rows.body_md: Though it mentions the same problem, this sentence wanders to roads outside the crew's work entirely, offering background rather than the requested example; a supporting detail must stay within the paragraph's own subject. Recheck which sentence shows the crew's own water-control work.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if the added sentence described looks instead of water — would it still serve the paragraph's point?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the paragraph's last sentence again and note what kind of example it sets up. Then test your sentence against that setup.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Raking the surface for photographs concerns appearance. Where in that sentence does any water get moved?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This sentence stays on the trail but serves an aesthetic purpose, not the water-control focus the paragraph establishes; an example must illustrate the actual work described. Re-filter the choices for the one that shows water being turned aside.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the sentences around it, could the underlined statement stand entirely on its own?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the fragment test: find the subject and a full verb, then check whether any opening word makes the clause lean on another sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A clause that opens with a relative pronoun reaches backward for something to attach to. Punctuated as its own sentence, what is it attached to?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A relative pronoun can only introduce a clause inside a larger sentence; set off by a period, this one becomes a fragment with nothing to modify. Re-test each version for a subject and finite verb that stand alone.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made this feel complete — can an '-ing' form by itself carry a statement's main verb slot?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the verb: some forms need a helper before they can anchor a clause. Ask whether this one has its helper.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Being' has no tense of its own. If the statement's only verb can't show past or present, what kind of construction is left?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This version swaps one fragment for another — the relative opener remains and the '-ing' form still lacks a finite verb, so nothing can stand independently. Rerun the test: subject, tensed verb, no dangling connector.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the sentence would be its subject if you read the statement alone?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Strip it down: what performs the action, and which verb carries tense? A complete sentence must supply both.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Starting with 'Being' leaves the statement with no subject at all — whose existence is it describing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A participial opener with no subject and no tensed verb produces a fragment, even though it feels descriptive; the statement must be rebuilt around a subject and a finite verb. Recheck which version supplies both.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship do you see between how the stringers looked and what the rot was doing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Name the logic in one word — addition, result, reason, or contrast — then check whether the connector matches it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Looking 'perfectly sound' and being 'hollowed out' pull in opposite directions. Does a simple additive link warn the reader of that reversal?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An additive connector merely stacks two facts as if they agree, yet these two facts contradict each other — appearance versus hidden decay — so the sentence needs a connector that signals opposition. Re-match each connector to that reversal.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through the cause and effect you had in mind — did looking sound make the beams rot?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Result connectors claim the second clause happened as a consequence of the first. Test that claim with these two clauses.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could an appearance from above cause hollowing from below? If not, what is 'so' falsely asserting?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'So' asserts that the rot followed from the sound appearance, a cause-effect link the sentence doesn't support; the real relationship is a clash between surface and reality. Re-test the connectors against that logic.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide the second clause explains the first — does the rot account for the healthy appearance?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'For' works like a reason-giver: the second clause must explain the first. Check whether that reading makes sense here.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read it as 'they looked sound, the reason being that rot had hollowed them' — does decay explain soundness, or undercut it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'For' presents the rot as the reason the stringers looked sound, which reverses the actual logic; hidden decay contradicts the healthy appearance rather than explaining it. Re-choose the connector that captures contradiction.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Take a second look at the two things being measured against each other — what exactly outlasts what?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Line up the comparison's two sides and check that they are the same category of thing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: On one side: stone steps. On the other: the people on newer crews. Can a staircase outlast a person 'by a decade' in any sensible way?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A comparison must weigh like against like, and this version weighs steps against workers; the sentence means to compare old stonework with newer stonework, so the second side needs a stand-in for the steps themselves. Re-balance the two sides before deciding.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — what action would 'do' be standing in for at the end?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When a helper verb closes a comparison, trace it back to the verb it copies and test the resulting sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Do' borrows 'outlast' — so newer crews outlast something? That still measures steps against people. Has the mismatch moved, or vanished?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Adding 'do' only re-asserts that the crews perform the outlasting, keeping the illogical steps-versus-people pairing; the fix must put the newer crews' stonework, not the crews themselves, on the second side. Recheck what each version actually compares.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made you reach for a pointing word here — and how many things is it pointing back to?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check agreement inside the comparison: the stand-in must match the number of the noun it replaces.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The stand-in must replace 'rock steps,' a plural. Does a singular pointer fit that job?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'That of' is the singular stand-in, and it must substitute for the plural 'steps,' so the pointer fails agreement even though the comparison's logic improved; the plural form is required. Re-verify both logic and number in each version.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the verb in the underlined phrase already tell you about where the volunteers ended up?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test each word for a job: if a word repeats meaning the verb already contains, it isn't earning its place.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can people assemble apart from one another? If not, what information does 'together' add?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Together' restates what the verb already guarantees — a coming-together — so the pair is redundant; every word must add new information. Re-inspect each version for words with no new job.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How many times does this version say that the volunteers came into one group? Count the ways.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Lay each phrase side by side with the verb's built-in meaning and cross out anything that repeats it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Together' and 'as a group' both restate the coming-together already inside the verb. What's left doing new work?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This version stacks two redundant phrases onto a verb that already means 'come into a group,' tripling the same idea; concision keeps only words that add information. Strip the repeats and see what remains.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking anything else, ask what 'in one place' could add to an act of assembling.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Redundancy hides in location phrases. Check whether the verb already implies where everyone ends up.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If an assembly necessarily happens in one place, does spelling that out give the reader anything new?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Together' and 'in one place' each duplicate meaning the verb already carries, so this version doubles the redundancy rather than trimming it; only information-bearing words should stay. Re-audit each version word by word.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about what each of these five words contributes — do any of them carry meaning the others don't?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Wordiness check: try compressing the underlined phrase down to its core function. What is the phrase's one job in this sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The phrase's entire job is to signal a cause. How many words does English actually need for that signal?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Due to the fact that' spends five words on a signal a single conjunction can send; the padding adds no meaning, only bulk. Re-weigh each version by meaning delivered per word.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the longer phrasing feel more polished — does extra formality here add any extra meaning?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Beware of dressed-up filler: test whether the phrase says anything a shorter cause word wouldn't.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'In light of the fact that' sounds official, yet its content is just 'this caused that.' Where is the added substance?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This swap trades one padded formula for an even more inflated one — the 'the fact that' scaffolding remains, doing no work; efficient prose signals cause in far fewer words. Re-compare the versions by what they trim.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the phrase you picked is the actual signal, and which part is packaging?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Circle the words 'the fact that' wherever they appear and ask what disappears from the meaning if they go.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Owing to' plus 'the fact that' still hauls the same empty scaffold. Has anything actually been trimmed?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This version keeps the identical 'fact that' filler under a different opener, so the wordiness survives intact; the sentence needs the cause marked and nothing more. Re-check which version deletes the scaffold entirely.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the underlined phrase and said it plainly, how would you describe when the leader checked the drains?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Concision test: find the single idea inside the phrase, then count how many of its words repeat that idea.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Regular intervals,' 'of time,' 'repeating basis' — how many of those chunks say something the others don't?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Every chunk of this phrase re-expresses one idea — recurring checks — so the phrase repeats itself twice over; trim until each remaining word adds something new. Re-measure each version for repeated meaning.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if 'of time' were deleted from your version — would any meaning be lost?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check each modifier: intervals are already stretches of time, and 'spaced' may repeat what 'intervals' implies. Test every word.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can an interval be anything other than 'of time' in this sentence? What does that phrase still contribute?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This version trims some padding yet keeps 'intervals of time,' a phrase whose last two words restate the first; meaning-free words remain. Re-audit each version until nothing redundant survives.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide 'regular' and 'repeating' were both needed — what does each one add?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Synonym check: when two describing words in a phrase mean the same thing, one is filler. Compare this pair.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Something done on a 'regular basis' already repeats. What extra information does 'repeating' deliver?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Regular' and 'repeating' duplicate each other, so this version still carries a redundant pair inside a padded 'basis' phrase; the idea can be carried far more economically. Recheck which versions eliminate every duplicate.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What information does the reader gain from being told the fact is interesting before hearing it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Look for throat-clearing: phrases that announce a statement instead of making it. Does the opener here do any announcing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the walls' eighty-year endurance is genuinely interesting, does labeling it 'interesting' add force or drain it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'It is interesting to note that' is an empty frame — it delays the subject and tells readers how to feel instead of letting the fact impress them; effective prose cuts straight to the statement. Re-test each version by what it puts before the real subject.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through the difference between your version and the original opener — did the filler go away, or just change costumes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the openers by function: does each one deliver information, or announce that information is coming?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'It should be pointed out that' still spends six words pointing instead of saying. What has actually been trimmed?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This swap replaces one announcement formula with another — the sentence still clears its throat before starting; the fix removes the frame entirely rather than rewording it. Re-inspect what each version puts in front of the subject.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What claim is 'as a matter of fact' pushing back against in this sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: That phrase works as a corrective — it needs a doubt or contrast to respond to. Search the sentence for one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Nobody has doubted the walls; nothing is being corrected. What is the phrase doing besides occupying space?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'As a matter of fact' signals a correction or emphatic contrast, and no such contrast exists here, so the phrase is filler wearing a purpose; the sentence is strongest with no preamble at all. Recheck which version starts with substance.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the sentence describes *how* the boulder travels — and does the underlined verb use any of that detail?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Precision check: the sentence stages a bar, a stump, leverage, and inch-by-inch progress. Rate how much of that staging your verb captures.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This verb could describe a forklift, a flood, or a shove. Does it honor the specific bar-against-stump technique the sentence sets up?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The verb is grammatically fine but generic — it discards the leverage detail the sentence works hard to establish, and precision rewards the verb that matches the exact physical action. Re-read the setup and match a verb to it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What register does your verb come from — a physics report, or a work scene on a mountainside?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Separate result from action: some verbs name where something ended up, others name how it was made to go. Which kind is needed here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Displaced' states that the boulder's position changed, in lab-report language. Does it show anyone straining against a bar?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This verb reports the outcome in clinical terms while erasing the method and effort the sentence describes; the context demands the verb for working an object loose with a lever. Re-match verb to scene.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Picture the action your verb describes — where are the worker's hands, and which direction does the force go?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the verb against the tools: does it fit a braced bar and leverage, or a rope and a straight pull?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Hauled' means dragged or pulled by main strength. Is that what bracing a bar against a stump accomplishes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This verb paints a pulling, dragging effort, which contradicts the lever-and-fulcrum technique the sentence stages; the precise verb must express levering a heavy load up and over. Re-check each verb against the physical setup.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — do any words here sound fine but do a job on paper that they cannot actually do?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This span hides two separate homophone traps; test the verb after 'can' and the little word before 'appearance' against the jobs they must perform.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'They're' expands to 'they are' — does 'alter they are appearance' make sense? And can lighting 'bring about' pigments that already exist?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Effect' as a verb means 'to bring about,' which does not fit here, and 'they're' is a contraction, not a possessive. Both words in the original need repair, so this version cannot stand — look for one that fixes each problem.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made you stop after checking the first word of the span — did the rest of it get the same scrutiny?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the expansion test on any apostrophe word: swap in the two words it stands for and listen to the result.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If 'they're' becomes 'they are,' the phrase reads 'alter they are appearance' — can that stand directly before a noun?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A noun like 'appearance' needs a possessive determiner in front of it, not a contraction of 'they are.' This version leaves the contraction in place, so reconsider with that second fix in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about the verb you kept — what does it literally mean in this sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: One classic mix-up pair splits into a noun (a result) and a verb (to influence); check which job the word after 'can' must do here.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: As a verb, 'effect' means 'to bring about or cause to exist' — can light 'bring about' pigments that are already on the paper?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When the meaning is 'to influence something,' the word spelled with an 'e' is the wrong member of the pair; this version keeps it, so return to the options and re-check the verb along with the possessive.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job is the underlined word doing — describing a thing, or describing how an action happened?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Locate the word being modified; if it is a verb, run the adjective-versus-adverb check before anything else.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Lifted' is an action — can an adjective form describe the manner of an action, or does that call for a different form?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Adjectives describe nouns; adverbs, usually ending in -ly, describe verbs. Since the word modifies 'lifted,' the adjective form in the original fails, so choose a form built to modify an action.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking the comparison, what part of speech does this word need to be in the first place?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try the substitution test: place the form you chose right after 'lifted the grime' and ask what it is describing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does '-er' on an adjective change its part of speech, or does it stay a word that describes nouns like 'formula'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Adding -er keeps a word an adjective, and adjectives cannot modify the verb 'lifted.' The comparison degree was right, but the part of speech is not — re-choose with the -ly requirement in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How many gels does the opening phrase say were tested — and does that number matter to your pick?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the degree of comparison: English uses one form for a pair and a different form for a group of three or more.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If only two formulas were in the trial, can one of them be the '-est' or 'most' of the group?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The superlative degree ('most') is reserved for comparisons among three or more items; with exactly two gels, the comparative degree is required, so this version overshoots — pick again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the sentence tells you exactly who spotted the flaw?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the people mentioned before the pronoun; a pronoun is only clear when it can match just one of them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could 'she' grammatically refer to either woman in the opening clause? If both readings work, what does that mean for the reader?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A pronoun with two possible antecedents leaves the reader guessing, and this sentence offers two women who both fit 'she.' The original keeps that guesswork, so look for a version that names the actor outright.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job does adding 'herself' perform in a sentence — emphasis, or identification?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test whether the extra word tells the reader which of the two women acted, or merely stresses that she did it personally.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'She herself' still leans on 'she' — has the number of possible antecedents actually gone down?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Intensive pronouns like 'herself' add emphasis but cannot resolve which noun a pronoun points to; the ambiguity survives untouched here, so re-examine how the other revisions identify who acted.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try reading the passive rewrite — does it now say who found the flaw, or just move the mystery to the end of the clause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Flipping a sentence into passive voice reshuffles the words; check whether the pronoun problem disappeared or simply relocated.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'By her' — her who? Can you point to exactly one woman with confidence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Passive voice only relocates the unclear pronoun: 'her' can still mean either woman, and the sentence grows wordier besides. Choose a revision that states the doer by role, not by pronoun.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the pronoun, how many nearby nouns could plausibly fill its slot?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: List the singular nouns earlier in the sentence; an unambiguous pronoun should match only one of them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could 'it' just as easily mean the whole case as the part that got swapped out? If yes, what does the reader actually learn?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When two singular nouns both fit a pronoun, the reference is ambiguous and the sentence fails the clarity test; the original leaves that double reading open, so pick a version that pins down the noun.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made a demonstrative feel more specific here than the word it replaced?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check what 'this' is attached to — a demonstrative usually needs a noun after it to point at anything.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'This yellowed' — this what, exactly? Has the guessing problem been solved or just reworded?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A bare 'this' with no noun after it is even vaguer than the pronoun it replaces, because it can gesture at an object or an entire situation. That revision fails the one-reading test, so choose again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before anything else, what number — singular or plural — must this pronoun carry?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the pronoun against its possible antecedents: do any of them agree with it in number?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If 'they' is plural, which plural noun earlier in the sentence could it stand for?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'They' requires a plural antecedent, but the case and its part are each singular, so that pronoun agrees with nothing in the sentence. Reject it and re-check which revision names the right thing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship did you decide these two sentences have before picking a connector?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Summarize each sentence in a few words, then ask whether the second one is a result of the first or a reversal of it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the move from beeswax to resins follow logically as an effect, or does it push in the opposite direction?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Cause-effect transitions require the second statement to flow from the first; here the studios abandoned the old standard, which is a reversal, not a consequence. The original connector misstates the logic — reread and rematch.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about what the second sentence would need to contain for an illustration cue to work.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An example transition promises a specific instance of the previous claim; check whether the second sentence delivers one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is switching to synthetic resins an example of beeswax being the standard, or a departure from it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A transition promising an example fails when the follow-up abandons the earlier topic instead of illustrating it; the second sentence turns away from beeswax entirely, so that connector misleads the reader. Re-test the logic and choose again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if the two sentences really were parallel cases, as your connector claims?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Similarity transitions assert that the second idea mirrors the first; compare the two practices side by side.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Are 'beeswax was standard' and 'studios now favor resins' alike in direction, or pulling opposite ways?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A similarity cue only fits when both statements point the same way; these two describe an old norm and its replacement, which are opposed. That connector asserts a false resemblance, so revisit the relationship and rematch.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where does the paragraph go after the opening slot — what pattern do sentences 2 through 4 follow?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An introduction should forecast what actually comes next; check whether the body discusses history at all.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the opener promises two centuries of continuity, where is the sentence that delivers on that promise?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The body is a first-next-finally walkthrough, not a comparison of past and present, so an opener about historical continuity promises content the paragraph never provides. Match the opener to the pattern that is really there.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is the one subject every body sentence returns to?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the opener against the paragraph's scope: does the body ever mention those other kinds of objects?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a reader primed to hear about flags and lace feel oriented when the very next sentence is about a quilt?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An opener that widens the topic to other textiles points readers away from the paragraph's single subject; nothing after it mentions those objects, so it fails the goal. Pick the opener that stays on the quilt process.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How much of the paragraph does your opener actually cover — one sentence, or all of them?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the opener's scope to the paragraph's scope; an introduction that zooms in on a single stage may be too narrow.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the screen step is the headline, what happens to the photographing and the rolling — are they still introduced?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An opener built around one stage previews only a third of the paragraph and leaves the other steps unannounced; the goal calls for a sentence that frames the entire procedure, so revisit the wider options.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the rest of the paragraph, what would a reader make of 'the cradle' in this sentence standing first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Track the definite articles: 'the cradle' signals something already introduced — find where that introduction happens.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can the liner be glued into an object that, at that point in the paragraph, has not been cut yet?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A sentence that refers to 'the cradle' cannot come before the cradle is created in Sentence 2; placing it first forces readers to meet an object before it exists. Re-test the slots against what each step requires.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through what physically exists after the tracing step — is there anything to glue a liner into yet?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Order-of-operations check: match each action to the object it requires, then see which sentence creates that object.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Between the tracing and the cutting, where does the brass form actually appear?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: After Sentence 1 only a paper tracing exists; the brass form is not cut until Sentence 2, so the liner step cannot logically squeeze in between. Place the moving sentence after its prerequisite is on the bench.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does Sentence 4 assume has already happened by the time the felt is curing overnight?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Look for backward references: any sentence that mentions the felt must come after the felt has been introduced.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the gluing were moved to the end, what would 'the felt had cured' refer to when readers first reach it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sentence 4 depends on the liner already being installed, so pushing the installation past it makes the paragraph mention curing felt before any felt appears. The moving sentence must precede that reference — reconsider the slots.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the phrase 'this long enclosure' need the reader to already know?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Pointer words like 'this' reach backward; check what has actually been established by the end of the paragraph's first sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: At the frass-under-the-pedestal stage, has any treatment even begun for the new sentence to describe?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Right after the opening, no tent, gas, or time span exists for 'this long enclosure' to name, so the added sentence would dangle without a referent there. Trace the pointer phrase to the sentence that creates what it points to.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which specific word in the added sentence — beyond the sealing itself — still needs support from the paragraph?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match every element of the new sentence to prior text: the tent is in place here, but check the time element too.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where does the paragraph first tell you the treatment is lengthy, and does that come before or after this slot?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: At this point the tent is sealed but no duration has been stated, so 'long enclosure' refers to a length of time readers have not met yet. Move the sentence to follow the spot where that duration is established.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about what Sentence 3 contributes — is it about time, or about something else in the tent?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Distinguish the treatment's ingredients from its schedule; the added sentence leans on one of those more than the other.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does knowing the oxygen level tell a reader anything about how long the objects stay inside?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sentence 3 establishes the atmosphere, not the time span, so 'this long enclosure' still points at nothing when placed there; the duration arrives one sentence later. Anchor the addition where the length of the seal is stated.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your own words, what is Sentence 3 about — the way plates are touched, or the way they are stored?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Label every sentence with a one-word topic tag, then find where the tags actually flip.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the masks-at-the-bench detail opens the second paragraph, does that paragraph really focus on storage?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sentence 3 continues the handling precautions, so splitting there drags a handling detail into the storage half and violates the writer's plan. Move the break to where the topic genuinely turns.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What work does the fourth numbered sentence do for the sentences that come after it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for an announcement sentence — a signpost that tells readers the subject is turning — and consider which half it belongs to.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the split comes after the pivot, which paragraph is left holding a promise about 'a different challenge' that it never keeps?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Beginning the second paragraph one sentence past the pivot strands the signpost at the tail of the first paragraph, where it introduces a topic that half never discusses. Start the new paragraph with the sentence that makes the turn.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the proposed opening of the second paragraph aloud — what does its first word lean on?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A paragraph should not open with a conclusion word whose cause sits in the previous paragraph; check what 'therefore' depends on.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where is the acid-releasing-materials problem that the sleeve solution responds to, and which side of your split does it land on?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Splitting at the final sentence separates the solution from the problem it answers and leaves 'therefore' pointing across a paragraph break; the storage discussion begins two sentences earlier. Re-draw the boundary at the true shift.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try lifting out the words between the punctuation you kept — does a complete, sensible sentence remain?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Commas that set off extra information work in pairs; scan the span for a partner to the comma that is there.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the comma after the name closes something, where did that something open?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An interrupting name must be fenced on both sides or not at all; a single comma before the verb merely severs the subject from 'believed.' The original has half a fence, so re-check which options complete or remove it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if you read the span straight through — does the name flow into the verb cleanly?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the punctuation for symmetry: whatever opens an aside must also close it before the sentence resumes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: After the comma introduces the name as extra information, what tells the reader the aside has ended?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This version opens the aside and never closes it, so the extra name collides with the verb; interrupters need matching punctuation on both ends. Look again for the version whose marks come in a complete set.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How many founding directors can one museum have — and what does that imply about the name?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the essential-versus-extra test: delete the name and see whether the reader still knows exactly who is meant.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If 'founding director' already narrows the field to a single person, is the name required to identify her, or is it bonus detail?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When a title picks out one unique person, the name that follows is nonessential and must be set off; leaving it bare treats needed punctuation as optional. This version drops the fence entirely, so revisit the ones that include it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read each half of this sentence on its own — could both halves stand alone as complete sentences?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Words like 'consequently' are adverbs, not true conjunctions; check what kind of mark two independent clauses need between them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If a comma plus 'consequently' were enough to join full clauses, how would that differ from a comma splice?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A conjunctive adverb cannot glue two independent clauses together with commas alone — that construction is a splice. The mark before the adverb must be strong enough to join complete clauses, so re-check the punctuation options.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which clause does 'consequently' belong to — the one before it or the one after it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A conjunctive adverb should stay attached to the clause it modifies; look at what the second heavy mark does to that attachment.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: After the connector is fenced off on both sides by strong marks, what is left standing on its own?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Placing a strong divider on both sides of the adverb strands it between the clauses and severs it from the statement it introduces; the mark after the adverb should be a light comma. Rebalance the punctuation and pick again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What jobs does that first mark usually perform — joining equals, or announcing what follows?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Recall the introducing mark's contract: it must set up a list, a definition, or an explanation of the first clause.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the second clause here an announcement being introduced, or simply a result being joined to a cause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The mark you chose introduces amplifying material; it does not pair with a conjunctive adverb to join a result clause. What is needed is the clause-joining mark before the adverb — return to the options with that in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before swapping marks, what test does the material after the mark need to pass for your choice to work?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: One of these marks joins two complete clauses; the other announces what is coming. Identify which job this sentence needs.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can 'flaking paint, a warped panel, and mold' stand alone as a sentence with its own subject and verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The mark you picked joins independent clauses, but what follows here is a string of noun phrases, not a clause. Introducing a list after a complete statement calls for a different mark — recheck what the original already does.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try reading your version aloud — how many things does the sentence now seem to list?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch what happens to the announced count of concerns when the introducing mark is softened to the same mark that separates the items.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If every pause in the series is identical, can the reader still tell where the announcement ends and the list begins?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Using the item-separating mark to also introduce the list collapses the announcement and the items into one blurry series; the boundary between clause and list needs a stronger, introducing mark. Reconsider whether the original span had it right.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Look at how each item in the series is separated — do all three get the same treatment in your version?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: List punctuation should be consistent: check whether these simple items contain internal commas that would justify heavier separators.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Why would the first gap in the series merit a stronger mark than the gap before the final item?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Semicolons between list items are reserved for items that contain commas inside them; these three are simple phrases, so mixing separators is inconsistent. The introducing mark was fine — it is the separator change that breaks the span.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking grammar, what exactly did the stem ask this verb to accomplish?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb can be correct yet colorless; weigh whether the current one adds any feeling of pace or care.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the original verb tell you anything about how the work felt — its speed, its delicacy — or only that it happened?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: On goal questions, a grammatically clean original still loses if it ignores the stated aim; this verb reports the action without any sense of patience or gentleness. Re-read the goal and find the verb that dramatizes it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What picture forms in your mind when varnish gets 'stripped' from a surface?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the verb's connotation against the goal: does it suggest a slow, delicate process or a quick, aggressive one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a reader who sees 'stripped' imagine six weeks of tiny swab strokes, or one afternoon with a scraper?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Stripped' connotes force and speed, which pulls directly against the stated aim of emphasizing slow, careful work. Choose the verb whose shading matches the goal rather than fighting it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about the register of your phrase — where would you expect to hear it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check two things at once: does the phrasing sound like the rest of the passage, and does it advance the stated emphasis?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'took off' add any hint of patience or delicacy that the plain original lacked?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: That phrasing is conversational and just as neutral about pace as the original verb, so it neither fits the passage's register nor serves the goal of stressing careful effort. Look for the verb that does both.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How would you describe the register of the passage's other phrases — 'demanded weeks of planning,' 'slightest jolt'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Judge the underlined phrase the way an editor would: does its level of formality match the sentences around it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would 'seriously iffy' appear in a museum's official condition report, or in a hallway conversation?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The passage speaks in a measured, professional register, and slangy hedging breaks that voice mid-sentence; keeping the original preserves the mismatch. Re-read the options for the phrase an editor of formal prose would approve.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made this phrase feel stronger to you — its accuracy, or its conversational punch?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Vividness and formality are separate dials; check which one the stem actually asks you to adjust.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does calling centuries-old plaster 'a total wreck' sound like careful description or like casual exaggeration?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: That phrase swaps precision for chatty overstatement, which collides with the passage's formal register just as badly as the original did. Find the option that stays both exact and professional.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the underlined words, which option would sound most at home beside 'could crumble at the slightest jolt'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for hedge words that soften a claim in speech but weaken it in formal prose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'kind of' sharpen the description of the plaster's condition, or blur it while lowering the register?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A colloquial hedge waters down the claim and drags the sentence into casual speech, so it fails the tone test the stem sets. Choose the phrasing that states the condition plainly and formally.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What one-sentence job is this paragraph doing, and how did you decide?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Weigh the proposed sentence's main point — not its passing mentions — against the paragraph's purpose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would knowing about a staff anniversary help a reader understand how infestations are caught and handled?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A warm personal note only earns its place if the paragraph is about people, and this one is about procedure; the anniversary detail serves a goal the paragraph does not have. Reconsider whether the sentence belongs at all.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the proposed sentence carries its real news — the clause about overseeing, or the milestone?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Separate what a sentence mentions from what it asserts; the because-clause you accepted must describe the assertion.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a twenty-year anniversary explain anything about how or why the procedures are enforced?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The sentence's main assertion is a personnel milestone; the overseeing detail is a passing aside, so the justification you accepted misdescribes what the addition would contribute. Re-judge the sentence by its central point.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: You said no — before settling, does the because-clause you picked actually describe this paragraph?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verdict and its reason must both be true; scan the earlier sentences for any prior mention of this material.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where earlier in the paragraph does anyone mention the security chief or an anniversary?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Nothing in the paragraph anticipates this sentence, so the repetition rationale is false even though the verdict is right; on these items the reason must be as accurate as the decision. Re-read the no options and test each because-clause.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What claim does this paragraph spend its first three sentences building?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A number is only evidence if it supports the actual argument; test what conclusion the cost detail points toward.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a price higher than the insured value make stitching look like the better method — or like a burden?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The paragraph's argument rests on reversibility and fiber health, and the cost figure supports neither point; a statistic that argues sideways is not proof. Re-weigh whether the detail helps or hijacks the paragraph.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in the deleted sentence do other museums or their adhesive choices actually appear?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check whether the connection you see is printed on the page or supplied by your own inference.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the sentence only names a price, who is doing the explaining about why institutions pick adhesives?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The justification you accepted describes a link the sentence never draws — it mentions no museums and no adhesives — so the keep-reason fails the accuracy test regardless of the verdict. Re-read each option's because-clause against the actual text.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before locking in your reason, which earlier sentence covers the same ground as the one being deleted?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: On keep-or-delete items, verify the because-clause the way you would verify a quotation: point to the line it describes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The earlier sentences discuss residue and stiffening fibers — where do any of them talk about money?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: No prior sentence raises cost, so the repetition reason is false even though removal is the right call; a correct verdict attached to an inaccurate reason is still a wrong answer. Compare the remaining reasons for deleting.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide this detail advances the paragraph's point rather than just mentioning its objects?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Relevance means feeding the paragraph's cause-and-effect claim; check what an object's age contributes to that claim.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does knowing a piece is centuries old show anything about what moisture cycles do to it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Age establishes value and history, but the stem demands evidence of harm from humidity swings; this detail shares a subject with the paragraph without supporting its claim. Look for the option that shows a consequence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What question does this detail answer — and is it the question the paragraph is asking?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for options that describe the equipment's backstory instead of the problem the equipment exists to prevent.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would naming the installer and the year persuade anyone that humidity swings harm wood?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The firm and date are logistics, unconnected to the paragraph's claim about what moisture does to artifacts; a supporting detail must demonstrate the harm, not the hardware's history. Re-test each option against the stated goal.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who benefits in this detail — the objects the paragraph is about, or the people walking past them?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the paragraph's actual concern: it is about what fluctuating moisture does to material, not about ambience.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can gallery comfort tell a reader anything about damage occurring inside wooden artifacts?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Visitor comfort shifts the topic from artifacts to audiences, leaving the paragraph's claim unsupported; the goal calls for a consequence of moisture cycling, so choose the detail that shows one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up everything between the commas, what would be left of this sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Bracket the which-clause and test the remainder for a subject paired with a tensed verb.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'The gilded frame ... at the lab' — where is the verb that tells you what the frame did?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An -ing form with no helping verb cannot anchor a sentence, and the only tensed verb here lives inside the which-clause; the main clause is a fragment. Find the version that gives the frame a true verb of its own.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try reading the whole sentence with your revision — how many times does the frame get named as the doer?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check for subject doubling: a noun and a pronoun should not both claim the same verb in the same clause.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If 'the gilded frame' opens the sentence, what work is left for 'it' to do before the verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Inserting the pronoun restates a subject the clause already has, producing 'The frame ... it arrived,' a doubled-subject construction; the sentence needed only a tensed verb, not a second subject. Re-select with that in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What two things is 'and' supposed to be connecting in your version?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A coordinator needs matching partners; look for the first verb that this one would pair with.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: After the which-clause is set aside, does 'and arriving' leave the main clause any better equipped with a tensed verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The added conjunction has nothing to join — the main clause still ends without a finite verb, so the fragment survives. Only a tensed verb can complete this sentence; look again for it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your own words, why do the conservators put on the gloves?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Name the relationship between the clauses first — agreement, opposition, reason, or result — and only then match a connector.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do the glove rule and the danger of skin oils pull against each other, or does one explain the other?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A contrast connector claims the clauses conflict, but the second clause states the very motive for the first; the logic is explanatory, not oppositional. Swap in the connector that signals a reason.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made a contrast word feel right here — the ideas themselves, or just the surface opposition of gloved and bare?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the connector by paraphrase: 'they wear gloves; even so, oils etch metal' — does that capture the intended point?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the second clause justifies the first, is a word meaning 'nevertheless' telling the truth about their link?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This connector, like the original, announces a conflict that is not there; the second clause supplies the motive for the glove rule. Choose the connector that presents one clause as the reason for the other.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which clause is the cause here, and which is the effect — walk me through the direction.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Result connectors declare that the first clause produces the second; check whether that direction matches reality.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does wearing gloves cause skin oils to etch the patina?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The result word runs the causation backward: the etching risk exists first and motivates the gloves, not the reverse. Pick the connector that lets the second clause explain the first.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What two things does this sentence literally set side by side for comparison?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check both sides of 'than' for category match: a rule or standard should be measured against another rule or standard.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a set of storage conditions be 'stricter than' a physical book?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: As written, the sentence weighs requirements against objects, comparing a standard to a thing; logical comparisons need matching categories on both sides. Rework the second term so it names the same kind of item as the first.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which earlier noun is your stand-in word replacing, and what is that noun's number?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the substitute pronoun to its antecedent the way you would match a verb to its subject.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the stand-in points back to 'requirements,' should it be singular or plural?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The singular stand-in cannot represent the plural 'requirements'; the comparison idea is right, but the number is wrong. Re-check which form agrees with the noun being replaced.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about the two measures in your version — are they the same yardstick?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Comparisons of unlike qualities fail even when both are abstract; verify that both sides name the same property.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is how much drift a book tolerates the same property as what its storage rules demand?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Strictness of requirements and degree of tolerance are related but distinct measures, so the mismatch persists in a subtler form. Keep the second term the same category as the first — a stand-in for the identical noun.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the distinct facts in your version — how many times does the reader learn how often the helmet was checked?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the added phrase to the words before it: does it introduce new information or restate old information in different clothes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is the difference between doing something 'twice' and 'checking its dimensions two times'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The tacked-on phrase repeats both the action and the number already stated, so it doubles the sentence's length while adding nothing. Cut every idea that appears more than once and re-evaluate the options.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Without adding anything, what single verb could replace 'took measurements of'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for a strong verb that has been unpacked into a noun phrase; that expansion often smuggles in a repeat.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you take measurements of something, haven't you already dealt with its size — so what work is 'of the size' doing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Turning the verb into 'took measurements of the size' repeats the measuring idea inside itself and weakens the verb; the leanest phrasing states the action a single time. Re-check which option does that.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Picture the workbench: what did the mount maker do differently when 'gauging' than when measuring?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the synonym test on the paired verbs — if the two words describe the identical action, one of them is dead weight.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'and also gauged' give the reader a second action, or a second name for the first action?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The two verbs are synonyms, so the pair announces one action twice; concise writing names an action once and moves on. Reconsider which version carries no duplicate.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Underline the words in this opener that carry meaning — how many actually earn their place?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the phrase for padding: could a single connector signal the same causal relationship?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does 'the fact that' contribute beyond delay before the real point?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Five-word formulas built on 'the fact that' are classic padding; the causal link they gesture at fits into one word with zero loss. Trim the scaffold and compare the options again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What changed between the original phrase and yours — the meaning, or just the first word of the padding?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check whether your revision removed the filler or merely repainted it; 'of the fact that' is still riding along.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the goal is tightening, how many words does your opener still spend before reaching the cause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This revision keeps the entire 'the fact that' scaffold and trims nothing; genuine concision deletes the filler rather than rearranging it. Look for the version that signals cause in the fewest words.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say the full sentence aloud — does your opener sound shorter than the original, or just different?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the words each option spends to say why the archive acted; concision is measured, not felt.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Beyond its length, what unfortunate echo does 'in light of' create in a sentence about lighting?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This variant is as padded as the original and stumbles into a pun beside the lamps; the sentence needs the briefest connector that keeps the causal meaning. Re-rank the options by working words.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Ask yourself what a reader learns from the second half of this span that the first half missed.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the two phrases as a pair: are they different locations, or two wordings of one location?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If something is under one thing and also under it, how many facts is that?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The span states a single spatial fact in two synonymous costumes, and concision requires deleting the duplicate outright. Strip the repeat, then see how little the sentence truly needs.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the word you added signal about the two phrases on either side of it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A connector like 'also' promises new information is coming; verify the second phrase delivers any.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does gluing the twin phrases together more smoothly make the sentence leaner, or just tidier about its repetition?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Adding a connector dresses up the duplication without removing it — the sentence still says one thing twice. The fix is deletion, not decoration; re-examine the shorter candidates.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which words did your trim remove, and which duplicated idea did it leave standing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Half-measures are the trap on concision items; check whether both synonymous phrases survived your cut.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: After removing the frame words, does the span still locate the portrait twice?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This trim deletes the harmless frame while sparing the actual redundancy — the paired synonyms remain. Cut the repeated idea itself and keep only what the meaning requires.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Look again at the clues around the verb — the counting task, the instrument, the hour. What kind of action do they add up to?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Vague verbs are rarely ungrammatical; test the current one for specificity instead of correctness.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the phrase you kept tell the reader anything about how carefully or how long the intern worked?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The context describes deliberate, sustained scrutiny, and a generic verb of seeing leaves all of that on the table; precision questions reward the verb that encodes the care the scene shows. Seek the sharper option.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How long does the sentence say the intern spent — and how long does your verb imply?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match each verb's built-in duration against the stated time; some verbs carry a stopwatch inside them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a person do something fleeting 'for more than an hour'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: That verb denotes a quick, momentary look, which collides with the hour of microscope work the sentence reports; the context needs a verb of sustained study. Re-match verb to evidence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What kinds of things does one usually witness — objects on a bench, or happenings?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the verb's typical object: some verbs of seeing take events, others take things.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would you say someone witnessed a coin, the way they might witness an accident or a ceremony?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This verb suits observing an event as it unfolds, not scrutinizing a stationary object; applied to a coin, it misfires. Pick the verb built for close study of a thing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the phrase 'rather than duplicate it' forbid the chosen verb from meaning?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the whole sentence as a contract: the verb must honor both the contrast clause and the purpose clause at the end.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If this verb means to copy something exactly, how can the sentence then deny that duplication happened?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb meaning 'copy exactly' collides head-on with the sentence's own 'rather than duplicate' and with the goal of keeping new paint tellable from old. The context needs deliberate near-ness, not sameness — re-test each option against that.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What sort of thing does one usually do with the verb you picked — colors on a canvas, or figures and quantities?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the verb's natural habitat: some words belong to mental arithmetic rather than visual comparison.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can pigments themselves perform a rough calculation of a palette?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: That verb describes judging an amount or value in the mind, not bringing paints visually close to older ones; it is the wrong domain for this sentence. Look for the verb about physical resemblance kept deliberately inexact.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the new paint truly did this to the old palette, could anyone later tell the two apart?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test your verb against the sentence's final clause — the stated reason the pigments were chosen this way.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does this verb allow the small, intentional difference the conservators are counting on?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb implying indistinguishable equivalence would defeat the plan spelled out after 'so that'; the context requires closeness that stops short of sameness. Re-read the options for the one carrying exactly that reservation.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through why you swapped the spelling in this spot — what pushed you toward the other version?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a part-of-speech check: what kind of word has to follow the helping verb 'would,' and does each spelling on offer truly work as that kind of word?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The spelling you picked usually works as a noun meaning 'a result' — can that meaning slot into 'would ___ the vision system's ability'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: As a rule, the a-spelling is the everyday verb meaning 'to influence,' while the e-spelling is usually the noun meaning 'a result'; your version forces the noun spelling into a verb slot, so re-test the options with that distinction.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the longer phrasing feel safer to you here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a two-part check: first whether the expansion adds any meaning, then whether the noun inside it is spelled as a noun.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In the phrase 'have an ___ on,' the blank must be a noun — which spelling is the noun meaning 'a result,' and is that the one your version uses?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When the word sits right after 'an,' it must be the noun, which takes the e-spelling; your version puts the verb spelling into that noun slot, so run the part-of-speech test on each option and pick again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — what do you actually hear between 'would' and the main action word?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check contractions against prepositions: say the full, uncontracted form of what you think you hear after 'would.'

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could the contraction 'would've' be tricking your ear here — what full helping verb does that contraction stand for?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Would of' is an ear-spelling of 'would have'; a preposition can never serve as a helping verb, so eliminate that version and re-test the remaining spellings for verb-versus-noun use.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking anything else, what word in the sentence do you think the underlined word is describing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the adjective-versus-adverb test: is the word describing a thing, or describing how an action was performed?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Held' is a verb — what form does a word usually take when it tells how an action happened?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Words that describe verbs must be adverbs, usually marked with -ly; the original leaves a plain adjective modifying 'held,' so look for the version that keeps the two-way comparison but uses the adverb form.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the -er ending feel right for this comparison?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check two things separately: how the comparison is formed, and whether the word should be an adjective or an adverb at all.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Even if that -er form were standard, it would still be an adjective — can an adjective describe the verb 'held'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A word modifying 'held' must be an adverb, and longer adverbs build comparisons with 'more' rather than with -er; your pick fails both tests, so re-check every option against them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How many claws are being compared in this sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a comparison count: -est and 'most' forms are reserved for a specific group size.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With exactly two designs on the table — the redesigned claw and the original — is a superlative the right degree?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Superlatives like 'most' require three or more items; comparing one claw with one other claw takes the comparative degree, so re-select using both the degree test and the adverb test.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about who you picture doing the concluding in this sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run an antecedent check: list every plural noun that comes before the pronoun and count how many could claim it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With two different plural groups mentioned earlier in the sentence, can a reader tell which one the plural pronoun points to?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A pronoun with two possible plural antecedents is ambiguous, and this sentence offers exactly two groups; the fix must identify the intended group beyond doubt, so re-read each option asking whether any confusion survives.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if a reader asked you exactly how many people your word refers to?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check for precision: does the replacement identify a specific, already-named group, or does it float free of the sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'some' tell the reader which of the two groups — or even how many people — actually reached the conclusion?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Indefinite words blur both the number and the identity of the actors; clarity requires an explicit, specific subject, so re-read each option asking which one leaves no doubt about who concluded.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the original sentence, what claim does your revision actually make about who agreed?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a meaning-preservation check: compare who performs the action in the original with who performs it in the revision.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The original credits the conclusion to one group after a comparison — does saying two groups concluded it keep that meaning or alter it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A revision must fix clarity without changing the claim; asserting that two groups jointly concluded something adds an agreement the original never states, so favor the version that is both clear and faithful to the original meaning.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the sentence tells you who committed the mix-up?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a two-candidate test: when a pronoun follows two names of the same gender, check whether grammar or context locks it to just one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Both names could own this pronoun — does anything in the pronoun itself settle who left the controller behind?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When two singular nouns of the same gender precede a pronoun, that pronoun is ambiguous and must be replaced by the intended name; use the apology to work out who erred, then re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What clue in the sentence did you use to decide who left the part behind?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the surrounding actions: match the person doing the apologizing with the person who made the error.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the message's sender is the one apologizing twice for the mix-up, who most likely left the controller in the pits?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An unambiguous rewrite must name the person the context implicates; the apology attaches the error to the sender of the text, not its recipient, so re-match the name to that role.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How many people does the sentence say left the controller behind?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run an agreement check: count the subject you intend and compare it with the number of the pronoun.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a plural pronoun stand in for one girl who misplaced one part?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Pronouns must match their antecedents in number, and this action belongs to a single person; a plural pronoun creates a new agreement error instead of resolving the ambiguity, so re-select the person the context implicates.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship do you see between passing the weight check and failing the height limit?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the logic connector: does the second sentence follow as a result of the first, or push against it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Did clearing one inspection cause the arm to be too tall — or is the second fact a setback despite the first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Therefore' claims the second sentence results from the first, but here good news is followed by bad news that cuts against it; the passage needs a reversal signal, so re-test each transition against that relationship.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Tell me why the height problem might count as an illustration of the first sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the example test: could you honestly say the second sentence is one instance of the claim made in the first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the too-tall arm an example of the chassis passing weight — or a different, conflicting piece of news?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'For example' only fits when the second statement illustrates the first, and a failed height limit does not illustrate a passed weight check; the two facts pull in opposite directions, so pick the transition that signals that turn.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In what way do you think the two inspection results resemble each other?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check for similarity: a likeness transition needs the second sentence to run parallel to the first.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: One sentence reports a success and the other a problem — are those parallel outcomes or opposed ones?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Likewise' asserts that the second fact mirrors the first, yet passing one check and failing another are opposite results; the sentences need a transition marking opposition, so re-evaluate with that in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you connect trailer costs to what the rest of the paragraph reports?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a coverage check: a good opener should preview most of the sentences that follow, not one passing detail.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The paragraph lists library demos, festival drives, and a booth, then ends with a roster jump — does a sentence about trailer prices set up any of that?

rows.subject: act-english
