rows.body_md: An introduction must preview the paragraph's actual content; scenic popularity never comes up again, while the body is entirely about shielding timbers from rain and snow. Pick the opener that forecasts that discussion.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made this sentence feel like a good first line?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Measure the opener's scope against the paragraph's scope — are they the same size?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is this paragraph about wood construction across all of history, or about one specific design decision?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This opener is far broader than the paragraph it introduces; a good introduction matches the paragraph's specific point about why these structures got their protective coverings. Re-choose with scope in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking anything else, reread the paragraph's two sentences and name their shared topic.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test whether the opener's subject ever reappears in the sentences that follow it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do the sentences about rot, roofs, and siding have anything to do with what visitors pay?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Tolls are never mentioned again, so this opener leaves the paragraph disconnected from its first line; an introduction must name the idea the following sentences develop. Re-select the sentence that does.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the paragraph aloud with your placement — what happens to the opening?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check what the moved sentence's words refer back to, and whether those references exist yet at the new spot.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sentence 3 says pumps drain 'the water trapped inside' — inside what, if the enclosure has not been introduced yet?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A sentence cannot precede the nouns it depends on: 'inside' needs the cofferdam and its walls already on the page. Track the physical steps — walls built, then water pumped out — and place the sentence where that order holds.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job is Sentence 4 doing, and what state is the site in when it happens?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk the construction timeline step by step and mark the moment the water must leave.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sentence 4 begins 'With the site dry' — can that come before the sentence that actually dries the site?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Draining must happen before workers can pour concrete on a dry riverbed; parking the pumping step after the pour makes the paragraph dry the site twice, out of order. Re-place it so the sequence flows: walls, water out, pour.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the paragraph told you the pumping step could wait until the end?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Number the physical steps in construction order, then compare that order with your arrangement.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the pier is already rising course by course, what work would be left for the pumps described in Sentence 3?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Putting the drainage step after the finished pier reverses the process — nothing can be poured or built until the water is out. Match the sentence order to the real-world sequence and reconsider.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about how the paragraph's timeline reads with the sentence where it sits.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Mark each sentence with a time stamp — before the failure or after it — and see whether the sequence ever doubles back.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Drivers were crossing and feeling seasick while the deck still existed; does that fit between the deck tearing apart and the design reforms?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The past-perfect 'had reported' flags an event earlier than the collapse narrative around it, so leaving it amid the aftermath forces readers to jump backward in time. Move the report into the part of the account when the bridge still stood and swayed.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship does this sentence have with the nickname story that opens the paragraph?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the sentence's pointing words — what must already be established for 'the undulating span' to make sense?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If readers meet 'the undulating span' before any bridge or rippling has been mentioned, what will they picture?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The sentence leans on details introduced in the opening — the bridge, its motion — so it cannot come first; a definite phrase like 'the undulating span' needs its referent already named. Re-place it somewhere that groundwork is already laid.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up this sentence, where would the paragraph feel like something was missing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the sentence's moment in time with the moment the paragraph has reached by its final line.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: By the last statement the bridge is gone and the lesson is being applied industry-wide — do queasy drivers on the intact deck belong after that?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Ending with a pre-collapse anecdote strands the paragraph in the past after it has already reached its conclusion; the drivers' reports belong with the description of the deck's swaying motion, early in the account. Reconsider the placement.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if you read the list one item at a time?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the items being ordered and check whether each one is fenced off from its neighbors.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Without a mark between them, do 'granite blocks' and 'steel pins' read as two materials or as one strange hybrid?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Every item in a series needs a separator; the first two materials here run together into a single mislabeled item. Re-punctuate so each of the three materials stands alone.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide where the pause before the last item should go?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read your version aloud exactly as punctuated, pausing at each comma, and listen to where the breaks fall.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Should the comma sit before the joining word 'and,' or after it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In a series, the final comma comes before the conjunction, never after it; placing it after 'and' splits the conjunction from its item. Re-check each version's comma positions.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Take a moment to list the separate materials the crew ordered.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the convention for punctuating three or more items in a row.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With no punctuation at all, how does a reader tell where one material ends and the next begins?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A series of three or more items requires commas between the items; running them together with none forces readers to guess the boundaries. Re-choose the version that fences off each material.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in the phrase is the ownership relationship shown?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Ask who or what possesses the span, then check whether that possession is actually marked.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Without an apostrophe, doesn't the first noun read as a plural — as if several structures were being named?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Possession must be marked with an apostrophe; leaving the noun bare turns a possessive into a plural and leaves the span unclaimed. Recount how many structures the passage describes, then re-pick.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Tell me how many structures you think this passage is describing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the apostrophe's position to the number of owners — the placement encodes singular versus plural.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An apostrophe after the s signals several owners; does the passage give you more than one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Apostrophe-after-s marks plural possession, but the passage describes a single structure suspended above the strait, so the possessive must be built on the singular noun. Re-examine the apostrophe placements on offer.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What clue led you to build the possessive this way?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Review how a singular noun forms its possessive, step by step, before adding anything extra.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does standard English ever pile an apostrophe-s onto a noun that has already been made plural?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A possessive is formed from the correct base noun first — singular noun, then apostrophe, then s; stacking apostrophe-s onto a plural creates a form standard English does not allow. Rebuild it from the singular base.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through how you would mark where the extra description starts and stops.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Find the interrupting phrase, then compare the punctuation at its entrance with the punctuation at its exit.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The aside opens with one kind of mark and closes with a different one — can a single interrupter switch styles midway?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Name the pairing test: the mark that opens an aside must be the same kind that closes it. Mixing two different marks around one interrupter fails — check each version's opening and closing marks against each other.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made this pairing of marks seem balanced to you?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Trace the appositive from its first word to its last, noting the mark on each side.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the description enters after one style of mark, what should the reader meet at the far end?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An interrupting phrase takes identical marks at both boundaries; entering with one mark and exiting with another leaves the aside lopsided. Compare boundaries in every version before settling.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking anything else, find where the extra description about the wires ends.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence without the aside; then check whether your punctuation lets a reader do the same.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With no closing mark, doesn't the verb get swallowed into the description of the wires?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An interrupter must be sealed at both ends so the main clause can reconnect; leaving it open lets the appositive run straight into the verb, garbling the sentence's core. Re-select the version whose aside is fully enclosed.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — where does the natural flow hit a speed bump?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Find the complete subject and its verb, then ask what stands between them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does anything grammatical justify a pause between 'the engineers who designed the glass footbridge' and what they did?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A subject must connect directly to its verb; a lone comma separating them is intrusive because nothing — no interrupter, no list — licenses it. Re-read each version, checking the subject-verb seam.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job is a semicolon supposed to perform in a sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test what sits on each side of the mark you chose — can each side stand alone?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can 'its deck to flex slightly underfoot' function as its own complete sentence once the verb is cut off by a semicolon?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, but here the second piece is just a predicate with no subject; the mark chops the subject off from its verb. Re-evaluate which versions keep the clause whole.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the sentence seemed to need dramatic emphasis?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Ask whether the words after the mark are an interruption or the sentence's own main verb phrase.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would you pause dramatically between a subject and the very verb that tells what it did?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Dashes set off interruptions or sharp turns, but the main predicate is not an interruption — it is what the subject has been waiting for; inserting any mark there severs the sentence's spine. Reconsider with the subject-verb link in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about how this wording serves the writer's stated purpose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Reread the stem's goal, then grade each option on how strongly it conveys sheer magnitude.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'holds back the pull' tell a reader anything about how enormous that force actually is?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The goal is emphasis on immense force; a neutral verb phrase reports the anchorage's job without conveying scale, so it leaves the writer's purpose unmet. Look for the wording that makes the magnitude vivid and specific.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship do you see between this verb and the writer's stated aim?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swap in each option and ask which one would make a reader's eyebrows rise at the size of the force.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'counters' any more vivid about magnitude than the original wording, or just a synonym for the same neutral idea?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Trading one plain verb for another leaves the emphasis unchanged; the stated goal demands wording that dramatizes how massive the load is, ideally with concrete detail. Re-rank the options by intensity, not by novelty.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the stem's goal, would this wording still mention force at all?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check each option for the core idea the writer wants foregrounded — resistance to a huge load.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does describing a mere connection convey any struggle or magnitude whatsoever?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This revision abandons the idea of force entirely, describing plain attachment; an option can be grammatical yet fail the writer's goal completely. Return to the goal and choose the wording that showcases an enormous load.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if this phrase appeared in an official county report?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sample the passage's diction — 'commission,' 'rigorous,' 'maintenance program' — and test whether the underlined words live in that register.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do 'totally' and 'mess up' sound like the language of a formal engineering report?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Tone must stay consistent: the passage is formal and technical, while this phrasing is casual conversation; the revision should describe the rust problem in measured, professional language. Re-assess each option's register.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide this idiom fits alongside words like 'commission' and 'rigorous'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Flag any slang or street idiom in each option, then compare it with the passage's established voice.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would an inspection report ever say a maintenance schedule 'kicks rust to the curb'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A colorful street idiom clashes even harder with the formal register than the original did; consistency of tone means choosing plain, professional phrasing. Re-read the options listening for the report's voice.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Take a moment to rank the four options from most formal to most casual.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for casual intensifiers — they often hide in otherwise acceptable sentences.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the word 'super' belong in the same sentence as 'load-bearing plates' in a formal report?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Super' is a conversational intensifier and 'stopping rust on' stays vague; formal prose needs precise, measured wording without chatty boosters. Compare each option's diction with the passage's first sentence and re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in the paragraph did you find support for a point about the community?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: State the paragraph's central subject in five words, then test whether kayakers advance it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Even if the detail is pleasant, does recreation on the river tell us anything about sensors, readings, or repairs?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A sentence earns its place by developing the paragraph's central subject — here, how engineers track the structure's condition; a kayaking detail, however friendly, develops nothing in that discussion. Reconsider whether the addition belongs at all.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Tell me the chain of logic that connects kayakers to the engineers' work.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the proposed reason: does the new sentence actually explain anything stated in the paragraph?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do engineers check strain readings because of summer paddlers, or because the data flags structural problems?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The justification must match what the sentence really does: it offers a recreational aside, not an explanation of the inspection program's purpose. Weigh whether the detail serves the paragraph before accepting any approving rationale.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What clue suggested a factual conflict between this sentence and the paragraph?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Separate two different flaws: a detail can be off-topic without clashing with anything.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which earlier statement, exactly, would kayakers on the river contradict?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Nothing in the paragraph conflicts with summer kayaking — the sentence's real flaw is irrelevance to the discussion of sensors and repairs, not contradiction. Match the reason to the actual problem and re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through how a passing mention of a tower would satisfy the stated goal.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Weigh coverage: how many sentences actually explain challenges of building in deep water?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is naming a tower during a sunrise walk the same as explaining how that tower was anchored?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A single scenic mention cannot carry an explanatory goal; the essay offers memories and imagery, not one word about construction methods or underwater challenges. Judge the essay by what it explains, then reconsider.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made pedestrian safety feel connected to the stated goal?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Restate the goal, then check whether the essay's evidence speaks to that goal or to something else.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does two people enjoying a walk demonstrate anything about anchoring a structure in deep water?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The stated goal concerns construction challenges, and safety for walkers is a different subject entirely — the essay supports neither, since it is a memory piece. Re-assess what the essay actually accomplishes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking anything else, reread the stated goal — does it require more than one structure?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Distinguish the right verdict from the right reason; both must be correct.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could an essay about a single bridge still explain deep-water anchoring perfectly well?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The essay indeed misses the goal, but not because it covers one bridge — a one-bridge essay could explain construction fully; the failure lies in the essay's storytelling approach, which ignores technical matters. Re-check each stated reason against the essay itself.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the paragraph again — what force is doing all the work in it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match each candidate sentence to the paragraph's cause-and-effect claim about the seasons.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does knowing who manufactures the joints show temperature moving the steel?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The paragraph's point is that heat and cold physically move the deck; a supplier detail is about commerce, not thermal movement, so it reinforces nothing. Seek the sentence that shows temperature producing real, observable change.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job would this detail perform for the paragraph's argument?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test relevance by asking whether the sentence would still matter if temperature never changed.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would painters' work zones exist to demonstrate expansion, or for a completely unrelated convenience?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The detail is incidental — a workplace convenience that says nothing about heat, cold, or movement; support must extend the paragraph's actual claim about seasonal expansion. Re-screen the options for thermal evidence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the paragraph's claim does this comparison strengthen?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for sentences that widen the topic instead of deepening the stated point.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does noting that other structures use similar joints prove anything about temperature's effect on this bridge?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Mentioning other structures broadens the scope without adding evidence of thermal movement here; reinforcement means specific proof of the paragraph's own claim. Pick the detail that shows temperature visibly changing the deck.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about what sits on each side of your comma.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test each side of the junction: can both halves stand alone as complete sentences?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If both halves are complete sentences, is a comma alone strong enough to join them?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two independent clauses cannot be fused with only a comma — that creates a splice; the junction needs stronger punctuation or a conjunction added. Re-test each option at the seam.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship do the two statements about fasteners have to each other?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Find where the first complete thought ends, and check what marks that boundary.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With nothing between 'together' and 'today,' where does one sentence stop and the next begin?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Running two independent clauses together with no punctuation creates a fused sentence; every boundary between complete thoughts must be marked. Re-inspect the junction in each version.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up everything before the semicolon, could the remainder stand on its own?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Remember what a semicolon demands from both of its sides.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does starting the second half with 'because' leave it a complete thought or a dependent one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A semicolon requires an independent clause on each side, but adding 'because' subordinates the second half, stranding a fragment after the mark. Recheck which versions keep both sides free-standing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if you read the sentence starting from 'Although'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the connecting words linking these two clauses — how many does the job need?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If 'Although' already signals the concession, what work is left for 'but' to do?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: One connector per clause pair: 'although' has already subordinated the first clause, so adding a coordinating conjunction doubles the link and breaks the structure. Re-read each option at the junction after the comma.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide a coordinator was needed after the comma?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Identify the sentence's skeleton: dependent clause, comma, then what must follow?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: After an 'Although' clause, does the main clause need any conjunction at all to attach itself?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A dependent 'although' clause attaches directly to its main clause; inserting 'and' leaves the sentence with a subordinate clause coordinated to nothing. Strip the junction to its required parts and re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Take a moment to map which clause depends on which.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check both the number of connectors and the logic your connector asserts.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does needing constant pumping follow as a result of the design being cheap, and can 'so' share the sentence with 'although'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'So' both duplicates the connection 'although' already makes and claims a cause-effect link the sentence does not intend; after an 'although' clause, the main clause needs no added conjunction. Re-examine the junction.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in the sentence is the thing that was weakened by salt spray?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Find the opening modifier's target: the first noun after the comma should be what it describes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Were the engineers weakened by decades of salt spray?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An introductory modifier attaches to the subject that immediately follows it; as written, the sentence claims the people, not the structure, were eroded. Re-check which version puts the weakened thing right after the comma.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Tell me what, literally, the opening phrase describes in your version.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the first noun after the comma — can that noun be salt-damaged?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a plan be weakened by decades of salt spray?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swapping in 'plan' still leaves the modifier dangling — an abstract plan cannot be weathered by spray; the noun following the comma must be the damaged object itself. Re-run the first-noun test on every option.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What clue told you 'it' could carry the opening description?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check what the placeholder pronoun refers to, and whether the modifier can sensibly describe it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In 'it was decided,' what exactly got weakened by the salt spray?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The dummy 'it' names nothing, so the modifier hangs with no logical target; the sentence must open onto the actual weathered structure. Apply the test — who or what was weakened? — and choose again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through what 'annually' already tells the reader.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Look for two expressions in the sentence covering the identical time span.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If inspections happen 'annually,' what new information does 'each year' add?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When two phrases state the same fact, one must go — keeping both is redundancy, and rewording the duplicate does not fix the doubling. Re-scan the options for the one that removes the repetition outright.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the longer phrase feel like an improvement?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the meaning of the adverb early in the sentence with the meaning of your phrase.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'every single year' say anything that 'annually' has not already said?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swapping one duplicate for a wordier duplicate deepens the redundancy instead of curing it; the fix is elimination, not elaboration. Reconsider which option leaves the sentence stating the fact exactly once.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking anything else, underline every time expression in the sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the sentence with the underlined words removed — is any meaning lost?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Isn't 'on a yearly basis' just 'annually' wearing extra words?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The phrase restates 'annually' with padding; since the sentence loses nothing without the underlined portion, the redundancy should be cut, not rephrased. Re-read each option asking what it truly adds.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — where does the phrasing start circling?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try a trim test: which words in the underlined stretch carry meaning, and which are filler?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'in connection with the matter of' add meaning beyond a simple linking word?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Concision favors the fewest words that preserve the full meaning; this five-word scaffold conveys a relationship one word can handle. Strip each option to its essential content and compare.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job is 'the question of' doing in this phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check for nested filler: a shorter start can still drag extra words behind it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Since 'whether' already introduces the question, why announce 'the question of' first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'The question of whether' doubles the job 'whether' does alone; concision means cutting words whose work is already done elsewhere in the sentence. Re-measure each option by that test.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of this phrase felt more precise than the original?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swap in each option and check what changes in meaning — if nothing changes, the extra words are decoration.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'pertaining to the matter of' clearer than a plain connective, or only fancier?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Formal-sounding padding is still padding: 'pertaining to the matter of' adds syllables, not substance. Judge each option by information conveyed per word, then re-select.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about what 'in a permanent way' contributes here.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Look for a phrase that a single-word modifier could replace without losing meaning.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could the idea of 'in a permanent way' be folded into one word?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When a prepositional phrase merely spells out a modifier's meaning, the compact form wins; 'in a ... way' constructions are classic wordiness. Compress each option mentally and compare the survivors.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship does 'in a manner that is permanent' have to a plain one-word modifier?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the words doing real work versus the words propping up other words.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'in a manner that is' add any information beyond what one word could carry?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This revision stretches the padding even further with a relative clause; concision collapses 'in a manner that is X' into a single modifier. Re-rank the options by meaning kept per word spent.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up 'there,' what meaning would the sentence lose?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Hunt for words with no referent or job — small words often stow away.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What location does 'there' point to that the sentence does not already state right afterward?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'There' duplicates the location given by 'to the tower's base,' and 'that are' props up a clause the sentence does not need; every surviving word should carry a fact. Re-inspect each version word by word.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if the subject were a carton of milk instead of a drawbridge?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the verb's usual companions — what kinds of things typically do this action?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do licenses and coupons expire, or do steel structures?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Expired' belongs to documents, deadlines, and perishables; applied to a structure the county stopped using, it is the wrong domain. Match the verb to what actually happens when a span leaves service, and re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide this euphemism fits a steel structure?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Flag verbs that are usually reserved for people, then test them against this subject.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a county report say a drawbridge 'passed on,' as though mourning a relative?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Passed on' is a gentle euphemism for a person's death; a machine or structure is withdrawn from use, not mourned. Re-match each verb with a subject made of iron.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Take a moment to consider what category of thing can go extinct.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check whether the verb describes an individual object or an entire kind of thing dying out.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can one particular drawbridge go extinct, or does extinction apply to whole species and types?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Extinction describes the disappearance of an entire category, not the end of one structure's working life; precision demands the verb used for equipment withdrawn from use. Reconsider with the single bridge in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where else in the sentence do you see language this casual?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the underlined words with the register of 'commission,' 'concluded,' and 'recommended.'

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a state commission's final report describe bearings as 'pretty much shot'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Slang cannot sit inside formal findings: the report's diction demands a precise, technical description of the bearings' condition. Re-weigh each option in the sentence's official voice.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Tell me how this phrase would land in an official document.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Listen for conversational intensifiers — they usually mark casual register.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'totally done for' more at home in a report or in a hallway conversation?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Totally done for' swaps one piece of slang for another; register consistency requires sober, exact wording that names the damage professionally. Re-audit the options for formality.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What clue made this hedge feel appropriately formal?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for vague softeners; formal writing states conditions plainly and exactly.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'kind of' convey the confident precision a commission's conclusion needs?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The hedge 'kind of' is casual and imprecise — the opposite of what a formal recommendation requires; the sentence needs an exact, professional description of the wear. Re-select with register and precision in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through the timeline of this sentence — when is everything happening?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the sentence for time markers and for the tense of its second verb before judging the underlined one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the singers 'competed' back then, can the radio hour be presenting its shows in the present moment?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: All verbs in a sentence must share one time frame; a present-tense verb clashes with the 1964 date and with 'competed,' so pick the form that keeps the whole sentence in that earlier era.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made a forward-looking verb feel right for this sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the tense you chose with the date that opens the sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a sentence anchored to 1964 describe something that has not happened yet?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A future-tense verb points ahead of the moment being described, but this sentence reports what was already true in 1964; choose the form that matches that finished time frame.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about why a 'has + verb' form seemed to fit here.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Think about what the perfect tenses signal about the connection between an action and the present day.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does anything in this sentence suggest the action stretches up to today, or is it sealed inside one earlier period?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Present perfect links an action to the present moment, yet every signal here — the date, the verb 'competed' — locks the events in a closed past period; re-choose with that timeline in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the phrase 'of these gatherings,' how would the sentence read?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a subject check: strip away any prepositional phrases sitting between the subject and the verb.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'gatherings' actually doing the action of the verb, or is it just part of a phrase describing something else?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb agrees with its subject, not with the nearest noun; here the plural noun inside the 'of' phrase pulled the verb plural, so find the bare subject and match the verb to it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide between the verb forms offered here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: There are two things to test in this form: the verb's number and the verb's tense.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Once the modifying phrase is crossed out, does the remaining subject call for a plural verb — and does the passage stay in the past?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This form is plural where the true subject is singular, and it drags a past-anchored description into present perfect; strip the 'of' phrase, confirm the subject's number, and stay in the established time frame.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change in meaning if the head noun of this phrase became plural?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Fixing agreement should never require rewriting the nouns themselves — test whether the nouns still make sense.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can 'these,' a plural pointer, sit correctly in front of the now-singular noun in this version?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Re-shuffling the nouns creates a mismatch between 'these' and its noun and distorts what the writer is describing; keep the original nouns and change only the verb so it matches the true subject.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — how does the verb-plus-preposition pair sound to your ear?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Some verbs travel with one fixed preposition; test this verb in a short sentence of your own.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would you say a friend 'insisted in leaving early,' or does a different small word belong after that verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Insist' is welded to one particular preposition in standard English, and 'in' is not it; try each option in a plain everyday sentence and keep the pairing that native idiom requires.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made an infinitive form seem natural after this verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Verbs differ: some take 'to + verb,' others take a preposition plus an '-ing' form — check which family this verb belongs to.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can you think of everyday sentences with 'insist' — does it ever lead straight into 'to' plus a verb?

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english

rows.body_md: If you cover up 'of donated costumes,' does 'have' still sound right next to what remains?

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'For' signals purpose or benefit, but this verb takes one conventional preposition to mean 'follow a rule,' and 'for' is not it. Re-test the remaining pairings aloud.

rows.body_md: What relationship do you see between the slow September sales and the sold-out weekend?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does weeks of structured drilling make the troupe seem more unscripted, or does it push against that impression?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check what grammatical job the words on each side of the comma perform in relation to each other.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Should any mark separate a verb from its direct object?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made a strong introductory mark feel necessary here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Recall the requirement for the sentence portion that comes before a colon, then test this sentence against it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could the words before the mark stand alone as a complete statement?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A colon must follow a complete independent clause, but here it interrupts a clause mid-thought, right between verb and object. Re-evaluate which version respects that boundary.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about what the dash is setting off in your reading.

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'every wireless microphone' extra, droppable information, or the very thing the operator checks?

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What image of Dana does your pick create — settled focus or something looser?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the verb's energy to the goal in the stem: the writer is after intensity.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does checking occasionally suggest a performer gripped by concentration, or one whose attention drifts?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The stem demands intensity of focus, and an intermittent, casual action signals divided attention rather than absorption; the strongest phrasing shows her attention fastened on one point. Re-read each option against that goal.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which details in the version you chose actually show concentration?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Separate physical location from mental state — the goal asks for the second.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does standing in a spot tell readers anything about how hard Dana is focusing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The goal is to dramatize concentration, but a bare statement of position carries no mental energy at all; the sentence needs an action that displays riveted attention. Compare the options for the one that shows it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is Dana doing, versus merely thinking, in the version you chose?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test each option for observable intensity rather than a passing thought.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does idly predicting when the light will come on convey urgency, or a relaxed wait?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A casual assumption about timing suggests detachment — the opposite of the gripping focus the stem requires. Look for the option whose action itself embodies concentration.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How would you describe the mood of the sentences leading up to this phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Weigh the phrase's register against the passage's: casual slang versus the surrounding reflective description.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a writer who lingers over dim work lights and reluctance to leave sum up the moment in throwaway slang?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Tone must stay consistent: the passage is subdued and wistful, and informal slang deflates that mood at the crucial moment. Re-read the options for the one that stays in the passage's register.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What feeling does your phrase's central image carry?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the intensity level: does the passage build toward a jolt of violence or a softer ache?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a punch-to-the-stomach image match the gentle, lingering sadness of performers reluctant to leave the stage?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The surrounding sentences are muted and tender, so a jarring physical-impact idiom spikes the tone far past the passage's register; the phrase should grieve softly, not strike. Reconsider with that register in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try reading your choice aloud in the middle of the paragraph — how does it sound beside the other sentences?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Tone can miss in two directions; check whether this phrasing is more formal and ornate than the passage's plain, reflective voice.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do elaborate words like these appear anywhere else in the passage's understated style?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Matching tone means matching level of formality, and this elaborately Latinate phrasing turns a simple, heartfelt moment into stiff ceremony. Re-select the phrase that keeps the passage's natural voice.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your own words, what does the proposed sentence actually say?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the justification you picked against the sentence's literal content, phrase by phrase.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the sentence mention repainting at all, or does it describe returning graduates?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A reason can only support adding a sentence if it accurately describes that sentence; this justification invents content about maintenance that the addition never mentions. Reread the proposed sentence, then re-evaluate each reason.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which earlier sentence, exactly, do you think already covers this information?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test for repetition by listing what the paragraph has stated and what the new sentence would state.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Has the paragraph said anything yet about what happens years after the signatures go up?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The paragraph covers the wall and the opening-night ritual, but nothing about graduates returning; the new sentence extends the timeline rather than repeating it. Re-judge whether the addition earns its place.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in the proposed sentence do you see money or donations come up?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the claimed focus-shift against the actual topic of the new sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is searching a wall for one's own signature a fundraising activity, or a continuation of the signing tradition's story?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Rejecting an addition requires a real flaw; this reason attributes a fundraising angle that appears nowhere in the sentence, so it cannot justify leaving the sentence out. Reconsider what the addition truly contributes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in the passage do awards or festivals appear?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A 'yes' verdict needs a reason that matches what the passage actually contains — verify the reason's claim first.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the passage celebrate trophies, or describe the tasks students perform each semester?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Even when the verdict is right, the justification must be true: no awards are mentioned anywhere, so this reason cannot support the goal. Re-read the passage and re-match verdict to evidence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made you place this passage in a professional setting?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the setting words in the passage before accepting a reason built on setting.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Whose platforms, lamps, and budgets are described — a Broadway crew's, or students' in a school course?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The passage names a school course and tracks its students from sketch to strike; a reason claiming a professional focus contradicts the text outright. Re-examine what the passage shows before judging the goal.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How many performances does the passage actually describe?

rows.body_md: Test the reason against the passage's scope: one night, or a semester-long process?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the passage evaluate a show for an audience, or trace what students learn to do over months?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A review of one performance would judge a single event, but this passage surveys a semester of skill-building across carpentry, electrics, and budgeting; the reason misstates the passage's scope. Reassess the verdict with the real scope in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is this paragraph tracking from sentence to sentence?

rows.body_md: Test the added detail by asking whether it advances the crew's story or describes the building instead.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do reupholstered seats move the crew any closer to being ready for opening night?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about how this fact connects to the crew described in the surrounding sentences.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for details that are on-theme but off-focus: related to lighting, yet not to this crew's work this week.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a note about famous designers' origins describe anything this crew is doing before opening night?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Topical relevance isn't enough — the sentence must serve the paragraph's specific focus on getting ready, and a career-history aside pulls readers away from the work at hand. Re-choose the detail that stays inside the paragraph's job.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the paragraph does a note about ticket fees develop?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Ask what question the paragraph is answering, then check whether your sentence answers that same question.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is building maintenance part of how the crew gets ready for the show?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The paragraph's throughline is rehearsal and readiness; a budgeting detail about fees answers a question no one in this paragraph is asking. Re-evaluate the options for the one that develops the crew's own process.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — how many complete statements do you hear?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Find each subject-verb pair, then check what's gluing the two complete thoughts together.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What, if anything, joins 'the fog machine hissed' to 'the audience gasped'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two independent clauses cannot simply run together with no connector or punctuation; that's a fused sentence. Look for the option that joins the clauses with a legal link.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is the comma doing between those two statements, in your reading?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the strength rule: can a comma alone hold two complete sentences together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If each half could stand alone as its own sentence, is a bare comma strong enough to weld them?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A comma by itself cannot join two independent clauses — that's a splice; the join needs a coordinating word with the comma or stronger punctuation instead. Re-test each option for a legal join.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where exactly did you place the pause, relative to the joining word?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When two clauses are coordinated, check which side of the connector the comma belongs on.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a comma go after the joining word, cutting it off from the clause it introduces?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In coordination, the comma comes before the connector, not after it; a pause trailing the joining word splits it from its own clause. Re-inspect the comma's position in each option.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How many connecting words are managing the relationship between these two clauses?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the contrast signals in the sentence; then recall how many a single two-clause sentence can support.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the opening word already sets up the contrast, what work is left for the second connector to do?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: One relationship gets one connector: pairing a subordinating opener with a coordinating conjunction doubles the link and leaves no independent clause. Strip the sentence to a single connector and re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try covering the second half — can each part stand on its own as a sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check what's joining the two complete thoughts once the opening connector is gone.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With no connector at all, is a comma strong enough to hold two independent clauses together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Removing the subordinator leaves two full sentences spliced by a comma; the contrast must be marked by a connector or stronger punctuation. Re-examine which option keeps a single, legal link.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship does the sentence's opening word promise, and what does the later connector deliver?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test whether the two connectors agree: one signals contrast, the other signals addition.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a clause be subordinated by its opener and coordinated by a following joining word at the same time?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A subordinate clause attaches directly to its main clause — inserting a coordinating word in between leaves the sentence with no independent clause at all. Re-read each option and keep the one connector that does the job.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who or what is balancing on the ladder in your version?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An opening descriptive phrase attaches to the first noun after the comma — identify that noun in your pick.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a lighting fixture balance itself on the top rung of a ladder?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Introductory modifiers must be followed immediately by the person or thing they describe; putting the equipment there makes the phrase claim the fixture is doing the balancing. Re-check what noun each option places after the comma.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the opening phrase, would your version still tell us who did the work?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check two things: what the opening phrase attaches to, and whether the doer of the action survives in the sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With only an angle being adjusted, who exactly is balancing on that ladder?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This version strands the modifier with no one to describe and hides the doer entirely; the sentence must name the balancer right after the comma. Re-test each option for that attachment.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the word at the start of your version refer back to?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Pronouns need a clear, stated antecedent — hunt for what this one could point to.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If a reader asks what exactly got angled, can this sentence say without guessing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The vague pronoun right after the modifier leaves both the balancing and the angling without a clear agent; the noun that follows the comma must be the one doing the balancing. Recompare the options on that basis.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What information does the underlined phrase add beyond what 'duet' already tells us?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the sentence for ideas expressed twice — the word for a two-person number may already carry this meaning.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If two leads practice a duet, can they do it any way other than jointly?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Redundancy repeats what the sentence already guarantees: a duet performed by the two leads is by definition a joint effort, so restating that adds words without meaning. Re-judge each option by what it adds.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What do the commas change about the phrase you kept?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Punctuating a phrase doesn't create new meaning — test whether the idea itself is already present elsewhere in the sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do the pauses make 'together' and 'with each other' any less repetitive of what 'duet' implies?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Setting a redundant phrase off with commas dresses it up but doesn't earn it a place; the sentence still says the same thing three times. Weigh the options by information, not punctuation.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try the sentence with the phrase's parts in a different order — does the meaning shift?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When rearranging words changes nothing, ask whether the words are needed at all.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does reshuffling two phrases that both mean 'jointly' fix the fact that 'duet' already says it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Reordering redundant words leaves them redundant — the pairing still repeats what the noun already conveys, in an even clumsier sequence. Re-assess which option leaves only words that add information.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare your version's length to the job it does — what did the extra words buy?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for verbs smothered into noun phrases; check whether the action could be stated directly.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'engages in the posting of' say anything that a single direct verb doesn't?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Wordiness turns one action into a ceremony: nominalizing the verb adds syllables but zero meaning. Re-read the options asking what each extra word contributes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the inserted phrase feel necessary?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test each added phrase: does it give new information, or duplicate something already in the sentence?

rows.body_md: Given that the schedule goes up every Monday morning, what does an extra timeliness phrase add?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The sentence already fixes the timing with 'Each Monday morning,' so an inserted phrase about timeliness duplicates it while interrupting the verb. Re-evaluate the options for padding.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your own words, what does 'makes it a point to' contribute here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check for filler frames wrapped around the real verb — could the sentence lead with the action itself?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is there any difference between deliberately posting the schedule and simply posting it, as far as the reader's information goes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Empty frames like this delay the verb without informing the reader; effective prose keeps the action and drops the wrapper. Reconsider what each option adds beyond the plain action.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up 'the kind of people that,' what meaning would the sentence lose?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Hunt for scaffolding phrases around the real action; test the sentence without them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does classifying the volunteers as a 'kind of people' add anything beyond the action they perform?

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does 'happen to' suggest about how the volunteers arrive?

rows.body_md: Check each added word for unintended meaning as well as bulk.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Are these early arrivals accidental, as your phrase implies, or is arriving early just what these volunteers do?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Happen to' both pads the sentence and miscolors the action as chance; the context treats early arrival as a habit, not luck. Re-weigh the options for accuracy and economy together.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How does being 'known for' something differ from actually doing it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for revisions that swap the action itself for a reputation about the action.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do volunteers get first choice because of their reputation, or because they are actually there early?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The sentence rewards the act of arriving, but this version substitutes fame for the act while adding words; the meaning shifts and the bulk grows at once. Re-examine which option preserves the plain action.

rows.body_md: Picture the moment: what exactly is the light doing as the soloist moves?

rows.body_md: Test the verb for precision — the soloist is weaving, so the verb must handle continuous motion.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a fixture 'look at' someone, and does that phrase capture following a moving target?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Precise word choice matches the action: the light continuously follows a moving performer, and a vague personified glance conveys neither the motion nor the mechanism. Re-try each verb against the actual action.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What settings usually call for the verb you picked?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the verb's connotation — some observation words carry courtroom or bystander overtones.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a spotlight observe a performance the way a person observes an accident, from the sidelines?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Connotation matters: this verb casts the light as a passive legal observer, while the sentence needs a verb for actively following motion. Re-match the verb to the action.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What attitude does your verb give the spotlight?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for verbs that add emotional charge the scene doesn't support.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the light menacing the soloist, or simply following her path through the dark?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This verb injects hostility into a neutral technical action; precision means conveying steady following without aggression. Re-evaluate the options for the verb that fits both motion and mood.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where will readers encounter this sentence, and what voice do they expect there?

rows.body_md: Match the phrase's register to a printed program note — a formal, public document.

rows.body_md: Would slang like this fit alongside the rest of a director's published note to an audience?

rows.body_md: Register must suit the setting: casual slang undercuts the formal, printed context of a program note. Re-screen the options for the one written in the document's own voice.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you weigh the formality of this phrasing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check both parts of the phrase — the hedge and the slang verb — against formal written English.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do 'pretty much' and that verb belong in a document families will read from their seats?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about what this phrase tells the reader the ensemble actually did.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test for both register and precision: conversational praise words often carry little specific meaning.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does calling the dancing 'awesome' describe the achievement, or just cheer for it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Colloquial praise is both too casual for a program note and too empty to describe the accomplishment; the sentence needs a formal verb that names what was achieved. Re-assess each option on register and content.

rows.body_md: Walk me through the sentence from the beginning — what did the team do first, second, and third?

rows.body_md: Compare the three actions in the list, and check whether they all sit in the same time frame.

rows.body_md: What made you place this action in the future?

rows.body_md: Look for the time marker near the start of the sentence and test each verb against it.

rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — does the third action feel finished or still in progress?

rows.body_md: Check whether the -ing form you chose agrees with the time frame of the other verbs in the list.

rows.body_md: If the trip wrapped up before 'the weather turned,' can one action in the series still be ongoing today?

rows.body_md: The progressive describes action unfolding at the moment of speaking, but every event here was completed last July; choose the form that matches the rest of the series.

rows.body_md: Which part of the sentence is actually performing the action here?

rows.body_md: Try crossing out the phrase that begins with 'of' and see what noun is left in charge.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'sensors' the subject, or is it tucked inside a phrase describing something else?

rows.body_md: A verb must agree with its subject, not with the closest noun; the head of this subject is singular, so a plural verb fails — re-examine the options.

rows.body_md: Say more about why you wanted an ongoing '-ing' form here.

rows.body_md: What time frame does your verb place these readings in?

rows.body_md: Can 'have,' a plural helper, pair with the singular 'array' — and does a completed action fit readings sent 'hourly'?

rows.body_md: If you covered up the rest of the sentence, would 'marvel on' sound right in a short test sentence?

rows.body_md: This is an idiom check: some verbs demand one specific preposition no matter the sentence.
