rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who or what is the actor in your version of the sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch the passive: it can mute both the actor and the vividness of the action.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Was heard' reports reception — does it say anything about the texture of the noise itself?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A flat passive tells us only that listening happened, discarding the noise's character; the sentence wants the sound rendered, not merely registered, so re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the sentence sets the level of formality — and what level is it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made this phrasing feel more at home in an investor report than the original?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare each word against the sentence's formal frame — one slangy word can sink the register.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Huge' in the sense of important — is that usage formal enough for financial correspondence from 1901?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This option trades one casual idiom for another, staying at conversational pitch while the sentence demands boardroom diction; re-choose the phrasing an investor report would actually print.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read your selection aloud — do all of its words come from the same register?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Inspect word by word: formal wrappers can hide one informal intruder.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Represent a significant development' sounds official — but what register does 'majorly' come from?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: One colloquial intensifier contaminates an otherwise formal phrase, and mixed registers fail the tone test just as surely as slang does; re-choose the option whose every word is businesslike.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through the order of events in this sentence — what happened first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the time marker at the start of the sentence and ask what era each verb belongs to.

rows.subject: act-english

rows.body_md: Consider what point in time a 'has + participle' verb connects an action to.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the sentence anchor her preparation to right now, or to the moment the round began?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Has' plus a participle links an action to the present, but this preparation was finished before a past event — the sentence needs the earlier-past form, so revisit the remaining verbs.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about the direction of time you pictured here.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test whether the underlined action points forward or backward from the sentence's anchor event.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would 'will have' describe something already finished before the round began, or something yet to happen?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Future perfect projects an action forward to a coming deadline; this studying was already complete when the past event occurred, so choose the form that reaches further back in time.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking anything else, which word in the sentence is actually doing the narrowing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide among the different verb forms here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two things need checking: the verb's number, and whether an ongoing form adds anything.

rows.body_md: Which noun is the true subject — the group itself, or the people inside the phrase describing it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This version still pairs a plural verb with a singular head noun; agreement comes before aspect, so find the option whose verb matches 'lineup' in number.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if you read this verb as an action rather than a description?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Ask whether the sentence describes something the subject did over time or a finished state imposed on it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'since the opening weekend' suggest a gradual process, or a completed passive condition — and is the subject singular or plural?

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — does the verb-plus-preposition pattern sound like set English?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Idioms travel in fixed pairs; identify which little word this particular verb demands.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: You may be hearing the pattern that follows 'forbid' — does 'prohibit' take that same partner?

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the pairing against other verbs you know: which verbs actually take this preposition?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Are you recalling the pattern after 'warn' or 'advise' rather than the one 'prohibit' requires?

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the sentence were you trying to repair with this longer verb phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check two layers: the preposition the main verb demands, and whether the progressive form adds meaning.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does stretching the verb into 'to be' plus -ing repair the idiom, or just pad the original problem?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship did you see between the two sentences when you picked this word?

rows.body_md: Does the second sentence really happen as a result of the first, or do the two pull in opposite directions?

rows.body_md: Tell me why an example word fit here — what would the example be illustrating?

rows.body_md: Is a statement about classical time controls a specific case of blitz rewarding instinct — or a different, opposing point?

rows.body_md: If you covered up the transition, would you say these sentences agree or disagree?

rows.body_md: Similarity words claim the second sentence runs parallel to the first — verify that claim.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do speed-and-instinct and hours-of-checking point the same way, or opposite ways?

rows.body_md: 'Likewise' asserts parallel ideas, but these sentences reverse direction; select the connector that marks a contrast between them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide the second sentence was a brand-new point?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the scope of the two sentences — is one general and the other specific?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the arbiter's questioning of four witnesses a separate claim, or a single concrete case of the habit described first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Addition words stack up new, coordinate points; here the second sentence zooms in to illustrate the first sentence's general claim, so choose the connector built for that move.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What in the second sentence seemed to push back against the first?

rows.body_md: A contrast word promises that the second sentence undercuts the first — verify whether it actually does.

rows.body_md: Does an arbiter carefully questioning witnesses contradict the claim that arbiters hear players out, or confirm it?

rows.body_md: The anecdote supports rather than opposes the opening claim, so a contradiction signal misleads the reader; pick the connector that introduces a supporting illustration.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about how you read the second sentence — a restatement, or something new?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Restating transitions require the second sentence to say the same thing in different words; test that here.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the anecdote merely paraphrase the first sentence, or does it supply a specific scene with new details?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A rephrasing signal fits only when no new information arrives; this sentence adds a concrete case with fresh details, so select the connector that introduces one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What's the one idea every sentence in this paragraph feeds?

rows.body_md: A closing line should circle back to the paragraph's core claim — check whether yours does.

rows.subject: act-english

rows.body_md: Ask whether your closer reinforces the paragraph's actual subject or swerves toward a new one.

rows.body_md: What made a fact about antique pieces feel like an ending here?

rows.body_md: Does bone-and-ivory history reinforce a paragraph about today's swelling club rosters?

rows.body_md: If you covered up Sentence 5, where would its details feel most missed?

rows.body_md: Track the pronoun and the phrase 'every stop' — find the sentence that gives them their meaning.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What signal told you the topic turns at that point?

rows.body_md: Is the founder buying clocks part of the early struggles, or part of the recent success story?

rows.body_md: How did you decide the early-years section ends there?

rows.body_md: Test the sentence on each side of your break: do they belong to different chapters of the story?

rows.body_md: What job is the phrase about the arbiter doing in this sentence?

rows.body_md: Extra, droppable descriptions need punctuation on both ends — count what this version provides.

rows.body_md: Distinguish describing from arguing. Ask whether the passage makes a recommendation or lays out a mechanism.

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A purpose must reflect what the passage does, and this one lays out a natural process rather than pushing a course of action. Select the purpose that matches its descriptive aim.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the paragraph most want its new sentence to prove?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: There is a difference between background about a person and evidence for a claim. Ask which one your sentence provides.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Your pick tells us when and where the theory was first dreamed up. Does that show whether it was ever checked against reality?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The paragraph is building toward proof that the theory held up, so a detail about the theory's origins adds background but no test. Choose the sentence that supplies real confirmation of the claim.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How does a note about atolls being photogenic connect to the paragraph's point?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Judge the candidate against the paragraph's goal, not against the general subject of reefs. Ask whether it moves the argument forward.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Your choice praises how these formations look. Does their beauty have anything to do with whether the theory was verified?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A supporting sentence must advance the paragraph's point about testing the theory, and a decorative comment on scenery does not. Pick the sentence that actually bears on whether the theory was confirmed.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is your sentence true — and, separately, does it touch the question the paragraph is asking?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A statement can be accurate yet off the paragraph's point. Weigh whether this fact speaks to how the theory was tested.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Your pick states the temperatures coral tolerates. Does that information help show the sinking-island theory was proved?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Relevance, not mere truth, decides whether a sentence belongs, and a correct fact about temperature limits says nothing about testing the theory. Select the detail that provides confirmation of the claim.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read each side of the comma on its own — could each stand as a full sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When two complete sentences meet, a comma by itself isn't strong enough. Test whether both halves are independent.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Both parts here can stand alone. Is a single comma enough to hold two complete sentences together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two independent clauses cannot be linked by a comma alone, which is exactly what the original does. Join them with a small linking word after the comma, or use stronger punctuation.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say the two halves aloud with no pause between them — does it run together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two complete sentences need something between them. Ask whether your version supplies any join at all.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Your pick puts no mark or word between the two complete statements. Can two sentences simply collide with nothing between them?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Dropping all punctuation between two independent clauses creates a run-on, which is even less acceptable than the original. Supply a proper connector so the two statements are correctly joined.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What kind of word did you add after the comma, and does it change how the clauses must be punctuated?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Some linking words still demand heavier punctuation than a comma. Ask whether the word you chose can follow a mere comma.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: You placed a 'therefore'-type word after the comma. Does that kind of adverb repair a comma between two full sentences?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A conjunctive adverb needs a semicolon before it, so putting one after a comma leaves the splice unfixed. Use a true coordinating conjunction after the comma instead.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the words after the period by themselves — do they form a complete sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A group of words needs a subject and a working verb to stand alone. Check whether the second 'sentence' has both.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The stretch after the period starts with an -ing word and has no subject. Can that stand as its own sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An -ing phrase with no subject and no helping verb is a fragment, so ending the first part with a period strands it. Reconnect it to the clause before it with lighter punctuation.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What has to follow a semicolon for it to be used correctly?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Semicolons and periods share a requirement about what sits on each side. Test whether the second part meets it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The words after your semicolon can't stand on their own. Does a semicolon allow a fragment to follow it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A semicolon must join two complete sentences, but the trailing -ing phrase is not one, so a semicolon is as wrong as a period here. Attach the phrase to the main clause with a comma instead.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try reading your version's second part aloud — does 'they providing' sound like a finished verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An -ing word alone can't serve as a full verb. Ask what the phrase would need to become a real clause.

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An -ing form needs a helping verb to act as a predicate, so 'they providing' is still not a clause. Rather than forcing a clause, join the phrase to the main sentence with a comma.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who or what is actually doing the drifting in that opening phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An opening -ing phrase describes whatever noun follows the comma. Check whether that noun can really perform the action.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Right after the comma, the sentence names the equipment as the thing drifting. Can a camera drift over the reef on its own?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An introductory modifier must attach to the person or thing performing its action, but here it lands on a piece of gear that can't drift by itself. Rewrite so the one actually moving through the water is the subject.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your version, who is doing the drifting the opening phrase describes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Switching to a passive construction can dodge naming a subject. Ask whether the drifter is clearly identified now.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Your rewrite still never says who drifts, and it adds extra words. Does the introductory phrase finally have a logical doer?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A passive rewrite leaves the opening modifier without a real subject and only pads the sentence, so the problem survives. Recast it so the living thing doing the drifting is the plain subject.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is the phrase you moved still describing after you shifted it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Relocating a modifier doesn't change what it attaches to. Ask which noun the phrase now sits next to.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: You tucked the phrase beside the equipment. Does that stop the sentence from claiming the equipment drifts?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Merely repositioning the modifier keeps it tied to the same illogical noun, so the gear still seems to be drifting. Make the true agent of the drifting the subject of the main clause.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the two verbs you've joined — do they mean different things or the same thing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for pairs where the second word just echoes the first. Ask whether the added verb contributes any new meaning.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'cut back' tell the reader anything the first verb hasn't already said?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When a second verb only repeats the meaning of the first, the pair is redundant and one word should go. Keep the single verb that already carries the whole idea.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which words in your phrase are doing real work, and which just repeat the idea?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Extra particles and synonyms can stack redundancy. Strip the phrase to its core and see what survives.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do 'down' and 'shortened' add meaning the first verb lacks, or do they restate it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Piling an adverb and a synonym onto a verb that already means the same thing is redundant padding. Reduce it to the one word that says it all.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read your longer phrase and ask what it adds beyond the first verb.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A tacked-on clause can simply restate what came before. Test whether it delivers new information.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'thereby reduced in length' describe anything different from what the first verb already describes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Restating a verb's meaning in a longer phrase is redundancy, not emphasis, so the addition should be cut. Keep the concise single verb on its own.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How many of the words in the underlined stretch are doing separate jobs?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Long strings of qualifiers often collapse into a short phrase. Try compressing it and see if meaning is lost.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you delete 'specific,' 'underlying,' and 'responsible for,' does the sentence lose any real information?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When several words all point at the same idea, most are padding and can go. Choose the trimmed phrase that keeps the meaning with far fewer words.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Look at the two verbs in your phrase — are they saying two things or one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A phrase can be shorter than the original yet still carry dead weight. Check whether both halves are needed.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do 'lies behind' and 'produces' express different ideas, or the same notion said twice?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Even a rewrite can stay wordy if it doubles the same idea, so this version isn't lean enough. Pick the phrase that states the idea a single time in the fewest words.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the opening 'what it is that' actually contribute to the meaning?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Frames like 'what it is that' often add length without content. Test whether the sentence loses anything if it's gone.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Strip 'what it is that actually' from your phrase — is any real information missing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An 'it is that' frame is empty scaffolding that pads the sentence, so it should be removed. Choose the direct phrase that names the idea without the filler wrapper.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the underlined phrase do beyond announcing purpose?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Some phrases can shrink to a single word without any loss. Try swapping this one and check the meaning.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you replaced the whole phrase with a one-word purpose marker, would the sentence lose anything?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A multi-word purpose phrase usually carries no more meaning than the single word 'to,' so it is just filler. Pick the shortest form that still signals purpose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read your phrase aloud — is it any leaner than the original?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swapping one wordy purpose phrase for another doesn't fix the padding. Compare its length to the simplest option.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'so as to' say anything the plainest purpose word doesn't already say?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Trading one bulky purpose phrase for a different bulky one leaves the filler in place. Choose the single-word form that conveys purpose most directly.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What extra idea does 'in an effort to' slip in, and is it needed?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Some purpose phrases sneak in a sense of striving. Ask whether that shade of meaning belongs here.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the sentence need to suggest the researchers are struggling, or just state their purpose?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'In an effort to' adds both length and an unwanted hint of struggle, so it overshoots a plain purpose. Use the concise form that simply marks purpose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the underlined phrase the sharpest way to name what the proteins do with light?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Casual phrasal verbs are often less precise than a single technical term. Ask whether a more exact word exists.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Your phrase is loose, everyday language. Does a scientific description of light deserve a more exact verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A vague phrasal verb works in speech, but a precise process calls for the exact term for sending out light. Choose the single word that names that action precisely.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Picture what 'release' usually describes — is it light, or something being let go?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Near-synonyms can carry the wrong image. Test whether your word fits producing light specifically.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'release' suggest giving out light, or letting go of some stored-up substance?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Release' implies freeing something held rather than producing light, so it misfits the optical process. Pick the verb that exactly means sending light outward.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does 'reflect' physically mean when we talk about light?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Some verbs name a completely different optical event. Check whether your word matches producing new-colored light.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The proteins create light of a new color, not bounce back the old light. Does 'reflect' describe creating light or bouncing it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Reflect' means bouncing existing light back, which contradicts how these proteins generate a new color, so it is technically wrong. Select the verb that means giving out light.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the underlined phrase in the middle of this scientific sentence — does the register match?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Quantifiers range from casual to formal. Ask whether this one fits writing about marine biologists.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would 'a ton of' appear in a formal research report, or does it sound like everyday speech?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A breezy, conversational quantifier clashes with formal scientific prose even though its meaning is clear. Choose the more elevated phrase for a large, valuable amount.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How formal does 'loads of' sound next to talk of databases and research teams?

rows.body_md: Match the quantifier's tone to the sentence's tone. Test whether casual slang belongs in a scientific description.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'loads of' the kind of phrase you'd find in a serious scientific write-up?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Loads of' is informal slang that undercuts the passage's formal register. Pick the dignified phrase suited to a large, valuable quantity.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say 'a whole bunch of' aloud in a formal report — does it fit?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Chatty quantifiers signal casual writing. Ask whether this phrase suits the scientific tone here.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'a whole bunch of' read as precise, formal language, or as everyday conversation?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'A whole bunch of' is conversational and vague for formal prose, so it breaks the register. Choose the polished phrase that names a large, valuable amount.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through the timeline of this sentence — when is everything happening?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try listing the sentence's time markers, then check whether the underlined verb points to the same moment they do.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the crews met at Promontory Summit in May 1869, can an action tied to that very day still lie in the future?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb must match its established time frame; 'will' points forward from now, but this sentence narrates a dated event that was already over long ago. Look again at the options that stay in past time.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made a perfect-tense form feel right to you here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a time-frame check: does the sentence describe an action completed at a specific, dated moment or one that continues to the present?

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english

rows.body_md: Say more about why a perfect-tense verb appealed to you here.

rows.body_md: An opener should act like a promise the paragraph keeps — check what promise this fact about length makes.

rows.body_md: Pointer phrases like 'that' must look backward at something already stated — check what Sentence 3 can see behind it from each position.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the hours detail arrives only later, what exactly was 'that grueling load' referring to when readers first hit it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A summarizing pointer works only when its evidence comes first; parking the workload detail behind the contrast sentence leaves the pointer starved and the detail stranded. Re-place the sentence so the pointer has its referent.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where does the paragraph's story reach its destination, and what happens if new hardship details come after that?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch the chronology: the paragraph moves from hiring to duties to a 1925 milestone — test each slot against that arc.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Once the union's victory closes the story, does circling back to monthly hours push the paragraph forward or drag it backward?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Supporting details belong before the conclusion they justify; adding workload facts after the climactic milestone breaks the timeline and blunts the ending, so slot the sentence where it feeds the hardship discussion.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try labeling each sentence with its city — where does the label actually change?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A paragraph break belongs at a change of subject; check whether the second sentence has left London yet.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Smoke-filled tunnels and soaring ridership describe which system — the one just introduced, or a new one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Dividing here strands London's opening sentence alone while its own story continues below; the split must fall where the passage crosses to its second subject, so re-scan for that crossing point.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the switch to electric power feel like a new topic to you?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Distinguish a topic change from a development within a topic — same city, new technology is which one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When the Tube electrifies and expands, has the paragraph stopped discussing London's underground?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A new paragraph marks a new subject, not a new phase of the same subject; electrification is still London's story, so look for the sentence where the geography itself changes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up everything before Sentence 4, which system would it seem to describe?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the place references: whose network reaches those suburbs?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a sentence about the network reaching London's outskirts belong with the London discussion or the American one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The suburban-growth sentence still develops the first city's system, so breaking here puts London material under the American heading; begin the new paragraph where the passage leaves Britain.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — where did your voice naturally pause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Identify the introductory chunk and the main statement, then check whether anything marks the border between them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Without a mark after 'arrived,' could a reader momentarily attach 'the platform' to the wrong clause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An opening dependent clause needs a comma at its close so the main clause can start cleanly; leaving the seam unmarked invites a misread, so re-inspect where the intro ends.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job is the word 'When' doing at the head of this sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check whether the comma you chose separates whole sentence parts or cuts inside one of them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can 'When' be peeled away from 'the evening express arrived' and still steer that clause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A subordinator belongs welded to its clause; a comma directly after it severs the word from what it governs. The single comma should sit where the intro clause hands off to the main one — re-place it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which words form the subject and verb of the opening clause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Scan for any comma standing between a subject and its own verb — that pairing must stay unbroken.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does a pause between 'express' and 'arrived' do to the clause they build together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Commas never split a subject from its verb; the boundary that needs marking is where the whole introductory clause ends, not the middle of it. Re-position the comma at that seam.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship connects the underlined word to the flagship express?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run an ownership test: if one noun possesses the next, some mark of possession has to appear.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a noun show that the express belongs to it without any apostrophe at all?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Possession in writing requires an apostrophe; a bare s shows neither plural sense nor ownership here. Decide how many owners there are, then pick the form that marks possession for that number.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How many railway firms does this sentence actually talk about?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Separate two questions: is the noun plural, and does it own something? Each answer changes the spelling.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the word merely named several firms, what in the sentence would connect any of them to the flagship?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A plain plural cannot express ownership; since the express belongs to a single firm, the noun needs the possessive built on its singular form. Re-check the options for that construction.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What evidence in the sentence points to more than one owner?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before placing the apostrophe, settle the head count: the mark's position encodes how many possessors there are.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'flagship' suggest a fleet shared by many firms or the prize train of one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An apostrophe after the s claims plural owners, but this sentence describes one firm and its showcase train; build the possessive from the singular and choose again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What information tells the reader which of the three gauges won the contract?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Decide whether the clause is removable background or essential identification — commas around it claim it could be lifted out.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you lifted the clause out entirely, would 'the gauge won the contract' still tell you which gauge, given that three were tested?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Commas around a clause mark it as removable extra detail; here the clause is the only thing distinguishing the winning gauge from the other two, so it must stay welded to its noun without punctuation. Re-test each option with the lift-out check.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where exactly does the comma in your version fall — between which two sentence parts?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Find the whole subject, clause included, and check whether anything separates it from its verb.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a comma stand between 'the gauge that handled the sharpest curves' and what that gauge did?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A subject may never be cut off from its verb by a single comma, even when the subject is long; the identifying clause rides inside the subject with no punctuation at all. Choose again with that seam in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about why a comma felt necessary before the clause.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check which relative pronouns can follow a comma — the punctuation rules differ for the two common ones.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Have you ever seen a comma placed directly before 'that' in a clause that identifies its noun?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'That' introduces essential clauses and never takes a comma in front of it; since this clause identifies which gauge won, it must attach directly to its noun. Re-inspect the options for the clean attachment.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — did you pause where the comma sits, or did the comma invent the pause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test whether the comma separates two complete sentence parts or interrupts one continuous action mid-stream.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'reset their clocks' feel finished before the reader learns what the clocks were reset to?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb and the phrase completing its meaning form one unit, and no comma may interrupt that unit on its way to completion. Strip out any comma that breaks the flow, then re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which two words does the comma in your version stand between, and what job does each do?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the verb-object check: a verb and the thing it acts on should touch, with nothing wedged between them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What happens to the action 'reset' when a pause cuts it off from the clocks being reset?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Punctuation never divides a verb from its direct object; 'reset' must connect straight to what was reset. Re-examine each option for a barrier inside that pairing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made a pause feel right inside the phrase 'the new standard time'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check whether the two describing words are interchangeable equals — the swap test settles whether a comma belongs between them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would you say 'the standard, new time' or 'the new and standard time'? What does that tell you?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Commas separate only coordinate adjectives that could swap places; here 'standard time' is a single named unit that 'new' describes as a whole, so nothing may intrude into it. Re-check each option against that test.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What picture does your chosen verb put in the reader's mind?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the verb against the writer's stated goal — the goal asks for motion the reader can almost feel.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a train that simply 'moved' seem to be crawling, rolling, or flying?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When the goal is vivid emphasis, a generic verb of motion fails the assignment even though it is grammatical; the sentence needs the verb whose sound and sense convey startling velocity. Compare the options for that energy.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How fast does a train that 'proceeded' seem to be going?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Weigh connotation, not just correctness: formal words often slow a sentence's felt pace.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a stiff, procedural verb convey a machine outrunning every steam schedule in the country?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A bureaucratic-sounding verb drains the motion of its drama; the writer's goal demands wording that makes the speed felt, not merely reported. Re-rank the choices by intensity.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the rest of the sentence, what pace would 'made its way' suggest?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test each option against the goal: which phrasings suggest wandering, and which suggest velocity?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Doesn't 'made its way' sound more like a hiker picking a path than a record-setting train?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A leisurely idiom contradicts the very speed the writer wants to spotlight; the goal calls for the verb whose connotation matches a machine tearing across open country. Re-weigh the options against that standard.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How would you describe the passage's voice in the sentences before the underlined part?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the emotional temperature of the underlined phrase with the calm, factual sentences around it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a paragraph about polished levers and memorized timetables build naturally toward a declaration about humanity's eternal struggle?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Tone must stay consistent: this passage speaks in a low, observational register, and a swelling, grandiose flourish breaks that voice. Re-read each option and keep the one that stays as level as the rest of the paragraph.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which audience does the phrase 'totally awesome' usually address?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the register: match the underlined words against the vocabulary the passage has used so far.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a historian describing signal boxes in measured prose suddenly drop in chatty slang?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Casual, conversational wording clashes with the passage's restrained voice; the revision must sound like the same writer who described the levers and timetables. Re-screen the options for that consistency.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try reading your choice in the same breath as the sentence before it — do they sound like one writer?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Puffed-up, technical phrasing is as much a tone break as slang; test the option for inflation.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'considerable operational significance' share the plain, human vocabulary of polished levers and memorized timetables?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Matching tone means matching plainness too: bureaucratic jargon overshoots the passage's simple register just as slang undershoots it. Look for the option written in the passage's own quiet manner.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What claim does the proposed sentence actually make — can you restate it in your own words?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the reason, not just the yes-or-no: does a fact about an 1840 stamp explain anything about mail volume on trains?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in the added sentence do you find a cause for railroads carrying so many letters?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An addition earns its place only when its content does the job the reason claims; a stamp's debut in Britain says nothing about why letters rode the rails, and it pulls the paragraph away from the sorting clerks. Re-judge the addition against the paragraph's focus.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When did the sorting clerks' profession begin, according to anything in the paragraph or the new sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Separate two different origins — the first stamp and the first onboard sorters — and ask whether the sentence dates the one that matters here.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a British stamp of 1840 tell you anything about when men began sorting letters on moving cars?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A supporting sentence must actually supply what its justification promises; the stamp's date marks postal prehistory, not the start of this profession, and the detail steers readers off the paragraph's subject. Reconsider what the addition really contributes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: You agreed the sentence doesn't belong — now test your reason: which earlier statement does it supposedly repeat?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Scan each existing sentence for any mention of stamps or of 1840 before calling the addition repetitive.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a fact appear 'again' if it never appeared a first time?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The right rejection names the real flaw: the sentence is not a repeat but a detour into postal background that the paragraph never opens. Match your reason to what the sentence actually does, then re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which sentences in the passage actually mention job titles Dennis held?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A 'yes' answer needs a reason that matches both the goal and the passage — check whether the passage catalogs her positions at all.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a list of career titles, even if it existed, show passengers' experience changing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The essay succeeds through what it shows travelers gaining, not through career labels it never enumerates; a justification must describe the essay as written. Re-match each reason to the passage's actual content.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where does the passage discuss freight?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before accepting a 'no,' verify its factual claim against the passage's actual subject matter.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Reclining seats, softer lighting, cinder-free vents — do those serve boxcars or people?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A reason built on a false description fails no matter its verdict; this essay never touches freight, so a rejection on those grounds cannot stand. Re-read the passage and test each option's claim against it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Whose experiences does the passage actually describe — point to the people in it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the claim inside this reason: find even one sentence about company officials reacting.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Did the passage quote a single executive, or did it follow what ordinary passengers gained?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Rejecting the essay requires an accurate account of it; no boardroom reactions appear anywhere, while the passage tracks what travelers experienced. Discard reasons that misdescribe the text and judge the goal again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job does the paragraph's first sentence perform for everything after it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before cutting an opener, check whether every later sentence depends on the idea it introduces.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the steep-grade claim vanished, would the details about gearing and powered axles still have a point?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The first sentence states the very focus — steep grades mastered by geared engines — that the writer wants to keep; deleting it beheads the paragraph. Hunt instead for whichever sentence drifts away from the machines entirely.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your own words, what does the second sentence explain?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the sentence against the stated focus: does the gearing explanation support how these engines gripped steep track?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could readers understand why the engines could climb without knowing the pistons drove a geared-down shaft?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The mechanism of trading speed for grip is the heart of the paragraph's focus, not a detour; the true stray is whichever sentence never touches the locomotives at all. Re-scan for it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would the paragraph lose if its last sentence disappeared?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the final sentence's subject: is it still about how these engines handled rough, temporary track?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Powered axles crawling over derail-prone rails — is that off the topic, or is it the topic?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The closing sentence extends the exact focus the writer names, so it earns its place; the intruder is whichever sentence turns from the engines to a different camp activity. Re-examine each sentence's subject.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How many complete statements do you count inside this sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Find each subject-verb pair, then ask what is holding the two statements together.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is a comma by itself strong enough to weld 'the turntable balanced perfectly' to 'a single worker could spin a locomotive'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone — that is a splice; they need a stronger separator or a comma teamed with a linking word. Re-test each option for a legal joint.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What kind of word is 'however,' and what punctuation does it normally demand around it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Words like 'however' and 'therefore' are movable adverbs, not glue — check whether the two clauses are still legally joined.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you dropped 'however' out of your version, what error would be staring back at you?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A conjunctive adverb set off by commas never repairs a splice, and this sentence sets up a cause-effect, not a contrast; the clauses stay broken unless a true conjunction or a stronger stop joins them. Re-inspect which options supply that.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read your version aloud without stopping — where does one statement end and the next begin?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Deleting all punctuation between two complete statements creates its own boundary problem; check for it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does removing the comma cure the joint between the clauses, or just hide it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Running two independent clauses together with nothing between them is a fused sentence, one step worse than a splice; the fix must add a legal connector, not subtract the comma. Choose again with that test.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where did you hear the break when you read this sentence out loud?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the subject-verb pairs, then check what stands at the border between them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can 'the special left at dawn' and 'its coaches were packed' share one sentence with no mark at all between them?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two complete statements need a genuine boundary — a full stop, a strong mid-sentence mark, or a comma with a joining word; leaving nothing there fuses them into one tangle. Re-screen the options for a real boundary.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made a comma feel sufficient at that spot?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Apply the both-sides test: if each side could stand alone as a sentence, a lone comma cannot hold them together.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try reading each half by itself — do both halves work as full sentences?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a splice; the border needs a full-strength mark or a comma plus a connector. Re-check which options meet that bar.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does adding 'because' claim about the relationship between the two halves?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check both the logic and the mechanics: a subordinating word changes what kind of clause follows, and the mark before it must match.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Once 'because' demotes the second half to a dependent clause, can the strong mid-sentence mark still stand in front of it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: That mid-sentence mark joins only two clauses that could each stand alone; bolting a subordinator onto the second half breaks the rule and invents a cause the sentence never claims. Re-evaluate the options against both tests.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who or what was restored plank by plank, according to your reading?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An opening modifier grabs the first noun after the comma — check who it grabs in this version.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Were the visitors themselves rebuilt over ten summers?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An introductory phrase must describe the subject that immediately follows it; here the restored thing is the building, so the building must stand right after the comma. Re-screen the options for the one that puts it there.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your version, what noun sits directly after the introductory phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Ask whether the thing named in that slot is something volunteers could restore.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can 'touring' — an activity — be the thing rebuilt plank by plank?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The modifier needs the restored building itself as the very next subject; an activity or abstract noun in that slot leaves the phrase dangling. Re-aim your search at what actually got restored.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the word 'there' refer to in your version?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Empty placeholder subjects cannot receive an opening modifier — test who the phrase describes now.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the sentence starts by naming what was restored, can a placeholder like 'there' claim that description?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A dummy subject gives the modifier nothing real to modify, so the phrase still dangles; only a version whose grammatical subject is the restored structure works. Compare the options on that single point.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is each time word in the underlined phrase doing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Scan the span for two expressions that answer the same question about when the planning happened.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If 'in advance' already places the planning early, what new information does the next time expression add?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When two phrases carry the same time meaning, one of them must go; keeping both says 'early' twice. Trim the doubled idea and re-select.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Talk me through how your revision changes the original phrase.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the time expressions your version contains — a fix should reduce that number, not reshuffle it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does swapping one early-time phrase for another remove the repetition, or just disguise it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Redundancy is fixed by deletion, not substitution: a version that still stacks two same-meaning time markers repeats the flaw it was meant to cure. Look again for the version that says 'early' exactly once.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the longer phrasing feel more complete to you?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test each connected phrase in your version: do they make different claims, or the same claim twice?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If both parts of your phrase mean 'earlier than the departure,' what does keeping both accomplish?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Piling up synonyms adds bulk, not meaning; a pair of same-meaning time phrases is redundancy no matter how they are joined. Re-choose the version that keeps a single time marker.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What extra work do you think the added words are doing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try a subtraction test: remove the introductory helper words and see whether any meaning disappears.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the log do anything different when helper words stand in front of its action?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Helpers that merely announce a verb add syllables, not sense; a phrase built on such scaffolding is wordier without being clearer. Re-run the subtraction test on every option before deciding.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before settling, ask yourself: is the sentence about what the log can do or what it does?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check whether your version reports a fact or merely a capability — the sentence's evidence is a doubled tonnage, an actual event.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the log records that tonnage doubled, is 'capable of' the right claim, or an inflated hedge?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Shifting from action to ability both pads the sentence and weakens its claim; the record states a fact outright. Strip each option down to the claim it makes, then pick again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How would you state this sentence's point aloud in one breath?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for phrases that turn a single action into a chain of nouns — count the words standing between the log and its point.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does 'an indication of the fact' accomplish that one direct verb could not?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Burying an action under nouns and 'the fact' is classic padding: it slows the reader and adds no content. Favor the version that states the action directly and re-decide.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you dropped the added word from your version, what meaning would vanish?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Some adverbs qualify a claim and some merely fill space — decide which kind this one is.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Was the line only 'basically' hauling slate, or did it haul slate, full stop?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Qualifiers earn their place only when something is genuinely approximate; here the hauling is a plain fact, so the added word is filler. Re-test each option by deleting its extras.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say the revised sentence aloud — what does the inserted phrase contribute?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Measure the phrase against the fact it interrupts: does it sharpen the claim or just delay the slate's destination?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a reader doubt that the line hauled slate without that four-word reassurance?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Stock idioms like this one hedge a claim that needs no hedging, and they wedge themselves between the verb and its object; empty phrases must be cut, not accommodated. Choose again with the deletion test.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which idea in the sentence needed hedging, in your view?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Ask whether the inserted phrase could be deleted with zero change in meaning — that is the test for filler.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In what other sense, besides a real one, could a railway haul slate?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A phrase that insists something is 'real' without adding information is pure padding; the sentence's claim was never in doubt. Strip the candidates to their working words and re-select.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How much detail does the underlined verb give about what the team actually did?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the verb to the evidence around it — measuring snowmelt, charting flood channels — and ask whether it works that hard.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could someone 'look at' a valley for a season without measuring anything at all?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A precise verb must match the described effort: a whole season of systematic measurement demands a verb of careful, sustained examination, and a vague catch-all undersells it. Re-weigh the options against the work described.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How long does the action named by your verb usually take?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Set the verb's built-in duration beside the sentence's time frame of an entire season.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a glimpse — a split-second, often accidental look — stretch across months of charting?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Word choice must respect a verb's core meaning: a term for the briefest possible look contradicts a season of deliberate measurement. Match duration and intent, then choose again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What picture of the surveyors does your chosen verb create?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test whether the verb describes an act of investigation or merely a way of viewing something.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'regarding' a valley involve instruments and records, or just a considered gaze?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb about attitude or gaze cannot carry the sense of methodical fieldwork the sentence details; precision means choosing the verb whose meaning includes that sustained investigation. Re-screen the options for it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where else in the sentence do you hear the same level of formality as the underlined phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Label the passage's register in two words, then label the underlined phrase the same way and compare.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a museum caption about an 1848 boiler plate call anything a 'big deal'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Register must stay consistent: conversational slang jars against the formal, historical voice of the rest of the sentence. Re-read each option in that voice and keep the one that belongs.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who talks this way — and is that the voice of this passage?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the vocabulary to the audience: which options could appear in a historical exhibit text without raising eyebrows?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'seriously cool' sound like the same writer who noted the original boiler plate and the 1848 completion date?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Casual intensifiers belong to speech, not formal description; the sentence needs measured wording that suits its historical register. Screen the options for that fit and re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What tone were you aiming for with the grander phrasing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Overshooting formality is as jarring as slang — check whether the phrase inflates beyond the passage's plain style.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a sentence of dates and miles support a sudden burst of 'ineffable, transcendent wonder'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Formal does not mean florid: the passage speaks plainly, so ornate abstraction breaks its register from above just as slang breaks it from below. Find the option pitched at the passage's own level.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through the timeline of this sentence — which event happened first, the cabled warnings or the landfall?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the tense frame: the sentence anchors everything to a moment in 1900, so test whether the underlined verb points to the present or to that past moment.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The helper verb in the original connects an action to right now. Can an action that ended before a 1900 landfall still be tied to the present?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Present perfect links a past action to the present moment, but this dismissal was completed before another past event; an earlier-than-past action needs a different perfect form. Revisit the options with that timeline in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made a future-pointing form feel right for events from 1900?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a timeline check: place the landfall and the dismissal on a line and ask which direction this tense points.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: That form describes something that will be finished at a future moment. Is anything in this sentence still ahead of us?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Future perfect marks completion before a future deadline, yet both events here sit firmly in the past, so a forward-looking verb cannot fit. Re-test each option against the 1900 time frame.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about why an in-progress form appealed to you here.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try an aspect check: does the sentence describe an action still unfolding at landfall, or one already over and done?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The phrase 'days earlier' tells you when the dismissing happened. Was it still going on as the storm arrived?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Past progressive shows an action in motion at a past moment, but this action had wrapped up days before the landfall; a completed earlier action needs a perfect form instead. Look again with that distinction.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up everything between 'array' and the underlined verb, how would the sentence read?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This is an agreement question: find the true subject before judging the verb, and watch out for nouns tucked inside describing phrases.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which word actually owns the verb — 'array,' 'sensors,' or 'anemometers'? Only one of them is the grammatical subject.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Name the agreement test: isolate the true subject, ignore the pile of nouns after it, then pick the matching verb. Here that subject is singular 'array' — re-choose after setting the pile aside.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made you add a completed-action helper verb to this sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two things to test here: whether the verb matches the subject in number, and whether the sentence describes a finished event or a routine that repeats.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The phrase 'every sixty seconds' describes an ongoing routine. Does a form meaning 'has already done it' capture that?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Every sixty seconds' calls for a simple present-tense verb agreeing with the singular subject 'array'; a plural perfect form misses on both counts. Test each option against subject and time frame.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the sentence did you treat as the subject when you picked a plural verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Strip the sentence to its skeleton: cross out every prepositional phrase and every clause starting with 'that,' then see what noun is left driving the verb.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Sensors' and 'anemometers' sit inside modifying phrases. Can a noun inside a modifier control the main verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The main verb belongs to 'array,' a singular noun, so a plural progressive form breaks agreement no matter how many plural nouns intervene. Cross out the modifiers and match the verb to what remains.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — do the three actions in the list sound like they wear the same uniform?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This is a parallelism check: line up the verbs in the series and compare their forms one by one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The first two actions are 'checks' and 'updates.' What form would the third action need to march in step with them?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Items in a series must share the same grammatical form; the first two verbs are simple present, so a helping-verb progressive breaks the pattern. Re-choose the form that matches the rest of the list.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made an infinitive feel right as the last item in this list?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare list items: read each verb in the series and ask whether they all start the same way.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would you say 'the meteorologist checks, updates, and to look over'? Test your pick by swapping it into the earlier slots.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A series stays parallel only when every item takes the same form; two simple present verbs followed by a 'to' form snaps the pattern. Match the third verb to the first two.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide between the '-ing' form and the forms used earlier in the list?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a series audit: the verb endings in a list should rhyme grammatically from the first item to the last.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Checks, updates, and' — what ending do the first two verbs share that a bare '-ing' word lacks?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Parallel structure requires matching verb forms across a series; a bare '-ing' participle cannot follow two simple present verbs. Re-pick the option whose ending mirrors 'checks' and 'updates.'

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship did you see between the two sentences when you chose a conclusion word?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a logic test: does the second sentence follow from the first as an effect, or does it push back against it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Imagery shows where clouds form, yet it cannot measure their rain. Is the second statement a consequence of the first — or a limitation of it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A cause-and-effect connector claims the second sentence follows from the first, but the second sentence actually cuts against the first by naming what the tool cannot do. Re-read both sentences and re-choose based on that relationship.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Tell me what the second sentence is doing — is it giving a sample of the first, or something else?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the transition category: an illustration word promises a specific instance of the previous claim.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'it cannot reveal how much rain will fall' an example of imagery showing where clouds gather?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An example connector must introduce a case of the preceding statement; here the second sentence instead points out what the tool fails to do, so an illustration word mislabels the logic. Re-examine the relationship and choose again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking anything else, ask: are these two sentences pulling in the same direction?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A similarity word claims the second idea echoes the first. Test whether these two ideas actually match.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: One sentence describes a strength of satellite imagery; the other describes a blind spot. Do those sound alike?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Likewise' signals two parallel, same-direction ideas, but this pair sets an ability against an inability — opposing directions. Re-check which logical relationship the pair really has.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your own words, what does the second sentence do with the information in the first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the connector's job: a restatement word promises the same idea repeated in a new way.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is widening the cone of uncertainty just a rephrasing of 'the models disagree' — or is it something the disagreement caused?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A restatement transition requires the second sentence to say the first thing again differently; here the second sentence is a consequence, an action taken because of the disagreement, so a rephrasing signal fails. Re-match the connector to that logic.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made a pushback word feel right between these two sentences?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Contrast connectors need tension: check whether the second sentence resists the first or flows from it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the models disagree, is widening the uncertainty cone surprising — or exactly what you'd expect?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Nevertheless' promises the second sentence happens in spite of the first, but widening the cone happens because of the disagreement, not against it. Re-read for the true cause-and-effect direction and pick again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where does the second sentence give a specific example of the first one, if anywhere?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An illustration transition must introduce one concrete case of the previous general claim — run that test here.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the hurricane center's action a sample of models disagreeing, or a response to it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Example connectors introduce instances, not outcomes; the second sentence reports what the disagreement led the center to do, so an illustration word mislabels it. Re-choose based on that cause-and-effect link.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the stated goal ask this final sentence to emphasize?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a goal check: the closing line should land on worldwide coordination, so test whether your pick even mentions how the launches are timed or connected.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the history of the device's design tell a reader anything about stations cooperating around the globe?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A concluding sentence must serve the stated goal, and a fact about when the device was invented drops the idea of coordinated launches altogether. Re-check which sentence keeps the paragraph's worldwide scope in view.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which detail in your pick did you read as evidence of coordination?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try a scale test: does the sentence you chose describe the network of stations acting in concert, or the journey of a single balloon?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A hundred-mile drift is vivid, but whose story is it — the worldwide system's or one balloon's?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The goal calls for emphasis on coordination across many stations; a close-up of a lone balloon's drift narrows the lens instead of widening it. Look again for the sentence that keeps the whole network in frame.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before settling, ask yourself: is this paragraph about all observing tools, or about one of them?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the paragraph's subject first: a strong closer deepens the topic already on the table rather than introducing new equipment.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the closing sentence turns to satellites and radar, what happens to the paragraph's focus on balloon launches?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A conclusion should complete the paragraph's own topic — the coordinated balloon launches — not open a catalog of other instruments; adding new tools scatters the emphasis the goal asks for. Re-choose with the topic held steady.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What has the reader already met by the spot where you placed the new sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a reference check: a sentence explaining why a group matters needs that group named beforehand.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the paragraph opens with the new sentence, has the reader heard of either radar or the spotters it compares?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An explanatory sentence must follow the sentence that first names its subject; placed at the very top, this one refers to people and equipment not yet introduced. Find the earliest point where both have already appeared.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is the paragraph doing at the point you chose — issuing warnings, or telling residents how to shelter?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Trace the paragraph's timeline and ask whether the new sentence continues the step where you dropped it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a note about what radar cannot see belong in the middle of safety instructions to residents?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A supporting sentence should sit beside the idea it supports; wedged into the sheltering step, this comment about spotters and radar breaks the warning-to-action sequence. Re-place it next to the material it actually explains.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the paragraph's last step — what stage of the storm does it describe?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try a timeline check: the paragraph moves from detection to warning to shelter to survey, so ask which stage the new sentence belongs to.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Spotters help while the storm is being detected. Is anything still being detected once survey teams are examining damage?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: New material goes where its idea is in play, not at the end by default; this sentence supports the detection stage, which is long over by the damage survey. Move it back to where spotters and radar are being weighed against each other.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What topic is the second sentence still working on?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try topic tracking: label each sentence 'old subject' or 'new subject' before choosing where to cut.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Almanacs bundling folk signs — is that the start of a new discussion or more of the first one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A paragraph break belongs where the subject changes, and the almanac material is still folklore prediction; cutting there strands the first topic across two paragraphs. Re-scan for the sentence that introduces a different kind of forecaster entirely.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the third sentence feel like a fresh start to you?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Ask what each sentence is about, not how it feels: a verdict on the old topic still belongs to the old topic.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When the paragraph says those predictions failed the test of records, which predictions is it judging?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Evaluating the almanacs' accuracy continues the folklore discussion rather than opening a new one; a shift in tone is not a shift in subject. Look instead for where a brand-new source of forecasts first appears.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try reading the fourth sentence on its own — what does its opening phrase lean on?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the transition first: a backward-pointing opener ties a sentence to what came before it, which matters when you are placing a break.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Even so' concedes something just stated. Can a paragraph comfortably begin by conceding a point its reader has not yet seen?

rows.subject: act-english
