rows.body_md: A new paragraph should stand on its own opening, but this sentence's first words reach back to the failed predictions before it, chaining it to the folklore discussion. Choose the sentence that starts the new subject with no backward tie.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try lifting the phrase about storm seasons out of the sentence — what punctuation is left behind?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do an interrupter check: count the marks fencing the aside and ask whether the fence is complete.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If a comma opens the aside, what should the reader meet where the aside ends?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An aside that can be lifted out needs punctuation at both its entrance and its exit, and the original marks only the entrance. Re-count the commas around the phrase in each version.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud without any pauses — does 'meteorologist a veteran' sound like one continuous title?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the drop test: if a phrase can vanish and leave a complete sentence, it needs to be set off, not welded on.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'a veteran of twenty storm seasons' essential to knowing which meteorologist, or is it bonus information about her?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Renaming phrases that add droppable detail must be fenced off from the main clause; running them straight into the noun blurs where the sentence's core resumes. Re-choose with the fence complete on each side.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where does the aside about her experience begin, and where does it end?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Apply a symmetry check: whatever punctuation closes an interrupter should have a matching mark where it opened.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Your pick closes the aside but never opens it — how will a reader know where the extra detail started?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Interrupting phrases take matching punctuation at both ends; a closing comma with no opening partner fences only half the aside. Re-select the version whose marks pair up.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Cover the punctuation mark and read each half of the sentence by itself — what do you notice?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a clause test: decide whether each side could stand alone as a sentence before judging the mark between them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Both halves have their own subject and verb. Is a comma by itself strong enough to hold two stand-alone statements together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone — that produces a splice; the joint needs either a full boundary mark or a connecting word added. Re-test each version against that rule.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job is each connector in your pick doing at the joint?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the joiners: between two clauses you need exactly enough glue, not glue twice over.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the mark already joins the clauses on its own, what work is left for the added word to do?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: One joint needs one connector: the mark you kept can link the clauses by itself, so stacking a conjunction after it over-punctuates the seam. Re-choose the version with a single, sufficient joiner.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence straight through without stopping — where does your voice want a boundary?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try a boundary check: find where the first complete statement ends and ask what, if anything, marks that spot.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Buoys record wave heights every hour the readings reach forecasters' — can two full statements share a sentence with nothing between them?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Independent clauses must be separated by real punctuation or joined by a conjunction; butting them together with nothing at the seam fuses two sentences into a run-on. Re-examine which versions actually mark the boundary.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the clause were dropped, would 'valleys' still mean the same valleys?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try a meaning test: setting a clause off with punctuation tells the reader it is skippable extra detail, so check whether this clause is skippable.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Are advisories issued for every valley, or only for the ones this clause singles out?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A clause that identifies which nouns you mean is essential and takes no punctuation around it; fencing it off turns 'only the cold-trapping valleys' into 'all valleys, by the way.' Re-read each version for what it claims about the advisories.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which noun is doing the trapping in this clause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run an agreement check: a describing clause borrows its number from the noun it points back to.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The word starting the clause stands in for 'valleys.' Should its verb be singular or plural?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The clause's verb must agree with 'valleys,' the plural noun it describes, so a singular verb breaks the match no matter how close 'air' sits. Trace the clause back to its noun and re-decide.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say the sentence aloud — did the pause you hear come from grammar or just from breath?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the punctuation pairing: certain clause-openers simply never take a comma in front of them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can you think of a well-edited sentence that places a comma immediately before this kind of identifying clause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Restrictive clauses beginning with this word attach directly to their noun; inserting a comma before it is never standard, whatever the spoken rhythm suggests. Eliminate on that rule and re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What did the stem ask this verb to accomplish beyond being correct?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Remember the goal check: on this kind of question, a perfectly grammatical original can still lose to a livelier verb.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Close your eyes and picture something that 'moved.' How fast was it going, and how hard could it hit?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When a stem names qualities like speed and force, the winning verb must carry them itself; the original verb is accurate but blank, showing motion with no pace or power. Re-judge every candidate against the stated goal, not against correctness.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What extra shading does your verb add that the original lacked?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try a vividness test: swap each candidate into the sentence and rate how much energy the picture gains.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Something can travel slowly and gently. Does that word by itself prove the storm was fast or fierce?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The goal requires a verb that itself displays speed and force; a neutral verb of motion leaves both qualities to the reader's imagination. Re-compare the candidates for the one that does that work alone.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When you picture your chosen verb, is the dust wall actually going anywhere?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a motion check: the sentence describes something crossing fields, so test whether each verb keeps that movement alive.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a wall of dust threaten a town in this sentence if the verb only says it became visible?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb meaning 'came into view' erases the advance the goal wants dramatized; without motion there can be no speed and no force. Re-select the verb that keeps the storm pressing forward.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does your verb tell the reader whose case this admission hurts?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a nuance audit: list what the goal demands — honesty, acknowledgment, damage to her own forecast — and score your verb on each.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: One can make a proud statement or a neutral one to a crowd. Does a verb of public declaration say anything about giving ground?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The goal needs a verb implying she yielded a point that worked against her; a verb of neutral public statement reports the news without any surrender in it. Re-test each candidate against the full goal, not the tone alone.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the quietest verb on the list feel like the safest fit?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try the subtraction test: remove your verb's meaning from the goal statement and see which requirements go unmet.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Someone can jot down an observation that costs them nothing. Where in your verb is the sense that this point stung her own case?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb of mere recording treats the model divergence as a neutral fact, but the goal requires an admission that undercuts her forecast — the reluctance is the point. Re-read the goal and match every part of it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How much sorrow does the stated goal actually ask for?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for overshoot: a verb can fail a goal by adding emotion the writer never requested, not only by lacking it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is grieving over the model runs the same act as honestly admitting they weaken your case?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The goal calls for candid acknowledgment, not mourning; a verb soaked in sorrow distorts her professional posture and overshoots the brief. Re-weigh the candidates for exact fit rather than intensity.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: You and the writer agree the sentence belongs — now, what does the sentence actually do for the paragraph?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Audit the reason: on add-or-delete questions, a verdict is only half the job, so check the justification against the sentence word by word.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in the added sentence is there any explanation of storm-track behavior?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: On these questions the stated reason must accurately name the sentence's function, and this sentence gives a decision-maker's deadline, not a meteorological explanation. Keep your verdict, but find the reason that matches what the sentence truly does.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which earlier sentence did you have in mind as covering the same ground?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a repetition test: point to the exact prior sentence that already states the supposedly repeated idea — if you cannot, the charge fails.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do superintendents, closings, or early-morning deadlines appear anywhere else in the paragraph?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A sentence repeats only if its information already exists in the passage, and no earlier sentence mentions school decisions at all; a new application of an established idea is development, not repetition. Re-evaluate whether the addition earns its place.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: After the added sentence, what would the very next thing on the reader's mind still be?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the scope: distinguish a sentence that changes the subject from one that shows the subject's consequences.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the sentence argue about whether schools should close, or does it show who must act on razor-thin forecasts?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A new example of the paragraph's point extends the topic rather than abandoning it; the sentence uses school closings to dramatize forecasting's tiny margins, not to launch a policy argument. Reconsider what the paragraph would gain from that concrete stake.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Point to the words in the final sentence that mention the crew or their safety.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Ground the relevance in the text: a keep-reason must come from what a sentence says, not from what we can imagine it implies.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the sentence only describes reinforcement and bolted instruments, where does the survival explanation come from?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Keeping a sentence requires a reason grounded in its actual content and the paragraph's purpose; this reason supplies a safety story the sentence never tells, and the paragraph is about measurements, not endurance. Re-test each option against what is really on the page.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Suppose the detail really is unique — does uniqueness alone earn it a place here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Apply the purpose filter: a paragraph keeps details that advance its main job, not every detail that appears nowhere else.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The paragraph follows what the readings do for intensity estimates. Does a hardware inventory move that story forward?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Unique information still gets cut when it serves a different subject than the paragraph's; being the only sentence about equipment mounting proves the sentence is an outlier, not a necessity. Re-judge it against the paragraph's purpose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: You concluded the sentence should go — now test the why. What two statements are supposedly in conflict?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A contradiction charge needs both claims to clash head-on, so line them up and compare them literally.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a plane be reinforced and carry instruments while satellites still fail to supply eyewall measurements? Do those facts collide anywhere?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The verdict is only half the task: the justification must be true, and no statement in the final sentence denies the satellite claim. Keep the deletion instinct, but pick the reason that accurately names the sentence's real fault.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What span of time does the passage actually cover?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Treat these as two-part questions: even a correct yes fails if its description of the essay is wrong.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the passage mention radar's invention, or anything before the 1980s baseline it opens with?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The justification must describe the essay accurately, and this one claims a sweep of history the passage never attempts — it examines one upgrade and its aftermath. Keep the favorable verdict, but re-match it to what the essay really does.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Re-read the stated goal — how many advances does it ask the essay to cover?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Measure the essay against the goal as written, not against a bigger essay you might imagine.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the goal asks how one advance improved warnings, is concentrating on the tornado warning process a flaw or a fit?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An essay fulfills a narrow goal by being narrow; the goal requested one advance and its effect, and faulting the essay for tight focus judges it against a goal nobody stated. Re-compare the passage with the goal's actual terms.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What numbers, if any, does the final sentence put in front of the reader?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before accepting a claim that nothing was measured, hunt the passage for quantities — durations, counts, distances.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Lead times moving from near zero to beyond ten minutes — is that an unmeasured claim or a measured one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A reason asserting that no measurable improvement appears is contradicted by the closing sentence's before-and-after lead times, so the objection collapses on the page itself. Re-verify each option's claim against the text before choosing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the middle statement by itself, then stop. Are you left waiting for something?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch the opener: a word like this one promises a second half, so see whether the period arrives before that promise is kept.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Although the sirens are tested...' — although what? Where does the sentence deliver the contrast its first word sets up?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A clause that begins with a subordinating word cannot end at a period without a main clause attached; the opener leaves the thought dangling. Look for the version that completes a thought on its own.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is the main verb in the version you picked?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a verb audit: a stand-alone statement needs a fully conjugated verb, not just a verb-like word.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can 'the sirens being tested' carry a sentence the way 'the sirens are tested' can?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An -ing form without a helper cannot serve as a sentence's main verb, so this version stays a fragment even with its opener changed. Re-check each version for a subject matched with a finite verb.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What changed, structurally, between the original and the version you chose?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the swap: replace one subordinating opener with another and ask whether the clause gained any independence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'While the sirens are tested...' complete a thought any better than the original opener did?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Trading one subordinating word for another leaves the clause dependent and the fragment unfixed; independence comes from removing the leaning word or attaching a main clause. Re-inspect which version actually stands alone.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Cover everything after the comma — could what remains end with a period instead?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Screen for a splice: whenever a comma sits between two would-be sentences, the join needs more than the comma itself.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The forecast promised sunshine; the committee acted on it. What is showing the reader how those two facts connect?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two independent clauses need a period, a semicolon, or a comma teamed with a coordinating conjunction; a comma alone is a splice no matter how short the clauses are. Re-screen each version for a legal join.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What kind of word is your connector — and is it licensed to join clauses by itself?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sort your connectors: some linking words are true conjunctions, while others are adverbs that merely comment, and only one kind can hold two clauses together with a comma.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Beyond the grammar, does a contrast word even fit here — did the committee act against the forecast or in response to it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A conjunctive adverb set off by commas cannot fuse two independent clauses, and this one also reverses the sentence's cause-and-effect logic into opposition. Re-pick a join that is both legal and logical.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read your version aloud at full speed — where did one statement end and the next begin?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Keep the run-on radar on: taking away punctuation never joins clauses; it only removes the evidence of the seam.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Promised unbroken sunshine the picnic committee left...' — what tells a first-time reader that a brand-new clause has started?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Deleting the comma turns a splice into a fused sentence, trading one boundary error for another; a legitimate join must add connective machinery, not subtract marks. Re-evaluate which version supplies that machinery.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the comma feel strong enough to hold these two statements together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Separate flow from grammar: referring back to the previous idea creates cohesion, but cohesion is not a grammatical join.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Each side of the comma has its own subject and verb. What rank of punctuation does that situation demand?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: However tightly the second clause points back to the first, two independent clauses still require a full boundary or a conjunction; a comma alone splices them. Re-choose the version with a legal seam.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered the second half, would the first half feel finished?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Hunt for the seam: read until the first complete statement ends, then ask what marks that ending in your version.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Locates each strike within seconds this speed lets...' — where is the signal that one thought has closed and another has opened?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Butting two complete statements together with nothing between them creates a fused sentence; the boundary must be marked, not erased. Re-inspect the options for a real stopping point.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: After the full stop in your version, read only what follows it. Does it stand on its own?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Mind the subordinator: a word like the one you added makes its clause depend on a main clause, so confirm one is still there.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Because this speed lets crews reroute power...' — where is the payoff clause that this opener promises?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Adding a subordinating word after a period strands the entire second statement as a dependent fragment; a repaired boundary must leave two complete sentences, not one and a half. Re-test what follows the stop in each version.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who, in this sentence, is capable of hoping?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Track the modifier: an opening action phrase reaches for the first noun after its comma, so identify what it grabs here.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: As written, what is doing the hoping — the people or the field?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An introductory participial phrase attaches to the subject that immediately follows it, and here that subject is a cornfield, which cannot hope; the sentence must be rearranged so the actual doer follows the comma. Re-check the first noun after the opener in each version.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What changed between the original and your version — and did the change touch the actual problem?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the attachment: whatever noun follows the opening comma inherits the action, so inspect that noun in your pick.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can flattened rows hope any better than a flattened field can?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Rewording the subject phrase without changing who follows the modifier leaves the dangle intact; the fix requires placing the people who hoped directly after the opening phrase. Re-examine which version does that.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where did the action phrase land in your version, and what noun now sits closest to it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Apply the proximity principle: a describing phrase points at its nearest neighbor, so trace whom yours points at after the move.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Tucked between commas right after the field, does the hoping phrase describe the field or the people?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Relocating a modifier does not fix it unless it lands beside its true doer; wedged against the cornfield, the phrase still assigns hope to a field. Re-select the version where the hopeful party stands next to the phrase.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the noun in this phrase already tell you about when the action happens?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Scan for redundancy: test every modifier against the noun's built-in meaning before letting it stay.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If getting ready is by definition done before the event, what do the surrounding time phrases add?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A modifier earns its place only by adding information, and both time expressions here restate what the noun already means; saying it twice pads the sentence without sharpening it. Re-compare the versions for the one that says it once.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How is your version different in meaning from the original?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Beware the swap trap: replacing a redundant phrase with a synonym of that phrase changes the words, not the problem.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'beforehand' tell the reader anything that the idea of preparing had not already guaranteed?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Trading one duplicate time-stamp for another leaves the meaning doubled; the cure for redundancy is removal, not substitution. Re-check which version actually drops the repeated idea.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the time cues in your version — how many point to the same moment?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Question the padding: more phrases feel more specific, but test whether each adds a distinct fact.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'In advance' and 'ahead of the storm' — what different information does the second phrase contribute?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Stacking time phrases that all mean the same thing compounds the redundancy rather than adding precision; each retained word must carry unique content. Re-select the version where nothing repeats.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Translate the underlined portion into the fewest words that keep its meaning — what did you get?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Audit for wordiness: hunt for multi-word formulas that a single everyday word could replace.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does 'were of the opinion that' say that a one-word verb of believing does not?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Concision on this test means the shortest version that loses no meaning, and each formula phrase here compresses to a single word with nothing lost. Re-rank the options by that standard.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What drew you to that phrasing over the original — is it actually shorter?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare by the syllable: set the candidate versions side by side and measure what each adds or trims.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'owing to the fact that' any leaner than the phrase it replaces?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Substituting one inflated formula for an equally inflated one changes the flavor, not the fat; the sentence still carries phrases a single word could do alone. Re-measure the options for real trimming.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Break your version into pieces — which pieces overlap in meaning?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for a doubled cause: some connectors already contain the idea of a reason, so a reason-phrase after them repeats it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the connector itself means 'for the reason that,' what is 'of the reason that' still doing there?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A cause connector plus a redundant reason-phrase states causation twice while adding no content; lean writing states it once. Re-check which option carries the cause in a single clean word.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What new information does your added phrase contribute to the sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the filler test: delete the inserted phrase and re-read — if nothing factual disappears, the phrase was empty.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Was anyone doubting the matter before 'as a matter of fact' arrived to insist on it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Phrases that assert nothing beyond what the sentence already claims are padding, and this insertion survives the delete test with zero loss. Re-judge the options by which one carries only working words.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try reading your version aloud in one breath — where did the sentence's engine stall?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the machinery: tally how many words your version spends before reaching the actual condition about temperature.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does 'in the event that it so happens that' accomplish that a single short time word does not?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Elaborate scaffolding around a simple condition is empty verbiage, not precision; the leanest version states the condition in one plain word. Re-weigh the options for wasted motion.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does your inserted phrase hedge, exactly?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sound the stock-phrase alarm: familiar ready-made expressions often occupy space without adding a single fact, so test this one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do the thermometer readings stay above freezing 'for all intents and purposes,' or do they simply stay above freezing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A hedge that alters nothing about the claim is filler dressed as caution; the sentence is stronger stating its fact outright. Re-pick the version with zero deletable phrases in it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What kind of thing is 'accuracy' — can it feel pain?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the collocation: some verbs pair naturally only with living victims, so test your verb's usual partners.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: You can do this to a knee or an athlete — but to a measurement's quality?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Precision questions turn on pairing the verb with its object, and a bodily-harm verb cannot act on an abstract quality like accuracy. Re-test each verb against the noun it must govern.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Picture the literal image your verb creates — what is bleeding here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Separate vividness from fit: a dramatic verb still fails if its literal meaning cannot apply to the object.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a careful science editor let a forecast's correctness be described as if it had flesh?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The verb must suit an abstract quality, and this one is even more tightly bound to bodily injury than the original; drama does not repair the mismatch. Re-choose by the object's nature, not by intensity.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When accuracy gets worse, does it take up less room?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Name the dimension: ask whether your verb describes a change in size, a change in number, or a change in quality.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Budgets, glaciers, and audiences can do what your verb says. Is a forecast's correctness that kind of thing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Accuracy worsens or improves along a scale of quality, not a scale of physical size, so a verb of physical contraction misdescribes the change. Re-match the options to the kind of change the sentence reports.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who is speaking in this sentence, and in what kind of document?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the phrasing to the setting: an official annual summary sets a formal bar for every word.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a state office publish the phrase 'out of whack' in its formal findings?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Word choice must match the document's register, and a slang idiom clashes with an official climate summary however clear it feels in conversation. Re-screen the options for the one written at the report's level.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say your version aloud as if reading a government report on the radio — how does it land?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the formality: casual intensifiers that work in speech often sink below a report's register even when they are short.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'way off' the wording of a scientist's summary or of a hallway conversation?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A formal document requires measured phrasing throughout, and this casual intensifier belongs to spoken English; brevity alone does not raise its register. Re-choose with the document's audience in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which half of your phrase got fixed — and which half did not?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Audit the whole phrase: run every single word past the register bar, because one casual word can sink an otherwise formal option.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Different from' passes a formal test; does the adverb attached to it pass the same test?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Register must hold across the entire phrase, and a slangy adverb keeps this version conversational despite its standard core. Re-inspect each option word by word for the fully formal one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through the time frame of this sentence — when is everything happening?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Scan the sentence for time-stamp cues, then check whether the verb form you kept belongs to the era those cues establish.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a verb built on 'have' plus a participle, which links an action to the present, sit comfortably in a scene anchored to last June?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A 'have' + participle verb ties its action to the present moment, but every event here finished in the past, before the kiln hit cone ten — so this form clashes with the sentence's time frame. Look for the form that marks an action completed before another past event.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made this verb form feel right when you read the sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the past events in this sentence and decide whether they happened simultaneously or one before the other.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Did the eighteen hours of watching happen before the kiln reached cone ten, or at the very same moment?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When two past actions are sequenced, the earlier one needs a form that flags it as already finished; a bare past verb here makes the two events sound simultaneous. Re-choose with the earlier-past marker in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking anything else, tell me: is this sentence describing the future or the past?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Look at the helping verb you picked and ask which direction in time it points.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How can 'will' describe hours of work that ended last June?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Will have' projects completion at some future moment, but 'last June' locks this scene firmly in the past; the verb must mark work finished before another past event, not work still to come. Revisit the options with that time frame in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about the word this pronoun points back to — who exactly is signing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before matching a pronoun, check whether its antecedent counts as grammatically singular or plural.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'every apprentice' name one person at a time or a whole group acting together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Name the number test: 'every' forces a singular noun, so the stand-in word must stay singular too. A plural pronoun cannot replace that antecedent — go back and rematch the numbers.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — what job is that little word doing right where it sits?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This spelling has sound-alike cousins with different jobs; decide whether the sentence needs a place word or an ownership word.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can the word that means 'in that location' tell readers whose name is being signed?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: T-h-e-r-e points to a place; showing ownership of a noun like 'name' requires a possessive form. Rule out any spelling that cannot show possession, then choose again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What kind of noun is this pronoun standing in for — a person or a thing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the pronoun not just in number but in humanness; think about what 'its' normally refers to.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would you ever call an apprentice 'it'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Its' is reserved for objects, animals, and ideas; an apprentice is a person, so the sentence needs a possessive used for people. Reconsider which version keeps the pronoun human.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the sentence is working as a list here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Line the three listed actions up vertically in your head and compare their opening forms.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do the first, second, and third actions in your version all start the same way?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Items in a series must share one grammatical shape; your version switches shape mid-list, so the middle action breaks the pattern the other two establish. Re-check each version for a matched trio.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the first two actions, how does the last one read on its own?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A series is only as strong as its final link — compare the ending item of each version with the items before it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the third action wear the same form as the two before it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Every item in a list must repeat the structure the list opens with; here the closing action slips into an -ing form while the earlier ones do not, so the series is broken. Pick the version whose three actions match.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if you read only the first listed action together with the verb 'learning'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check where the series begins and make sure its opening item sets the same pattern the later items follow.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the first action match the shape of the second and third?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A parallel series cannot open in one form and finish in another; your version starts with an -ing action while the rest use a different shape. Revisit the options and select the consistent trio.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship do you see between how the two clays behave?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the connector by restating each sentence in your own words and asking whether the ideas point the same direction.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If one clay thrives in high heat and the other fails in it, are the two statements really alike?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A likeness connector requires the second statement to echo the first, but these sentences pull in opposite directions — one clay endures the heat the other cannot. Pick the connector that signals that opposition.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide that the second sentence illustrates the first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An example must be a specific case of the previous claim — check whether that is what the second sentence actually does.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is earthenware's failure an instance of stoneware's toughness, or something set against it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An illustration connector only works when sentence two gives a sample of sentence one's idea; here the second sentence pushes against the first instead. Choose the connector built for two things behaving in opposite ways.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before judging the connector, ask yourself: did the first sentence cause the second?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Cause-and-effect connectors need a genuine trigger; see whether stoneware's strength makes anything happen to earthenware.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does stoneware surviving the kiln in any way produce earthenware's slumping?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A consequence connector asserts that the first statement brings about the second, but these clays behave independently — the sentences set opposites side by side rather than linking cause to effect. Re-choose with that relationship in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your own words, what does the second sentence do to the first one's claim?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An example connector needs the second sentence to be a sample of the first; test whether locked notebooks are a sample of free sharing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a formula kept secret be an instance of recipes circulating freely?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The second sentence carves out an exception to the general habit described first, and an example connector cannot signal an exception. Look for the connector that concedes a surprise despite what came before.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made you read the second sentence as strengthening the first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An intensifying connector doubles down on the prior claim; check whether this sentence doubles down or pulls back.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do the guarded notebooks make the sharing culture sound even stronger, or do they limit it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'In fact' promises an even bolder restatement of the previous idea, but this sentence retreats from that idea by naming holdouts. The passage needs a connector built for an exception, not an escalation.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Take another look at the pair of sentences — does the first one cause the second?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before accepting a cause-effect connector, name the mechanism: what in sentence one would produce sentence two?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would recipes being shared freely logically force other recipes to stay secret?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A consequence connector requires the first statement to bring the second about, yet nothing about open sharing produces the holdouts' secrecy — the second sentence resists the first rather than resulting from it. Re-choose accordingly.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is this paragraph mostly about, sentence by sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An opening sentence should forecast the whole paragraph, not spotlight one small prop inside it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do the plaster slabs drive this paragraph, or do they appear only in passing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This opener elevates a piece of equipment mentioned once, so it cannot frame the full process the paragraph walks through, from soaking to reshelving. Pick the sentence that previews everything the paragraph covers.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the paragraph does your opening sentence actually set up?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the scope: a good first sentence should be no wider and no narrower than what follows it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the paragraph survey millennia of human history, or one studio's routine?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An opener spanning twenty thousand years promises a sweeping history the paragraph never delivers; this paragraph needs a first sentence scaled to a single studio's routine for reusing its clay.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in the paragraph is the idea from your opening sentence developed?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Trace each detail of the paragraph and see whether any of them connect to the topic your opener announces.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do the sentences that follow say anything at all about workshops?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An introduction must announce the subject the paragraph pursues, and nothing after this opener mentions classes of any kind. Choose the sentence whose promise the paragraph actually keeps.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is happening in the paragraph at the exact spot where you placed the new sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Notice that the paragraph runs on a clock from dawn to noon; test whether your placement breaks that clock.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a jump back twelve years fit between the crowd gathering and the door coming down?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Origin backstory belongs where the event is still being introduced in general terms, not in the middle of the morning's minute-by-minute action; placing it there halts the timeline. Re-examine where the paragraph is still setting the scene.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through the sequence of events right around your insertion point.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check what the reader is watching at that moment and whether a history lesson belongs mid-scene.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a memory of a small potluck fit between pots leaving the kiln and reaching the tables?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Dropping the event's origin between two linked actions severs them; background about how a tradition started should appear while the tradition itself is being introduced, before the play-by-play begins. Reconsider the earlier positions.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How does the paragraph feel when it ends with your placement?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A paragraph's final position carries its closing image; ask whether new backstory belongs after the story has wrapped.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Once every pot is claimed and the day is over, does the reader still need to be told how the event began?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Tacking origin history onto the end leaves the paragraph trailing off after its natural conclusion; background information should sit where the event is first presented. Look again at the paragraph's opening moves.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made you draw the line where you did — what changes at that point?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Find the sentence where the paragraph stops explaining a method and starts reporting an event; the break belongs exactly there.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the second paragraph opens with the artists' contributions, which earlier sentence introducing that show gets left behind with the technique?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Your split abandons the sentence that first announces the gallery event, leaving it attached to the how-to material; a paragraph break must fall at the first sentence of the new topic, not one sentence late. Re-scan for where the event is first mentioned.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the two halves your division creates — does each feel whole?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Group the sentences by subject first, then place the break between the groups rather than inside one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the sentence about a vessel rising tall a new topic, or the payoff of the stacking description before it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Splitting here cuts the craft explanation in half mid-thought; the break should fall where the paragraph pivots from describing the method to covering the show. Re-sort the sentences by topic and try again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which sentences in this paragraph are working together on a single idea?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A new paragraph should begin only where the subject genuinely turns; check whether your chosen sentence continues or abandons the opening idea.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the sentence about rolling ropes of clay start something new, or explain the technique just named?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This division orphans the opening definition from the explanation that depends on it; both belong to the same idea, so the break must come where the paragraph turns to a different subject entirely. Re-examine the later sentences.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the phrase about the vessel's flaws, what would be left of the sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Identify the sentence's core subject and verb, then decide whether the descriptive phrase between them is essential or an aside.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could a reader tell where the renaming of the teapot begins and ends without any signals?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A nonessential renaming phrase must be fenced off on both sides so the subject can reach its verb cleanly; with no punctuation at all, the description crashes into the sentence's spine. Re-choose with the full frame in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job is the phrase between the two commas in your version doing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check whether your punctuation keeps the whole description together or slices it into pieces.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'with a drippy spout' describe the teapot separately, or does it belong inside the renaming phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The entire description — vessel, flaws, and all — is one unit, and a comma dropped inside it splits the unit apart while leaving part of the aside unfenced. Look for the version that wraps the whole description as one package.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where does the interrupting description begin in your version, and how would a reader know?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Interruptions need signals at both their entrance and their exit; audit your version for each.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: You have marked where the aside ends — what tells the reader where it started?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A closing signal without an opening one leaves the reader unsure where the main sentence paused; a nonessential phrase set inside a sentence needs matching punctuation on both ends. Re-check each version for the pair.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read each half of this sentence on its own — could both stand alone?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When two stand-alone statements meet, a comma by itself is the weakest possible weld; test whether yours holds.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is a lone comma actually joining here — a phrase to a clause, or one complete statement to another?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two independent clauses cannot be fastened with only a comma; that is the classic splice. The junction needs either a full-strength stop or a comma reinforced by a joining word, so re-test each version at the seam.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made you want both a strong stop and a joining word at the same seam?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Each connector type can do this job alone; consider what happens when two are stacked together.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the punctuation already fully separates the clauses, what work is left for 'and'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A semicolon and a coordinating conjunction are two different welds for the same seam — using both together is redundant joining. Pick the version that fastens the clauses exactly once.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say the sentence aloud — where does your voice insist on a break?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the complete statements here, then check what is standing between them in your version.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With nothing at all between 'midnight' and the crew's celebration, how does a reader know one statement ended?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Running two independent clauses together with no punctuation fuses them into a blur; every clause boundary needs a signal strong enough to end a complete thought. Re-examine which version supplies one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What kind of clause sits between those two commas, and what word introduces it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check which relative pronouns are allowed to head a clause that is set off by commas — English is strict about this pairing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When extra information is fenced off from the main sentence, can 'that' be the word that opens the fence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'That' introduces only essential clauses, the kind that take no commas at all; a comma-marked aside needs a different relative pronoun to lead it. Re-check each version's pairing of pronoun and punctuation.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made you decide the mixing detail is essential to identifying the glaze?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try the cover-up test: read the sentence without the clause and ask whether the glaze is already fully identified.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Since 'signature' already tells us exactly whose glaze this is, does the mixing detail narrow it down further or just add background?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A clause that merely adds background to an already-identified noun is nonessential and must be marked off with punctuation on both sides; stripping the commas wrongly treats the detail as identifying. Run the cover-up test again before choosing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where does the aside about mixing begin and end in your version?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Interrupting clauses need boundary markers at both ends; audit your version for a matched set.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: You have shown the reader where the aside starts — what signals where it stops and the main statement resumes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An aside opened with a comma must also be closed with one so the subject can rejoin its verb; a lone marker leaves the interruption dangling. Re-inspect each version for a complete frame.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which words in the stated goal should steer your judgment here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Weigh each version for vividness: does yours let the reader actually see what happens to the pot?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'an unfortunate effect' show damage happening, or just report that something bad occurred?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The goal calls for wording that dramatizes how fast careful work can be destroyed; a vague label like this hides both the speed and the loss. Re-read each version and keep the one that makes the damage visible.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How serious is the mishap your version describes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the scale of the damage in your wording with the scale the goal asks you to convey.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a pot that is 'slightly less even' persuade anyone that hours of work can vanish in one pass?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The writer wants the mistake to feel devastating, and wording that shrinks the damage to a minor flaw works directly against that aim. Look for the version whose stakes match the goal's.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read your version aloud — does it sound like the rest of this passage?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the register: the surrounding prose is polished and precise, so measure your phrase against that standard.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would 'big-time' fit comfortably in a formal essay about craft?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Slangy phrasing clashes with the passage's measured tone even when it conveys energy; the goal must be met in language that matches the register. Re-evaluate the options with tone and goal together in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is the stated goal asking this verb to accomplish?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the verb you kept: does it carry any sense of muscle and strain, or is it neutral about effort?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could 'works with' describe someone labeling jars just as easily as someone hoisting twenty pounds of clay?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb that fits any task, light or heavy, cannot spotlight physical exertion; the goal needs an action word that makes the reader feel the strain. Re-test each verb against that requirement.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What aspect of Imani's work does your verb spotlight?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Separate artistry from effort — decide which of the two the goal explicitly asks you to emphasize.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'shapes' tell us the clay is heavy and hard-fought, or only that it is being formed skillfully?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The writer's goal is effort, not craftsmanship; a verb about forming emphasizes skill while staying silent about exertion. Choose the verb whose whole job is conveying labor.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If a friend asked what your verb adds to the sentence, what would you say?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Some verbs whisper difficulty and others shout it; rank the options by how strongly each conveys hard physical work.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'manages' put the reader inside the physical struggle, or merely note that Imani copes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb of quiet competence keeps the labor at arm's length, understating the bodily work the goal demands; the sentence needs the verb that turns the task into a visible struggle. Re-rank the options with that test.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Look closely at the proposed sentence — what information does it add?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A justification must match the sentence's content; check whether this sentence describes a making process or a result.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in a dollar total for the food pantry is anything about how bowls get made?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verdict is only as good as its reason: this sentence reports what the event achieved, not how members craft anything, so the justification attached here misdescribes it. Re-match each reason to what the sentence really says.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which earlier sentence do you believe already covers this ground?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Scan the paragraph line by line for a dollar figure or a named recipient before calling anything a repeat.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the four-thousand-dollar total stated anywhere else, or would this be its first appearance?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Nothing in the paragraph mentions the money raised or the pantry it supports, so the sentence cannot be repeating anything; a claim of repetition must point to an actual earlier statement. Reconsider whether the sentence adds something new.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is the subject of the proposed sentence, and what is the paragraph's subject?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before ruling the sentence off-topic, test whether its content grows out of the event being described or abandons it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Doesn't a total raised for the food pantry belong to the story of a dinner held to fight hunger?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A sentence shifts attention only when it introduces a different subject; this one reports the outcome of the very event the paragraph describes, extending the topic rather than leaving it. Re-judge the addition with that in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is this paragraph teaching the reader, sentence by sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Even a true fact must serve the paragraph around it; check what job this new fact would perform here.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does knowing about a Tuesday class help the reader follow how raised lines of slip are made?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The paragraph explains one studio technique from start to finish, and a fact about Nadia's teaching schedule performs no job in that explanation, however flattering it is. Weigh the addition against the paragraph's subject before deciding.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you connect the wheel class to what this paragraph is explaining?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Ask whether the paragraph is building a portrait of Nadia or a walkthrough of one method.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is a class about a different skill an example of slip trailing, or a departure from it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This paragraph is a step-by-step walkthrough of one surface-ornament method, not a resume of Nadia's talents; a sentence about an unrelated class interrupts the sequence instead of illustrating it. Reconsider whether the addition serves the walkthrough.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Your verdict and your reason are separate judgments — what does the reason you picked actually claim?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the justification: would this sentence, if added, make the how-to explanation longer, or change the subject entirely?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Since the proposed sentence never mentions slip at all, can the level of detail in the explanation be the real problem with adding it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The right ground for rejecting this sentence is not that the explanation is finished; it is that the sentence belongs to a different subject altogether. Match your justification to what the sentence actually fails to do.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in the passage do you see prices or costs discussed?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A justification has to be grounded in the text; hunt for any sentence comparing handmade work with factory goods.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If no sentence mentions cost, can cost be the reason the essay succeeds?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The passage never discusses pricing, so even a correct verdict fails when tied to this reason; the essay succeeds on different grounds. Reread what the passage actually spends its sentences doing, then re-pair verdict and reason.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Reread the stated goal — does it ask for a comparison of any kind?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the goal's scope to the essay's scope before demanding material the goal never requested.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can an essay fail for omitting other programs when the goal names only how one place trains its people?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The goal asks only for a description of how a particular workshop brings newcomers along, so comparisons elsewhere are extra, not required; an essay is judged against the goal it was given. Re-evaluate with the goal's exact wording in front of you.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What time span does the passage actually cover — a day, a season, or years?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the reason against the text: count how many phases of learning the passage walks through.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a passage that moves from a first season to a third and beyond really follow one person's single day?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The reason attached to this verdict misreads the passage, which surveys years of progressive learning rather than one person's day; a verdict built on a misreading cannot stand. Reread the passage's structure, then judge the goal again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Find the main verb of your version — which word is doing that job?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An -ing word cannot power a sentence by itself; check whether anything else here can serve as the main verb.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With 'hanging' in place, what complete statement is left once the opening clause ends?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An -ing form needs a helping verb before it can act as a predicate; without one, the main clause collapses into a fragment. Re-test each version by asking whether it can stand alone as a full statement.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does your version ever deliver a finished statement, or does it leave the reader waiting?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A to-form of a verb expresses purpose or intention, not an action actually happening; look for a true predicate.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: After the opening clause, who does what in 'the aprons to hang on numbered hooks'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An infinitive cannot serve as a sentence's main verb, so this version never completes its thought; the main clause must contain a subject paired with a working verb. Check each option for that pairing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What happens to the sentence's main action when 'that' steps in front of the verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Words like 'that' fold a verb into a description of the noun; see whether any verb remains for the sentence itself.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If 'that hang' only describes the aprons, what are the aprons actually doing in this sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A relative pronoun swallows the verb into a descriptive clause, leaving the sentence without a predicate of its own — a fragment in disguise. Re-choose by hunting for the version with a free-standing verb.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How many stand-alone statements does this sentence contain?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two independent clauses need more than a comma between them; inventory what your version places at the seam.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With the joining word gone, what is holding the two clauses together besides a pause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Removing the conjunction leaves two complete sentences fastened by a lone comma — a splice; a comma can join independent clauses only with a coordinating word beside it. Re-inspect what each version stations at the junction.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship does your connector claim exists between the jam and the switch?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two checks apply at this seam: the connector's logic and its punctuation power; run both.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Did the class switch to slab rollers in spite of the jam, or because of it — and can this connector legally follow a mere comma?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This connector signals contrast where the sentence needs consequence, and as a conjunctive adverb it cannot ride on a comma between independent clauses without splicing them. Re-run both the logic test and the punctuation test on every option.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Your connector's meaning fits the sentence — so what should you double-check next?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Conjunctive adverbs and coordinating conjunctions carry different punctuation requirements; identify which kind you chose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What punctuation must come before a word like 'consequently' when it links two complete clauses?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A conjunctive adverb after only a comma still splices the clauses, no matter how apt its meaning; that word would need a semicolon in front of it. Compare each option's connector with the punctuation it legally requires.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the comma feel strong enough for this spot?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check both sides of the comma for a subject-verb pair; two full clauses change the punctuation rules.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If each half could end with a period on its own, what does that tell you about a lone comma between them?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A comma alone cannot fasten two independent clauses; that junction demands a full stop, a semicolon, or a comma teamed with a conjunction. Audit each version's seam for legal strength.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where does the first complete thought end in your version, and how would a reader know?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With no punctuation at all, check whether the reader can tell where one statement stops and the next begins.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read 'before every use sediment settles' — doesn't that string briefly send the reader down the wrong path?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Fusing two independent clauses with nothing between them creates a run-on and even garbles the reading; every clause boundary needs a marker. Re-examine which versions actually supply one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What logical relationship does your subordinating word set up between stirring and settling?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Subordinators carry meaning as well as grammar; test whether yours states the reason for stirring or contradicts it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would we stir the buckets despite the settling, or precisely because it happens?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Although' concedes something that works against the main claim, yet the settling is exactly why stirring is required — the logic runs backward. Choose the version whose grammar and logic both hold.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who or what is balanced on the bat, according to the opening phrase's position?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An opening modifier grabs the first noun after the comma; identify which noun yours grabs.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a grown potter be the thing perched on a disk barely wider than a pot?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A modifier at the head of a sentence attaches to the very next noun, and here that noun is the person rather than the pot he carries; the sentence must be rebuilt so the description sits beside what it describes. Re-inspect each version's word order.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your version, which noun follows the opening phrase, and what does the phrase now claim about it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swapping in a new subject helps only if that subject is the thing being described; test the new pairing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the studio — an entire room — the thing balanced on a narrow bat?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Handing the subject slot to a different noun cures a dangler only when that noun is what the phrase describes, and a room cannot perch on a bat; the misattachment survives the rewrite. Re-check which version finally unites the description with its owner.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What did adding a word at the front change about who the phrase describes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Cosmetic additions can leave the underlying attachment untouched; re-run the who-does-the-phrase-point-to test.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With 'being' in place, isn't the sentence still claiming the potter is the one balanced on the bat?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Prefacing a dangling phrase with 'being' does not reassign it; it still latches onto the first noun after the comma, which remains the wrong one. Hunt for the version that physically moves the description beside the object it fits.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which idea in the underlined phrase appears more than once?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Break 'collaborate' into its parts — 'co-' plus 'labor' — and ask what the adverb beside it still contributes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If working jointly is already baked into the verb, what job is the extra word doing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Collaborate' means to work together by definition, so pairing it with 'together' says the same thing twice; a sentence should spend each idea only once. Recheck every version for doubled meaning.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How is your revision different in meaning from the original phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swapping one word for a synonym cures redundancy only if the doubled idea disappears; test whether it did.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Doesn't 'jointly' repeat the same togetherness that lives inside the verb itself?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Replacing one adverb with its synonym keeps the redundancy fully intact — the verb still carries the idea the adverb repeats. Hunt for the version that trusts the verb to say it once.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What problem were you solving by moving the adverb to a new spot?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Redundancy is about meaning, not word order; check whether relocating a word can remove a doubled idea.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'together' stop repeating the verb's built-in meaning just because it now comes first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Moving a redundant word does not erase the repetition; redundancy is fixed by cutting the doubled idea, not relocating it. Re-examine the options with meaning, not order, in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How many words in the underlined phrase are pulling real weight?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Look for a buried action: when a noun like 'decision' hides a verb, the sentence usually swells.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could the idea of 'made the decision to go forward with' live inside one stronger verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Noun-heavy phrases bury the action under padding; strong prose converts such phrases back into direct verbs and drops the filler around them. Re-rank the options by how much dead weight each carries.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which words did you cut, and which did you keep — and why those?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Half-trimmed wordiness is still wordiness; test every remaining word for a job.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'made the decision to' doing anything that a single verb wouldn't do?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This version prunes one limb of the padding but leaves the noun-built opener intact; true concision converts the whole buried action into a direct verb, not just its edges. Re-audit each option word by word.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where does the new length in your version come from?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A direct verb can still drown in trailing clauses; count the words between the verb and its object.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Once the co-op 'decided,' what does 'that they would go forward with' add to the meaning?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Starting with a strong verb helps only if the rest stays lean; this version re-inflates the sentence with a clause that adds no information. Choose the version in which every word does necessary work.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What information does the interrupting phrase contribute to the instruction?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the phrase by reading the sentence without it — track what meaning, if any, is lost.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'as a matter of fact' tell the reader anything about wax, drying, or glaze?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Filler expressions assert nothing and slow the sentence down; when omitting a phrase costs zero meaning, keeping it costs the reader time. Reconsider what this sentence actually needs between its commas — if anything.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How does your replacement differ from the phrase it replaces?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swapping filler for filler is a sideways move; test the new phrase for actual content.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would the reader lose if 'in point of fact' never appeared here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Exchanging one empty formula for another leaves the sentence carrying the same dead weight; the real question is whether any such phrase belongs here at all. Re-test each option by what it adds.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What work do you expect this phrase to do in an instruction about drying time?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Long idioms need to justify their length; check this one for information about the process.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'for all intents and purposes' even fit a rule that is absolute — the wax must dry completely?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This idiom hedges a statement that allows no hedging, and it adds length without adding facts; empty qualifiers weaken instructions. Ask what the sentence loses without any interrupter, then choose again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Picture the action: how much water does a fine mist actually deliver?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the verb's intensity to the details around it — 'fine mist' and 'just enough' set a scale.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a light spray truly drench a tile, or does that verb flood the image?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This verb describes thorough saturation, but the sentence describes the lightest possible wetting; a precise verb must match the degree the context sets. Re-weigh each option against 'fine mist' and 'just enough.'

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What exactly does your verb say is landing on the tiles?

rows.subject: act-english
