rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Ending on an upcoming project introduces unrelated material rather than reinforcing the paragraph's point about what the correspondence shows; a strong closer circles back to that revelation. Re-choose the sentence that does so.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in the paragraph does the reader first learn what the documents actually are?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The added sentence generalizes about 'each document' — check how many documents the reader has met at your insertion point.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Placed this early, can 'each' refer to anything the reader has actually seen yet?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A summarizing sentence about 'each document' requires the inventory to come first; at this spot the reader has not met a single item, so the generalization has nothing to gather. Re-place it where the list is complete.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide the reader had seen enough of the collection at that point?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the items introduced before your insertion point and compare that with a sentence that sums up every one of them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With only the airline ticket on the table, does a claim about every document ring true yet?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Summaries belong after the material they gather; only one item precedes this spot, so 'each document' overreaches. Move the sentence to where all the papers have been named.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about what the sentence you are placing is doing — introducing, continuing, or gathering up?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check whether any documents are still to come after your insertion point; a gathering sentence should not leave items outside it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the visa application is introduced later, does the summary placed here cover it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Placing the summary before the final item strands the visa application outside the generalization; the sentence must follow the complete inventory. Re-place it at the paragraph's true end.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which of the early sentences still belongs to the legend, in your reading?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Track the topic sentence by sentence and mark where the source of information switches.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the grandmother's memory of the poster part of the legend or part of the archival record?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The second sentence still elaborates the legend, so cutting there splits the legend material in half instead of separating legend from record; the break belongs where the documents take over. Re-locate the pivot.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking anything else, find the sentence that announces the shift — where does the paragraph signal a turn?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A new paragraph usually opens with the sentence that introduces the new focus, not with the first piece of supporting detail.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the remark about a 'less romantic story' belong with the legend before it or with the records it introduces?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The announcement that the documents tell a different story is the doorway into the second topic; starting one sentence later strands that doorway in the legend paragraph. Begin the split at the announcing sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through what the fourth and fifth sentences have in common.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Group the sentences by what they describe — the tale or the paperwork — and place the break at the boundary between groups.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the labor contract is introduced earlier, can a paragraph sensibly begin midway through discussing it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Breaking here splits the contract discussion across two paragraphs and leaves the pivot sentence behind; the division must fall where legend ends and documentation begins. Re-place the break at that turn.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the phrase about the cedar box, would the sentence still stand on its own?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Identify the phrase's job: is it renaming the trunk, and how does punctuation usually signal a renamer?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How is a reader supposed to see where the renaming phrase begins and ends with nothing marking it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A nonessential appositive must be set off by punctuation on both sides; with no punctuation at all, the renaming phrase crashes into the main clause. Re-choose the version that marks both its start and its finish.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made a single comma feel sufficient for this phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Interrupters work like parentheses — check whether your version closes what it opens.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If a comma opens the aside, what tells the reader the aside has ended before 'still anchors'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Paired punctuation is required around a mid-sentence appositive; opening it without closing it leaves the aside leaking into the verb. Re-choose the version with both boundaries marked.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — where does your voice drop into the aside, and does the punctuation match that spot?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the front edge of the interrupting phrase, not just its back edge.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With no mark after 'trunk,' how does the reader know the description has started?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An appositive needs a boundary at its beginning as well as its end; marking only the close makes 'trunk a battered cedar box' read as one run-together noun pile. Re-choose the version fenced on both sides.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What sits on each side of that comma — could each half stand alone as a full sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the two-sentence test: read each half separately and check for a subject and a verb in both.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a comma by itself hold two complete sentences together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone — that is a comma splice; the join needs stronger punctuation or a conjunction. Re-choose a version with a legal connector between the clauses.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job is 'then' doing in the version you picked — is it a glue word or just a time word?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test whether an adverb has the grammatical power to join two complete sentences across a comma.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With 'then' added, are there still two full sentences sitting on either side of a bare comma?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Adverbs like 'then' add timing but no grammatical connection, so the comma splice remains; joining independent clauses requires terminal punctuation or a conjunction. Re-choose accordingly.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide that the coat purchase was caused by the twelve dollars?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check what a subordinating word does to the clause that follows it — can that clause still stand alone?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'because' make the second half a complete sentence or a dependent fragment, and what does the punctuation before it require?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The punctuation used here must have an independent clause on each side; 'because' demotes the second clause to a fragment and asserts a cause the sentence never claims. Re-choose the version with two free-standing clauses.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job is the clause about Naples doing for the noun it follows?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the essential-information test: drop the clause and ask whether the reader can still tell which item is meant.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the strongbox holds many papers, can the identifying clause be treated as a removable aside?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Commas around a clause mark it as removable extra information, but this clause is what singles out the notebook among the papers, so fencing it off strips the sentence of its identifier. Re-choose with the clause's essential role in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — what happens between the clause and the verb 'is'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check what that lone comma is separating; a subject should reach its verb without a barrier.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a comma belong after an identifying clause when nothing opened a pause before it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A restrictive clause takes no commas at all; inserting one only at its close cuts the subject off from its verb. Re-choose the version whose punctuation matches the clause's essential role.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before anything else, look at the word that opens the clause — which relative pronoun is it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Recall the pairing rules: one relative pronoun introduces essential clauses, and a different one takes the paired commas.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can 'that' ever head a clause set off as a removable aside?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The pronoun 'that' introduces only essential clauses and never takes commas around its clause; pairing it with commas mixes the two systems. Re-choose the version where pronoun and punctuation agree.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What feeling does the stem ask this verb to carry?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the original verb against the stated goal: does it show any emotion at all, or just motion?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a reader sense the grandmother's reluctance from a plain verb of motion?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The goal is to convey hesitation, and a neutral verb of motion reports movement without any reluctance; the original wording leaves the feeling unexpressed. Re-choose the verb that dramatizes her uncertainty.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about the mood you think this verb creates.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Picture the pace and posture the verb implies, then compare that picture with the stem's stated goal.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a leisurely, relaxed gait match a woman uncertain about the crowd below?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This verb paints an unhurried, carefree walk, the opposite of hesitation; the stem calls for reluctance, not ease. Re-choose the verb whose connotation matches her uncertainty.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide what emotion the grandmother feels on the gangway?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the direction of the feeling your verb implies — toward eagerness or away from it — against the goal in the stem.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would someone hesitant to meet a crowd of strangers rush toward it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb of speed signals eagerness or urgency, while the stem asks for hesitation; the connotation points the wrong way. Re-choose the verb that slows her down.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through what the cousin starts with — a finished map or scattered fragments?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the verb's built-in picture to the stem's goal about piece-by-piece effort.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does following a route that already exists demand the same labor as assembling one from scraps?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb meaning to follow an existing path implies the route is already known, which erases the painstaking assembly the stem asks you to emphasize. Re-compare the verbs against that goal.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What role do the manifests, census sheets, and ledger play in the cousin's work?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check whether your verb honors the sources listed in the sentence, or floats free of them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the route were merely dreamed up, why would the writer catalog three documents?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb of pure invention discards the documentary labor the sentence showcases; the goal is effortful work grounded in sources, not fantasy. Re-choose with the documents in view.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before comparing options, ask: is the route sitting there waiting to be written down?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Weigh how much effort your verb implies — copying something known, or piecing together something lost.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can you simply write down a route that survives only in scattered fragments?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb meaning to write down implies the information is already complete, which flattens the painstaking, bit-by-bit labor the stem highlights. Re-choose the verb that conveys that effort.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the proposed sentence actually talk about — the factory or the classroom?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Adding is only half the decision; test whether the stated justification matches what the new sentence does.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does staying late to practice conversation explain anything about why cannery shifts ran twelve hours?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A sentence should be added only for a reason it actually fulfills; this justification points at the factory's schedule, which the proposed sentence never touches. Re-choose the reasoning that matches what the sentence contributes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the proposed sentence with the notebook detail — do they report the same fact?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Repetition means the same information restated; list what each sentence tells you and look for overlap.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is practicing conversation after class the same fact as columns of copied vocabulary?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The notebook shows written drill while the proposed sentence shows spoken practice — a new fact, not a restatement — so the repetition claim fails. Re-weigh whether the addition strengthens the paragraph's focus.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who stays at the center of the proposed sentence — the teacher or the grandfather?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the sentence's grammatical subject and what he is doing before deciding whose story it tells.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does one mention of a volunteer teacher pull the spotlight away from the man staying late to practice?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The proposed sentence keeps the grandfather as its subject and shows his persistence; the teacher is background, so the focus-shift objection misreads it. Re-decide whether the sentence supports the paragraph's portrait of him.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your own words, what is the paragraph's last sentence able to claim because of the account book?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before cutting a sentence, trace what the closing observation would rest on without it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If only the census spoke, would the paragraph still show that the form missed anything?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The account book is the second voice that exposes what the census left out; removing it leaves the closing claim about the form's blind spots unsupported. Re-consider what the paragraph loses without that sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the sewing income feel off-topic to you?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Relevance is earned by connection — test how the account book relates to what the enumerator wrote down.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Doesn't the paragraph need her earnings on record to show that the census called her occupation 'none'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The earnings are the paragraph's counter-record: they clash directly with the census entry and set up the closing observation, so they are central rather than stray. Re-judge the sentence's role before removing it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which word in this justification goes beyond what the account book can show?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Keeping a sentence for an overstated reason is still an error — measure the claim against what the passage says.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does income from sewing show that the enumerator lied on purpose, or only that the form asked too little?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The passage blames the census's narrow forms, not a dishonest clerk; a justification alleging deliberate falsehood overreaches, even though keeping the sentence is right. Re-choose the reason that matches what the paragraph actually argues.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Restate the supposed goal in your own words before judging the essay against it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Distinguish narrating an event from explaining a process — which one does the essay deliver?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a scene of a pressed dress and a photograph teach a reader the legal steps to citizenship?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Describing the day a goal was reached is not the same as laying out the steps required to reach it; the essay gives scenes, not a how-to, so it cannot serve as a step-by-step account. Re-match the essay's content to the stated goal.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How much of the supposed goal does one detail actually cover?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A goal about a whole process needs the whole sequence — count how many legal steps the essay walks through.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Beyond the oath, where are the forms, the residency rules, the examinations?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: One requirement glimpsed in passing cannot carry a goal that demands the full sequence of legal steps; the essay never explains the rest. Re-evaluate whether the essay as a whole fits the goal.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test this description against the passage — what actually gets the most attention?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A justification must describe the essay accurately; reread and track who or what each sentence follows.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the building the essay's subject, or is the grandmother in every scene?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The essay follows the grandmother — her dress, her oath, her keepsakes — so a reason claiming the courthouse dominates misdescribes the passage even though its verdict is right. Re-choose the reason that describes the essay accurately.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the second word group aloud as if it stood alone — does it feel finished?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the complete-thought test on what follows the period: subject, verb, and no dangling subordinator.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a word group opening with 'Because' stand as its own sentence when nothing completes it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A subordinating word makes its clause dependent, so punctuating it as a separate sentence strands a fragment; the clause must attach to the statement it explains. Re-choose the version that connects the two.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is the verb in the second word group of the version you picked?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check whether an -ing form by itself can power a sentence, or whether it needs a helper.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who believes, and where is the finished verb that says so?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An -ing form without a helping verb cannot serve as a sentence's main verb, so the second word group is still a fragment; the thought needs to join the main clause. Re-choose the version that attaches it grammatically.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the punctuation mark you chose demand from each side of it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test both halves around the semicolon for independence — each must stand alone as a sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Once 'because' opens the second half, can that half still pass the stand-alone test?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A semicolon requires an independent clause on each side, but a clause led by a subordinator is dependent; the join fails on its right side. Re-choose the version that links the dependent clause correctly.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the complete thoughts in this sentence — how many subject-verb pairs could stand alone?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the strength of the mark between the two halves against what each half is.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is a lone comma strong enough to hold two full sentences together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma form a comma splice; the seam needs a conjunction alongside the comma or stronger punctuation. Re-choose a version with a legal connection.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What kind of word is 'then' — a connector with gluing power, or a time marker?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Remove 'then' mentally and see whether the underlying join has changed at all.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With 'then' added, what is actually holding the two complete statements together besides a comma?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Time adverbs cannot join clauses; the comma splice survives with 'then' riding on it. A true conjunction or a full stop is required — re-choose accordingly.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read your version's second sentence by itself, starting from its first word.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test what a subordinating opener does to a clause's ability to stand alone.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the half beginning with 'Because' finish its thought, or does it lean on something no longer attached?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Splitting with a period here strands a subordinate clause as a fragment, and it also asserts a cause-effect link the sentence never claims. Re-choose the version that joins two whole clauses legally.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where does the first complete thought end in this sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Find the two subject-verb cores and look at what stands between them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What punctuation, if any, separates the reading room's closing from the photographing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two independent clauses placed side by side with nothing between them form a fused sentence; a boundary mark or conjunction is required at the seam. Re-choose a version that marks that seam legally.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: You added a pause at the seam — is a pause the same as a boundary?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Rank the marks by strength and ask which ones may stand alone between two complete sentences.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a comma with no conjunction legally join the two full statements here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A comma alone between independent clauses creates a splice, trading one boundary error for another; the seam needs terminal punctuation or a conjunction with the comma. Re-choose the version with a legal boundary.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What part of speech is 'however,' and what powers does it have at a clause boundary?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test whether the word you added changed the punctuation problem or only the logic between the clauses.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Even with 'however' in place, what single mark is still carrying two complete sentences?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Conjunctive adverbs cannot glue clauses; with only a comma at the seam the splice remains, and the contrast it signals is not the sentences' actual relationship anyway. Re-choose a version whose boundary mark can do the job.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who or what, exactly, is yellowed and brittle in the version as written?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Find the noun that sits right after the opening description — that is who the description attaches to.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the mother the faded, fragile thing, or is it what she is holding?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An opening modifier grabs the first noun after the comma, so as written it calls the mother yellowed and brittle; the description must sit next to the paper it belongs to. Re-choose the version that puts describer and described together.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What did the added adverb fix about who the opening phrase describes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Ignore the adverb and re-run the attachment test on the noun after the comma.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does describing how she unfolded it change what 'yellowed and brittle' points to?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Inserting an adverb polishes the verb but leaves the opening description still attached to the person, not the paper; the misattachment survives untouched. Re-choose the version that moves the description next to what it describes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In this version, what noun follows the opening description — and can that noun be yellowed and brittle?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swapping in a body part still leaves something human wearing the description; test the fit.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Are the hands the aged, fragile objects, or is it the paper they hold?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Shifting the modifier onto the hands only relocates the error — the description still lands on the person's body instead of the aged document. Re-choose the version where the paper itself is described.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the second verb in your pair add that the first has not already said?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the delete test: strike one of the paired verbs and see whether any meaning disappears.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is accumulating money over three winters different in any way from saving it over three winters?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Paired verbs with one meaning say it twice, and the timeframe already conveys the slow gathering, so the doubling adds nothing. Re-choose the version that says it once.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What information does 'gradually' carry that the rest of the sentence lacks?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the phrase 'over three winters' — what pace does it already establish?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can saving across three winters happen any way other than gradually?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A modifier that repeats what a nearby phrase already guarantees is redundant; the three-winter span makes the slowness explicit, so the adverb duplicates it. Re-choose the version without the doubled idea.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare 'saved' with the longer verb phrase — what changed in meaning?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test each added word for a job; words without jobs are padding.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If he saved the sum, is there any doubt he was able to?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Wrapping a verb in an ability phrase adds no information once the action is stated as done; the extra words are filler. Re-choose the version that states the action directly.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What verb is doing the real work in the underlined phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try turning the noun in the phrase back into a single action verb and compare the two versions.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'made an ... of' add any meaning that the buried action word does not already carry?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Stretching one action into a verb-plus-noun package pads the sentence without adding meaning; a single strong verb does the same work. Re-choose the tightest expression of the action.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What drew you to the more formal-sounding verb here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Fancier wording and tighter wording are different things — count the words each version needs for the same fact.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'conducted an ... of' say anything that one direct verb would not?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swapping in a stately verb keeps the same padded noun construction; the sentence still takes four words to do one word's job. Re-choose the version that trims the construction itself.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say the full sentence with your version — does the idiom sound like standard written English?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check both economy and idiom: the phrase must be natural as well as brief.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do officials 'give an inspection to' luggage, or does another construction handle this action?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This wording is both unidiomatic and padded — the action hides inside a noun while the verb contributes nothing. Re-choose the version that expresses the action in its plain verb form.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which words in the underlined portion contribute facts to the sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Apply the strike-through test to the opening phrase and see whether the sentence loses anything.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does announcing that something is interesting make it interesting, or just delay it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Openers that merely announce interest are filler — they add no information and slow the sentence; the detail should start immediately. Re-choose the version with the empty phrase removed.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What did the replacement phrase fix about the original problem?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the new opener the same way you would test the old one: does it carry any content?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is there a disputed claim here that 'as a matter of fact' needs to push back on?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Trading one contentless opener for another leaves the padding in place; the phrase asserts nothing the sentence needs. Re-choose the version that simply begins with the fact.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who is doing the noting in your version, and does the reader need to be told to note?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Weigh the opener for content: is it an instruction to the reader, or information about the family?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the sentence works without the announcement, what is the announcement for?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An impersonal announcement that something should be noted is academic filler; the sentence delivers its detail faster without any throat-clearing. Re-choose the opening that gets straight to the detail.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How much certainty can a five-word register entry actually deliver?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the verb's strength to the strength of the evidence in the passage.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could the two brothers have left separately in the same spring, for all the entry shows?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A claim of proof requires evidence that rules out every alternative; a terse register line cannot do that, so the verb overstates the case. Re-choose a verb whose certainty matches the source.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What earlier belief would this entry be verifying, according to the passage?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the verb's built-in assumption — it implies something was already established and awaited support.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in the sentence is the prior claim that the register line could back up?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb of confirmation presupposes an existing claim being verified, but the passage presents the line as the only source; the verb both overstates certainty and invents a backstory. Re-choose a verb that fits a lone, terse clue.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Look at the quoted entry itself — does it state outright that the brothers traveled as a pair?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Separate what the line says from what a reader infers; your verb must match the saying, not the inferring.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a source mention a fact it never explicitly states?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A source mentions only what it actually states; the entry never says the brothers left together — that idea is an inference — so the verb misdescribes the evidence. Re-choose the verb that signals inference rather than statement.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Whose voice is this sentence written in — a newsletter's or a hallway conversation's?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the underlined phrase's register with the words around it, like 'praised,' 'curators,' and 'collections.'

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a historical society's publication call the documents 'a bunch'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The passage speaks in a formal register, and casual phrasing like this clashes with it; the diction must match the newsletter's professional tone. Re-choose the version written at that level.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What impression does your phrase give about how the curators worked?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check both tone and connotation: the verb should respect the passage's formal voice and the curators' effort.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does scraping things up sound like careful curation or like a last-minute scramble?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This phrasing is even more slangy than the original and belittles the curators' work besides; the sentence needs standard, respectful diction. Re-choose the phrase that fits a professional publication.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read your version aloud — does it sound formal, or inflated?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Formal register means clear standard English, not the longest Latinate words available; test each word for plainness.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a careful editor keep 'effectuated the amalgamation,' or trim it as puffed-up?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Overcorrecting into pompous diction is as much a register error as slang; formal writing stays clear and natural. Re-choose the phrasing that is professional without being inflated.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through how you checked the verb in this sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: There's a helping verb sitting right before the main verb—run your irregular-verb check on that pair.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Irregular verbs use one form for the simple past and a different one after 'had.' Which of the two forms is this?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: After has, have, or had, a verb must take its past-participle form, not its simple past; the original pairs 'had' with a simple past form, so it cannot stand—pick the version with a true participle.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made this verb form sound right to you?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test whether this verb takes a regular '-ed' ending or changes its vowel instead—say its three forms out loud.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would you say a lake 'shrinked' last summer, or does this verb change internally rather than adding '-ed'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This verb is irregular: it never takes '-ed' in any form, so a manufactured '-ed' participle is not a real word; select the irregular participle instead.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking anything else, what time frame is this sentence describing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two things to verify here: whether the helper matches the timeline, and whether the main verb is in participle form.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The rangers found something already complete by the time they measured—does a present-tense helper fit an already-finished event, and is the verb after it a true participle?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A present-perfect helper misplaces an event already finished in the past, and this version still attaches a simple-past form to the helper; a past-perfect helper with a genuine participle is required, so re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which word in the sentence do you think this pronoun stands for?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Cross out the prepositional phrase after the opening word, then re-check what the pronoun refers to.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Each' is the word that owns the permit here—is 'Each' singular or plural once you set aside the phrase that follows it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Words like 'each,' 'either,' and 'neither' are singular no matter what plural noun follows in an 'of' phrase, so a plural pronoun clashes with the subject; select a singular pronoun that fits a person.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about who or what owns the permit in this sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: You've handled number—now check whether the pronoun's category matches the antecedent: person or thing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would you use this pronoun to refer to a human guide, or is it reserved for objects and animals?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A singular pronoun is right here, but the antecedent is a person, and this pronoun can refer only to things; re-choose a singular pronoun suited to people.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the rest of the sentence, who would 'one' point back to?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check for a pronoun shift: does this word keep referring to the same people the sentence already named?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The sentence talks about specific guides—does switching to the impersonal 'one' still point clearly at them, or does it introduce a brand-new generic person?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A pronoun must stay tied to the noun already in the sentence, and this impersonal form abandons the named guides for a generic stand-in; pick the singular, person-appropriate pronoun that stays tied to 'Each.'

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — what pattern do the first two activities set up?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This is a three-item list; compare the grammatical shape of each item against the first one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Clearing' and 'rebuilding' are matching verb forms—does the third item keep that shape, or does it restart with a new subject?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Parallelism requires every item in a series to share one form; inserting a subject pronoun turns the last item into a full clause that no longer matches, so select the version shaped like the first two items.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made you switch verb forms for the third item in this list?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Line up the three list items side by side and check whether their endings match.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The first two items end in '-ing'—can an infinitive sit as the third item without breaking that match?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A series must stay parallel from start to finish; an infinitive clashes with the two items before it, so the final item needs the same form as its partners.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What time relationship does 'having' plus a participle usually signal?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check two things at once: whether the form matches the other list items, and whether it changes when the action happens.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'having repainted' suggest the crew finished the blazes before the summer even started, and do the other two items carry any such time stamp?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Perfect participles mark an action completed before another one, which this sentence does not intend, and the form also breaks the series' pattern; re-pick the simple form matching the first two items.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship do you see between what visitors picture and what the park really is?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Summarize each sentence in a few words, then ask whether the second one echoes the first or pushes back against it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Similarly' promises the second idea resembles the first—does a mistaken swamp image resemble a corrected description, or collide with it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A similarity transition requires two ideas pointing the same direction; here the second sentence overturns the visitors' impression, so a corrective, contrast-flavored transition is needed instead.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide the second sentence follows from the first as a result?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the cause-effect test: could you honestly insert 'as a result' between these two sentences?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the park drain and refill *because* visitors picture it as a swamp, or is that picture simply mistaken?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Therefore' asserts causation, but the visitors' impression causes nothing about the park's hydrology; the sentences are related by correction, not consequence, so pick the transition that signals setting the record straight.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the transition, what would you call the job the second sentence does?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Apply the example test: an example must be a specific instance of the idea before it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is a floodplain forest an *instance* of the gloomy-swamp picture, or a replacement for it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'For example' works only when the second sentence illustrates the first claim; this one discards that claim and substitutes an accurate description, so select the transition that flags a correction.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Tell me how the road lottery connects to the animals' behavior.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before swapping transitions, test whether the second sentence opposes the first or flows from it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If barely any cars enter the park, would unafraid animals be a surprising contradiction of that, or a natural outcome of it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A contrast transition needs two ideas in tension, but few cars leading to unwary wildlife is cause and effect; the original connector already names that relationship, so reconsider whether any replacement is needed.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if the second sentence merely restated the first in different words?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Apply the restatement test: could sentence two be deleted with no loss because it repeats sentence one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'animals never learned to fear traffic' say the same thing as 'few cars win the lottery,' or does it report what that scarcity produced?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'In other words' fits only a rephrasing, and this sentence introduces a new downstream effect, not a paraphrase; the cause-and-result connector already in place is the logical one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What time relationship, if any, links these two sentences?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check whether the sentences describe two independent events running side by side or one event producing another.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Meanwhile' sets two unrelated scenes running in parallel—do fearless animals merely coincide with the car limit, or result from it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Simultaneity transitions strip out causation, and causation is precisely the link here: limited traffic explains the animals' calm, so keep the connector that expresses result.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What's the one idea every sentence in this paragraph serves?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check whether your closing sentence returns to the paragraph's core subject or opens a fresh attraction.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Fireflies are certainly in this park—but did the paragraph discuss tourist spectacles, or the people who maintain the place?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A concluding sentence must reinforce what the paragraph argued; a new detail about an insect display starts a different topic instead of sealing the point about who sustains the park, so re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking each option, how would you state this paragraph's main idea in one line?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch the zoom level: a conclusion should match the paragraph's scope, not the whole park system's history.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a claim about when parks were founded follow from sentences about volunteers, budgets, and donated hours?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Conclusions that leap to broad background information leave the paragraph's actual argument hanging; this paragraph is about volunteers offsetting a thin budget, so the closer must return to that idea.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about how a closing sentence should relate to the sentences before it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test for setup: has anything earlier in the paragraph prepared the reader for advice to hikers?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in the paragraph did weather or trip preparation come up, if anywhere?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A conclusion cannot introduce advice the paragraph never grounded; packing tips have no root in the volunteer-and-budget discussion, so pick the sentence that echoes that discussion.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try reading the paragraph straight through—where does the timeline jump?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Track the time cues: 'back then,' 'today,' 'at first.' Do they run in one direction as the paragraph stands?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the canyon is already peaceful in the previous sentence, does circling back to the initial protest keep events in order?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A phrase like 'at first' must come before the long-run outcome, not after it; leaving this sentence at the end rewinds the story, so move it to sit right after the event that sparked the protest.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the phrase 'the ban' in Sentence 5 point back to?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before placing the sentence, find where its referent is first introduced in the paragraph.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If readers hit 'the ban' immediately after learning only that shuttles are new, what ban would they think is meant?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A sentence cannot precede the noun it points to: the ban is not announced until later, so resistance to it must follow that announcement, not the opening sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which earlier sentence does Sentence 5 most directly react to?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match cause to reaction: the resistance is aimed at a specific decision—check whether that decision has appeared yet at this spot.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Right after the traffic description, has anyone actually banned anything for businesses to resist?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Reactions follow their triggers: at this position readers know about traffic jams but not yet about any vehicle ban, so the resistance sentence must wait until the ban itself has been stated.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the sentence numbers, where would you say the subject changes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Label each sentence's topic with a single word, then look for the first label that differs.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sentences 1 and 2 both describe how the cave formed—what happens to that pair if a paragraph break separates them?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A paragraph break belongs at a topic change, not inside a unified explanation; splitting the two formation sentences strands the opener, so find the sentence where the subject actually turns.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job is the word 'though' doing in this paragraph?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the sentence just before your break point—does it belong with the old topic or the new one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the paragraph breaks here, the sentence contrasting geology with bats stays attached to the geology—does it fit there?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The pivot sentence announces the new subject and must lead the new paragraph; breaking one sentence too late leaves that announcement stuck with the material it turns away from, so shift the break to the pivot.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide these last sentences belong to separate topics?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Group the sentences by subject first, then see whether your break separates two groups or cuts one group in half.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can the ranger-program sentence stand at the head of its own paragraph when the bat flight it describes sits in the previous one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Breaks must fall between topic blocks: the amphitheater detail depends on the bat exodus before it, so cutting between them severs one subject—place the break where the geology ends instead.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — can you hear where the descriptive phrase starts and stops?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Interrupters need punctuation on both sides; count the marks fencing this one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If a comma opens the phrase about Roosevelt's hobby, what closes it before the sentence's verb arrives?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Nonessential phrases require a matched pair of marks, and dropping the closing comma leaves the interrupter fused to the verb; restore the complete pair.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the sentence could you lift out and still have a complete statement?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the boundary where the name meets the description—is there a mark separating them?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Without an opening comma, does 'Theodore Roosevelt an avid outdoorsman' read as a name plus an aside, or as one garbled unit?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An appositive's fence must begin where the aside begins; a closing comma alone leaves the front gate open, so the phrase needs marks on both ends.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made you pair those two particular punctuation marks?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Look at the marks on each side of the interrupter—are they the same species?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If a dash opens the aside, what mark does the rule require at its other end?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Paired punctuation must match: dash with dash, comma with comma; a dash opening closed by a comma is a broken fence, so keep the pair uniform.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What's on each side of that comma—test both halves for a subject and a verb.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the two-sentence test: could each half stand alone with a capital letter and a period?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If both halves are complete sentences, is a comma by itself strong enough to hold them together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses—that's a splice; the joint needs a full-strength separator or a comma teamed with a conjunction, so re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try reading this version aloud without pausing—where do the two ideas collide?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the boundary between the temperature statement and the recommendation: what is marking it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When two complete sentences touch with nothing between them, what is that error called?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Removing all punctuation creates a fused sentence, which is even less acceptable than a splice; the boundary between two independent clauses needs a genuine separator, so pick one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide to use two connectors at that joint?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the joining devices in this version—how many are doing the same job?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A semicolon can join clauses by itself, and 'and' can join them with a comma—what happens when you deploy both at once?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Connectors do not stack: a semicolon replaces a conjunction rather than accompanying one, so strip the joint down to a single correct device.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you deleted the clause after 'system,' would readers still know which system is meant?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Classify the clause first—essential identifier or removable aside? The pronoun follows from that call.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The clause is doing identifying work with no commas around it—does the pronoun 'which' match an essential, uncommaed clause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Essential clauses take the plain identifying pronoun without commas, while 'which' belongs to comma-fenced asides; this version mismatches pronoun and clause type, so re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through what a single comma before a clause like this one signals.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two checks here: is the clause removable, and if you fence it, are both ends fenced?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the clause were a true aside, it would need commas at both ends and the sentence would still identify the system without it—does either condition hold?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Turning an essential clause into a half-fenced aside fails twice: the sentence needs the clause to say which system, and the lone comma never closes; keep the clause restrictive and unfenced.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who—or what—is doing the limiting in this sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the relative pronoun to its antecedent's category: person or thing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a pronoun reserved for people attach to 'the quota system'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Who' refers only to humans; a system requires a thing-pronoun, and since the clause identifies the system, it needs the restrictive thing-pronoun with no comma—re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What temperature does this phrase actually conjure for you?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the verb against the writer's stated goal: does it deliver *extreme* heat or something gentler?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would 'get warm' describe a July noon in the hottest place in North America, or a spring afternoon anywhere?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The stem demands intensity, and this phrasing communicates comfort rather than severity; go with the verb whose heat could genuinely punish.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What did the word 'steadily' add toward the writer's goal?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Separate pace from power: which one does the goal ask for?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does warming gradually make the heat sound fiercer, or merely slower?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An adverb of pace does not raise the temperature; the goal is severity, so pick the verb that conveys scorching force, not gradual mildness.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before comparing options, what single quality is the writer trying to amplify?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check whether your phrasing even mentions the quality the stem names.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where is the heat in 'sit in the sunshine'—does the image sound punishing or postcard-pleasant?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A version that drops temperature entirely cannot emphasize heat; return to the goal and select the verb that makes the flats sound dangerously hot.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about the level of attention 'looks over' suggests to you.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Grade the verb's intensity—skim, read, or examine: which does the goal require?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If a colleague 'looked over' your lab report, would you expect line-by-line checking or a thirty-second glance?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The goal specifies painstaking care, and this phrasal verb leans casual and quick; swap it for the verb whose definition centers on minute, critical examination.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if the biologist 'researches' the signals rather than reading them each dawn?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the verb's scope: does it name this one morning task, or an entire profession's activity?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can you 'research' a single night's collar data at dawn, or does that verb describe a months-long enterprise?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb covering a whole scholarly process is too broad for one careful daily reading; the goal needs a verb of close, detailed inspection of the data at hand.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How much effort does the verb 'notices' imply the biologist is spending?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sort the candidates into active versus passive attention—the goal tells you which pile to draw from.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do you *notice* something on purpose, painstakingly, or does noticing simply happen to you?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Passive awareness contradicts deliberate care: the writer wants effortful, detail-level examination, so pick the verb that makes the effort explicit.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What kind of work does the proposed sentence do—give a reason, or give another example?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Separate the verdict from the justification; both halves of the statement have to be accurate.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'even at fifty, most have yet to sprout their first arm' tell us *why* growth is slow, or *how slow* it is?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The sentence illustrates slowness with another age milestone; it never supplies a cause, so a justification claiming explanation misdescribes it—re-choose with the accurate reason.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the proposed sentence next to the two-inch claim—do they pull in the same direction?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test for contradiction: could both statements be true of the same cactus?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If a saguaro is two inches tall at ten and armless at fifty, is the second detail fighting the first or piling on more evidence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The two benchmarks reinforce each other—both dramatize slow growth—so rejecting the sentence as a contradiction misreads it; reconsider with the sentence's actual function in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is this paragraph about, in one word?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the topic claim inside the justification against the paragraph's actual subject.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where do desert animals appear in a paragraph about cactus growth rates?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A justification built on a topic the paragraph does not have cannot stand: the paragraph is about the saguaro itself, and the new sentence fits that topic, so re-decide on accurate grounds.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which earlier sentence do you think already covered this detail?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the repetition test: find the first mention, then the repeat—can you point to both?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the paragraph mention fishing tournaments anywhere before the italicized sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A deletion justified by repetition requires an actual earlier occurrence, and there is none—the sentence's true flaw is that it is a side trip from the paragraph's focus, so re-choose the reason that names that flaw.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the italicized sentence actually tell us about pythons?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the justification's claim against the sentence's content, word by word.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is bass fishing on weekends information about python biology, or about a contractor's spare time?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Keeping a sentence requires that it serve the paragraph, and this one describes a hobby, not snake science; the paragraph's job is tracking the removal effort, so reconsider whether the hobby belongs.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship do you see between weekend fishing and the 11,000-python figure?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the transition claim: a bridge sentence must connect the idea before it to the idea after it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does knowing a contractor fishes for bass prepare the reader in any way for the removal total?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A true transition links its neighbors logically, and this sentence links to neither the devastation before it nor the tally after it; a detail with no connective work is a detour, so re-evaluate keeping it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in the passage did you find the details this justification mentions?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Verify the reason against the text: a justification can be wrong even when its verdict points the right way.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can you quote a single activity a child completes, anywhere in the passage?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The passage traces decades of development but never enumerates activities, so a reason built on such a list fails even though its verdict is right; re-select the justification the text supports.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would an *evaluation* of the program look like, compared with what this passage does?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sort the passage's sentences: are they judging quality or narrating change across time?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where does the writer say whether the program works well or poorly?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Every sentence marks a stage in time—1930s, 1960s, 1990s, today—and none renders a judgment; a passage that narrates development satisfies a development-tracing goal, so re-decide the verdict.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How many distinct programs can you actually name in this passage?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Track the thread: do the clubs, booklets, and badge belong to separate initiatives, or to one initiative changing form?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When the 1990s standardization arrives, what earlier things is it standardizing—new programs, or earlier stages of the same one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The passage presents one continuous program passing through phases, not a catalog of unrelated ones; since a single program's growth is exactly the supposed goal, the verdict needs rethinking.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up everything after 'bison,' what does the herd actually *do* in this version?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the complete-sentence test: subject, tensed verb, full thought—does this version pass all three?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can an '-ing' word all by itself carry the tense a main verb needs?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A participle cannot anchor a sentence: 'bison grazing in the valley' is a picture, not a statement, so restore a verb that carries tense.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made you tuck the action inside a 'that' clause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check what remains outside the clause—does the leftover part still make a statement?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Hundreds of bison that graze in the valley'—where is the verb telling us what those bison do?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A relative clause only describes its noun; moving the sole verb into one leaves the main clause verbless and the sentence a fragment, so keep a tensed verb in the main clause.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try reading this version aloud—does it feel finished, or does it leave you waiting?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test whether the verb form can carry tense: past, present, or future.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Hundreds of bison to graze...'—is that a statement about what happens, or a plan with no verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Infinitives are tenseless and cannot serve as a sentence's main verb; without a tensed verb the line is a fragment, so return to a form that asserts the action.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What's holding the two halves of this sentence together in your version?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Both halves pass the stands-alone test—so check which joining devices are legal between two such clauses.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With the conjunction gone, what is a lone comma being asked to do between two complete sentences?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Deleting the conjunction creates a comma splice; a comma can join independent clauses only when a coordinating conjunction rides along, so reconsider what the original joint already had.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide this joint needed both of those marks?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Audit the connectors: a legal join uses exactly one strategy, not two stacked together.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If a semicolon can join the clauses alone, what work is left for 'and'—and vice versa?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Semicolon-plus-conjunction is a doubled weld treated as an error; one device must go, and the sentence as first written already used a single legal combination.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What part of speech is 'however,' and what punctuation does it demand?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Distinguish true conjunctions from conjunctive adverbs before choosing the surrounding marks.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Set between two commas, can 'however' legally join two independent clauses the way 'and' or 'but' can?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Conjunctive adverbs are not conjunctions: with only commas, 'however' leaves a splice that would need a semicolon before it; the original comma-plus-conjunction pairing was already legal, so re-examine it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Cover the first sentence and read only what follows the period—can it stand on its own?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Apply the stand-alone test to everything after the end-stop mark.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What idea does 'Which' point back to, and can it survive when a period walls it off from that idea?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A relative clause severed by a period becomes a fragment; it must stay attached to the clause it comments on, so pick punctuation that connects rather than terminates.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does a semicolon promise about the words on each side of it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check both sides for independence before allowing a semicolon.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is a clause opening with a relative pronoun a complete sentence, as a semicolon requires?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Semicolons join only two independent clauses; the trailing clause here is dependent, so the joint needs the lighter attaching mark, not a semicolon.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What kind of material do you expect after a colon?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the colon rule: the part before must be complete, and the part after should deliver a list, definition, or payoff—not lean backward.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a clause that reaches back to modify the whole first statement behave like the announcement a colon sets up?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Colons introduce forward-looking material; a backward-leaning relative clause is not that, so the dependent clause should be attached with the ordinary connecting mark instead.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who is doing the paddling in this sentence, as written?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Introductory '-ing' phrases attach to the first noun after the comma—identify that noun and test the match.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can loons paddle kayaks through island channels at dusk?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The opening phrase describes the paddlers, so the paddlers must be the first noun after the comma; as written, the birds inherit the paddling, which is absurd—re-choose the version that seats the right doer there.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made this rearrangement feel like it fixed the problem?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Re-run the modifier test on the new version: first noun after the comma, matched against the action in the opening phrase.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Even reworded, which creature still sits right after 'at dusk,'—and is it the one holding a paddle?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Shuffling the predicate does not cure a dangler while the wrong noun still follows the modifier; the paddlers themselves must come first after the comma, so look for the version that puts them there.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In this version, what exactly is paddling through the channels?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Strip the sentence to modifier plus first noun and ask if the pairing is possible.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can cries—sounds—paddle a kayak?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swapping in the birds' cries makes the mismatch worse, since a sound now owns the paddling; the fix is structural: the humans in the boats must immediately follow the opening phrase.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the prefix at the front of 'collaborates' already tell you?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check each word after the verb: does any of them restate something the verb has built in?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If 'collaborates' means 'labors together,' what new information does 'together' contribute?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A modifier that repeats meaning already inside the verb is redundant and must go; drop the duplicate and keep only what adds information.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made 'jointly' feel like an improvement over the original wording?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the built-in-meaning test on the adverb: is its idea already inside the verb it modifies?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is collaborating ever done un-jointly—alone?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swapping one redundant word for a fancier redundant word fixes nothing; the verb needs no togetherness modifier at all, so cut the duplication rather than re-dress it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the words in this version that all mean 'together'—how many do you find?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Unstack the phrase: identify the core verb idea, then see how many wrappers repeat it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'works in collaboration together with' say anything that a single working verb plus its preposition would not?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Three layers of the same idea is the heaviest redundancy on offer; concision keeps each idea stated once, so strip every duplicate layer before re-choosing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job is the underlined phrase doing between the two parts of the sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the words doing that one job—could fewer carry the same link?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'the fact that' add any information the sentence would lack without it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Five words performing a one-word job is padding; the causal connection survives intact in a single conjunction, so trim to it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How does this version differ from the original underlined phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare word counts and meanings side by side—did the substitution actually tighten anything?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'owing to the fact that' any leaner than the phrase it replaces?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Replacing one five-word formula with another leaves the padding untouched; the sentence needs just one causal word, so re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is whitening shirts something that happened inside the print shop this paragraph describes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Vividness cannot rescue a detail set in the wrong workplace; the sentence illustrates laundering, not the shop's routine, so this reasoning misfires. Reconsider whether the material belongs at all.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which earlier statement did you think the new sentence duplicates?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Scan the paragraph for any prior mention of the new sentence's specific content.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do launderers or linen appear anywhere else in the paragraph?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The verdict may point the right way, but this reasoning fails: nothing earlier covers laundering, so no duplication exists — the sentence's true flaw lies in its subject matter. Re-select the justification that names it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about what the final sentence is mainly doing in the paragraph.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Separate the sentence's incidental details from its central claim before judging the reason offered.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the mention of a Lyonnaise workshop the sentence's point, or just the address of the copycat?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This justification seizes on a geographic detail while the sentence's real work is showing what imitation and a legal plea reveal; a keep-or-cut reason must name the sentence's actual contribution. Re-read the sentence for its central point.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What earlier claim did you match the final sentence against?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the kind of evidence each sentence gives: sales figures and legal battles are not the same testimony.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a competitor forging the letters tell readers the same thing as customers buying the books?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Brisk sales and a competitor's forgery are distinct pieces of evidence — the closing sentence escalates the story rather than restating it, so the duplication reasoning collapses. Reassess what the sentence adds.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which sentences, if any, describe the process of designing the slanted letters?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the interruption claim: identify the thread the paragraph actually follows from start to finish.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a sentence interrupt an account of design work if no such account appears in the paragraph?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The paragraph follows the invention's fortunes — motive, success, imitation — and never narrates design work, so nothing exists for the final sentence to interrupt. Re-examine what thread it continues.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which evidence in the essay did you feel this reasoning points to?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Verify the justification against the text: a supporting reason must describe something the essay truly contains.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can you find a single named person credited with inventing one of these terms?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The essay attributes no term to any individual, so this reasoning praises evidence that does not exist; the verdict needs support the essay actually supplies. Re-check what the essay really does.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How would you state this essay's subject in one sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Distinguish where the terms came from and what the essay is about — those can differ.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If every example explains how a term entered English, is the essay about arranging pages or about language?

rows.subject: act-english
