rows.body_md: The essay uses shop practice as source material for a story about English usage, so the claim that it ignores language mistakes the subject entirely. Re-read with the goal in one hand and the essay in the other.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which of the essay's examples did you test this reasoning against?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Audit every example in the essay, not just the first ones, before accepting a claim about 'only.'

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a person who has never touched a press still say they feel 'out of sorts'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: At least one example is everyday idiom rather than specialist vocabulary, so the 'only professionals' claim fails on the essay's own evidence. Weigh the verdict again with all examples counted.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the opening 'Because' clause, could the remaining words stand alone as a sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Hunt for a verb that carries tense — one that tells you when the action happened.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does an -ing form by itself ever anchor a complete sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An -ing form carries no tense, so nothing after the comma can stand on its own and the whole sentence collapses into a fragment. Look for the version with a fully finite verb.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which words here would serve as the subject and main verb of the sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Strip away the opening clause and test the leftovers for completeness.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With the workers gone from this version, what word is left to carry the sentence's tense?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This version leaves the sentence without any tensed verb, so the dependent opener has nothing to lean on. Re-test each version for a complete main clause.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What kind of grammatical unit does the word 'with' begin?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Label each chunk of the sentence — clause or phrase — and see whether any chunk can stand alone.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a sentence be built entirely from a dependent clause plus a prepositional phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A 'with' phrase can only modify; it can never serve as a main clause, so this version is a fragment from end to end. Seek the version containing a true subject-verb core.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — how many complete statements do you hear on either side of the joint?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Classify the linking word: is it a true conjunction like 'and,' or an adverb wearing a conjunction's clothes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a lone comma hold together two clauses when the word between them is only an adverb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Otherwise' is a connecting adverb, not a conjunction, so a bare comma before it splices the clauses; a stronger stop must precede it. Re-inspect the joint's punctuation.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What did the extra comma around the linking word seem to fix?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Look past the decoration and test the actual joint between the two complete statements.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the mark before the adverb is still only a comma, has the splice actually been repaired?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Wrapping the adverb in commas changes nothing about the weak joint itself — two independent clauses still hang on a single comma. Strengthen the stop that precedes the adverb.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if all punctuation vanished from this junction?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Find where the first complete thought ends, and check what signals that ending to a reader.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Without any mark, how does a reader know the temperature claim has finished before the warning begins?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Removing punctuation entirely fuses two independent statements into one breathless run-on; the boundary needs a firm mark before the adverb. Revisit the junction.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where does the first complete thought in this sentence come to an end?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Scan the junction for any signal separating the two statements.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How would a reader know the claim about buyers has closed before the next action begins?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two complete statements stand here with nothing between them — a fused sentence — and the boundary must be marked with a full stop or its equivalent. Re-mark the junction.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What role is 'therefore' playing at this junction, grammatically speaking?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sort connectors into two bins — true conjunctions and adverbs — and place this one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does an adverb give a comma enough strength to hold two complete clauses together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Therefore' is an adverb, so a comma before it merely splices the clauses; the junction demands a stronger separation. Re-choose with the connector's true part of speech in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: After the strong mark in this version, what words remain to form the second statement?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the right-hand side of the junction for a subject and a tensed verb.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can 'therefore printing' stand alone as a complete statement about anyone?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A strong mark requires a complete clause on each side, and the -ing form with no subject leaves the second half a fragment. Verify both sides before settling.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who, in your reading, actually did the inking described by the opening phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check which noun sits immediately after the comma and whether it could perform the opening action.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a sheet of paper ink a set of rollers by hand?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The opening phrase must describe the very next noun, and here that noun is an object incapable of the action — the modifier dangles. Re-position the true performer right after the comma.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What did trimming the end of the clause accomplish for the opening phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Re-run the modifier test on the shortened version: identify the subject that now follows the comma.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Even shorter, is the thing named after the comma any more able to wield an ink ball?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Cutting words does not cure a dangler; the subject after the comma is still the wrong performer for the opening action. Restructure so the doer takes the subject slot.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which single word functions as the grammatical subject of this version's main clause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Strip the possessive down and see what noun the verb actually belongs to.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does putting a person's title in a possessive make that person the one performing the sentence's action?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A possessive only marks ownership; the clause's true subject remains the object being pulled, so the opener still describes the wrong thing. Give the performer the subject position itself.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the base word here already promise about how often the mold works?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Unpack the word's built-in meaning, then examine what the added phrase contributes beyond it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If something can be reused, has 'more than once' told the reader anything fresh?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The tacked-on phrase restates the meaning already packed inside the word, and repetition without new content is redundancy. Trim the sentence to its essentials.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about what the second half of this wording adds to the first half.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Translate both halves of the phrase into plain meaning and set them side by side.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Are 'reusable' and 'could be used repeatedly' two facts, or one fact said twice?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The added clause repeats the adjective's meaning in stretched form — one fact stated twice is padding, not thoroughness. Favor the version that says it once.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the appositive phrase feel like it deepened the description?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the phrase between the commas: remove it and note whether any meaning disappears.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'capable of repeated use' name a different property than the word it follows?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The interrupting phrase re-dresses the same idea in longer words, so it burdens the sentence while informing no one. Prefer the leanest wording that keeps the meaning.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How many separate facts does the underlined portion give about the press?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the two halves of the span and check whether each earns its place.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the second verb phrase add that the words before 'and' have not already established?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Both halves report the same single fact, and a sentence should state a fact once; the doubled phrasing is excess. Keep only what carries meaning.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if the words after 'and' disappeared from this version?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test each piece of the span for new information versus echo.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is a machine described as working not already, by definition, running?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The added participle echoes the phrase before it rather than extending it, so the wording remains padded. Reduce to the single statement of the fact.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through what each verb in this long version contributes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count how many times this wording asserts that the machine works.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do 'continues,' 'remain,' and 'running' describe three conditions or one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This version says the same thing three ways and even adds stray commas; concision demands the fact be stated once, cleanly. Strip the span to its core.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job is the five-word opening phrase performing in this sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Look for a formula built around 'the fact that' and consider what such formulas usually hide.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could a single ordinary connector express this same cause-and-effect link?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Formulas built on 'the fact that' add packaging, not meaning; prefer the wording that states the link most directly. Re-weigh the candidates for economy.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the longer formula feel more precise than the original?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Weigh the phrase's word count against the information it delivers.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'in light of the fact that' add any shade of meaning the sentence needs?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swapping one bulky formula for a bulkier one moves backward; empty scaffolding around a simple link should be removed, not extended. Reconsider with economy in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How would this phrasing sound in a formal essay read aloud?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the phrase against written-English standards, not just conversational habit.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'being as how' something you would expect in an edited publication?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: That phrasing is a colloquialism that formal prose rejects, and it is no more economical than the original; the link needs standard, direct wording. Re-screen the candidates for register and economy.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What specific quality of the gap between the letters should the verb capture?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Grade the verb for specificity: does it commit to a manner of motion or stay generic?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would this verb distinguish a slow optical spreading from a sudden jump?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A generic verb reports motion without character, and precision questions reward the verb whose shading matches the effect exactly — a slow, unintended spreading. Re-grade the candidates for specificity.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What connotations does this verb carry from its everyday uses?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the verb's implied purpose: some motion words suggest intent and an itinerary.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do letterforms on a page journey anywhere, or do they merely seem to sit too far apart?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This verb implies deliberate movement across distance, but the effect is a passive optical impression with no journey involved. Match the verb's connotation to a subtle, unintended effect.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How fast is the motion this verb usually describes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the verb's speed and suddenness against the effect in the sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a spacing flaw strike the eye as a sudden dash or as a quiet, gradual impression?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This verb means to spring away abruptly, clashing with the slow, subtle separation the sentence depicts. Re-test each verb's speed against the effect.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — does every phrase sound like it belongs in a formal history?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the underlined phrasing's register with the register of 'guarded their designs jealously.'

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would a scholarly account of the 1800s describe competitors as ripping anything off?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The phrase is modern slang, and its casual register breaks the essay's formal voice; the sentence needs standard written diction for the same act of copying. Re-screen the choices for register.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What exactly would competitors be doing, according to this idiom?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the phrase twice: once for register, once for whether it keeps the original meaning.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is following a trend the same act as reproducing a rival's design?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The idiom is conversational and it swaps the specific act of copying for vague trend-chasing — a double failure of register and precision. Re-check each candidate on both counts.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which era does this word choice belong to, and which era does the sentence describe?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the noun at the phrase's center against the vocabulary of formal historical writing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could a word coined for casual talk about moods sit naturally in a sentence about Victorian foundries?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The slang noun is jarringly contemporary and imprecise about what was copied; formal prose demands exact, standard wording. Re-evaluate the candidates' diction.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through how the verb in this sentence is built — how many words make it up?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: There's a helping verb right before the underlined word. Check what form of a verb that helper is allowed to pair with.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: You'd say 'they began' on its own — but does 'they have began' follow the same pattern? Recite the three forms of this irregular verb.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: After have/has/had, English requires the past participle, and for this irregular verb the simple past and the participle are different words — so the original pairing is ungrammatical. Take another look at the verb forms offered.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the -ing form feel right after the helping verb here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Different helping verbs demand different verb forms. Which helper is actually in this sentence — a form of *be* or a form of *have*?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'They are ___ing' works, but the sentence doesn't say 'are.' What form does *have* call for instead of the -ing form?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An -ing verb needs a form of *be* as its helper; *have* takes a past participle instead, so the -ing pairing breaks the verb phrase. Re-check the remaining forms with that rule.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking anything else, read just the verb phrase aloud: does 'have' plus this bare form sound like standard English?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Think about the three principal parts of an irregular verb — base, past, and participle. Which slot does a verb after *have* need to fill?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: You can say 'they begin' in the present, but with *have* in front, is the bare base form still the right part?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The base form only works alone, after 'to,' or after modal verbs; after *have*, the past participle is required, so this pairing is ungrammatical. Apply that test and pick again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What word in the sentence is this pronoun standing in for — say it out loud.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch out for the noun that sits closest to the blank; the real antecedent may be further back, at the head of the subject.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the subject 'each' or 'stations'? Strip away 'of the twelve solar-powered stations' and see what's left to own the readings.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Each' is grammatically singular even when a plural noun follows it in an of-phrase, so a plural possessive can't refer back to it. Rework the number match and pick again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the apostrophe for a second, what is this word actually built from?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the expansion test on any apostrophe-plus-s pronoun: swap in the two words it abbreviates and re-read.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'transmits it is readings' make sense? What does that tell you about putting a contraction in a possessive slot?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An apostrophe in this pronoun always signals the contraction 'it is,' never possession — the possessive form carries no apostrophe. With that rule in hand, reconsider the choices.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about what this word expands to when you write it out fully.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two separate checks apply here: number (singular or plural?) and form (possessive or contraction?). Run both.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The subject is 'each' — singular — and the sentence needs a word showing ownership of the readings. Does a plural contraction pass either test?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This word fails twice: it abbreviates 'they are,' so it isn't possessive, and it's plural while the antecedent 'each' is singular. Apply both tests and choose again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the three things the analysts confirm, one at a time — do they all start the same way?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When a sentence lists clauses, the first item sets a template. Compare how each item in this series opens.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The first two items each begin with a little marker word before their subject. What happened to that marker in the last item?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Once a series starts repeating 'that' before each clause, every item must keep it; the version you chose drops the marker and falls out of parallel. Re-scan for the item matching the template.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the -ing phrasing feel like it fit at the end of this list?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check two things for the final list item: does it open like the earlier items, and does it contain a full, finite verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Tremor is intensifying' has a subject plus a complete verb. Does an -ing word by itself give the last item the same kind of verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A bare -ing form is not a finite verb, and this item also lacks the marker the other clauses carry, so it breaks the parallel twice. Match the last item to the first two and pick again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the sentence convinced you the fix was only about the opening word?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Adding the right opener is half the job — now test whether the words after it could stand as a complete statement.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try saying the last item alone: does 'gas output rising' contain a verb that finishes the thought, the way 'the ground is swelling' does?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A that-clause needs a finite verb; an -ing participle alone leaves the clause incomplete, so this version fixes the opener but not the verb. Re-test each version against the first two items.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How would you sum up each of these two sentences in just a few words?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A transition is a promise about the logic ahead. Test whether the second sentence keeps a promise of sameness.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: One tool is stopped by night and cloud; the other sees through both. Are those two facts alike, or pulling in opposite directions?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A likeness transition requires the second sentence to echo the first, but here the satellite succeeds exactly where the webcam fails — an opposing relationship. Pick the connector that signals that difference.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if the second sentence really were an illustration of the first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An example transition means: here is one specific instance of the claim just made. Test the second sentence against that job description.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the satellite's ability to see through clouds serve as an instance of the webcam's limitations — or does it push against them?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The second sentence doesn't illustrate the first claim; it counters it, so an example connector misstates the logic. Choose the transition that names opposition, not illustration.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through the cause-and-effect chain you saw between these two sentences.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A result transition asserts that the first sentence produces the second. Ask: did anything in sentence one make sentence two happen?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the webcam's blindness at night cause satellites to see through clouds — or are these simply two tools with opposite strengths?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: No causal link connects the sentences; they compare a limited tool with a more capable one, so a consequence word misleads the reader. Re-select with that opposition in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking the connector, what did the instruments lead everyone to expect — and what actually happened?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A conclusion word claims the second sentence follows naturally from the first. Verify that the outcome matches the prediction.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The forecast named the summit; the fissure opened far down the flank. Is that the predicted result, or a surprise that broke the prediction?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A result transition only fits when expectation and outcome line up; here the eruption defied the forecast, so the sentence needs a concession word instead. Re-choose with that reversal in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What likeness did you spot between the forecast and the eruption itself?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the connector's claim: would a reader nodding along agree that the second event resembles the first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Predicting a summit eruption and getting a flank fissure — do those parallel each other, or does the second undercut the first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The second sentence departs from the forecast rather than mirroring it, so a similarity connector misleads. Look for the word that admits the expectation failed.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about how the second sentence restates the first one, if it does.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A rephrasing connector promises the same idea in new words. Compare the content of the two sentences carefully.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'the fissure opened far from the predicted spot' another way of saying 'the instruments pointed to the summit' — or is it new, conflicting information?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The second sentence contradicts the forecast instead of restating it, so a clarification connector misdescribes the logic; a concession is needed. Weigh the connectors again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is this paragraph actually doing — arguing a position, or laying out how something works?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An opener sets a contract: if it promises criticism, the body must deliver criticism. Scan the body sentences for any critique.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do the green-to-red sentences ever question the scale's usefulness, or do they simply explain each step of it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The paragraph explains the scale step by step and never challenges it, so an opener casting doubt promises an argument the body never makes. Match the opener to the body's neutral, explanatory purpose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the first-sentence slot, what one phrase names what the rest of the paragraph is about?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare the scope of your pick to the scope of the body: an opener can be too wide as easily as too narrow.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The body sentences all describe steps of a single color-coded ranking. Does a sentence about instruments in general point the reader to that?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A strong opener previews the specific subject the body develops — the ranking system — while this one gestures at monitoring in general and never mentions it. Find the sentence whose subject every body sentence expands.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which sentences of the paragraph does your opener actually connect to — all of them, or just one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the opener against the whole body: every following sentence should feel like it grows out of the first.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Aviation hazards surface only in the final sentence about the highest level. Can a detail from one step introduce the entire ladder of steps?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An opener built on one late detail leaves the earlier levels unintroduced; the paragraph needs a first sentence that frames the whole ranking system. Re-check which candidate covers all the body sentences.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the movable sentence aloud — which words in it point backward to something else?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Phrases like 'this ___' lean on whatever was just described. Check what the sentence right before currently describes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In its present spot, the pointer follows a description of burying sensors on the summit. Is that the stage the inspection sentence names?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'This indoor stage' must sit directly after the sentence describing indoor work; where it stands now, it follows outdoor fieldwork, so the reference dangles. Trace the pointer to its true referent and re-place the sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the very top of the paragraph feel like the right home for this sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A sentence with a backward-pointing phrase can't come before the thing it points to. Locate where the indoor work is first described.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the inspection sentence follows the opener, has any indoor work been mentioned yet for 'this indoor stage' to name?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Placed that early, the pointer phrase arrives before its referent exists, forcing readers to hold an unexplained reference; the sentence belongs immediately after the indoor work it describes. Re-check the sequence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through the timeline of steps as you understand it — what happens where?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the movable sentence's content to a step: during which task would cables and connectors be checked twice?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The crate-packing sentence is about wrapping gear for a flight. Is that when connectors get inspected, or does that checking belong with assembly and testing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The inspection describes bench testing, not packing, so attaching it to the packing step splits the assembly description in two. Put the sentence right after the step it actually details.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try labeling each numbered sentence with a two-word topic — where do the labels shift?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A paragraph break should fall between ideas, not between a topic sentence and its own supporting details.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the break comes that early, the opener about paper records gets separated from the drums and cabinets that illustrate it. Do those belong apart?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Splitting after the first sentence orphans the paper-era details from the sentence they support; the break belongs where the subject itself turns. Re-scan the paragraph for that turning point.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which sentences describe the old way of keeping records, and which describe the new?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Group the sentences by era before deciding anything. A clean break keeps each era whole.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The slow-afternoon sentence — is that a complaint about the paper system, or the start of something new?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The retrieval frustration still belongs to the paper era, so breaking before it splits one idea across two paragraphs. Find the sentence where the era actually changes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What signaled a fresh start to you at the spot you chose?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Words like 'Today' feel like openings, but check whether the sentence just before it already launched the new idea.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Doesn't the arrival of digital networks begin the modern story — and doesn't 'Today...' continue that same story rather than start another?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Breaking at the final sentence leaves the digital turning point stuck in the paper-era paragraph; the new idea starts where the technology changes, not where 'Today' appears. Re-draw the boundary at the true shift.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the phrase about gases, would the sentence still stand on its own?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Removable descriptions get fenced off. Count how many fences the underlined version puts around this one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: There's a comma after the phrase — where is its partner before the phrase begins?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A nonessential appositive needs punctuation at both its start and its end; a single comma leaves the reader entering the interruption with no signal. Check each version for a complete pair.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — where do you naturally pause around the describing phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A comma that opens an interruption makes a promise: a matching mark will close it before the sentence resumes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: After 'gases,' the main verb arrives. Did anything signal the reader that the detour was over?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Opening an appositive with a comma but never closing it lets the aside collide with the verb; interrupters take a matched pair. Re-count the marks in each version.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job is the phrase about volcanic gases doing — is it required to identify the person, or is it extra background?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the removal test: essential phrases stay unfenced, extra ones get set off. Which kind is this?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Since the sentence already identifies the person as the team's lead, is the specialty essential — and if not, what punctuation does an extra aside demand?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The specialty is removable background, so leaving it completely unpunctuated welds an aside onto the main clause; paired marks are required. Re-examine which version fences the phrase on both sides.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Look at the two halves on either side of the mark — could each stand alone as its own sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: List what is legally allowed between two complete statements. Is a lone comma on that list?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Magma does not rise quietly' is complete; so is everything after the mark. What does joining two complete statements with only a comma create?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A comma by itself cannot join two independent clauses — that is a comma splice; a stronger mark or a joining word is required. Test each version against that rule.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try reading just the second part aloud, starting from the capital letter — does it finish a thought?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Adding a subordinating word changes what a clause can do on its own. Test the second statement for independence after the addition.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Because it cracks the rock... toward the surface' — where is the payoff clause that this reason attaches to?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Starting a stand-alone sentence with a subordinator and never completing the frame leaves a fragment; the second statement must remain able to stand alone or be properly attached. Re-test each version for completeness.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the version with no mark at all feel smooth when you read it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the seam where the first statement meets the second — say each half separately, then together.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Without any mark, 'quietly it cracks' runs two complete sentences head-on into each other. What is that error called?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two independent clauses joined with no punctuation form a fused sentence; some boundary must separate or connect them. Reconsider which version marks the seam correctly.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What sits on each side of the mark you chose — a full clause, or something smaller?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Different marks introduce a reveal versus balance two statements. Identify which situation this sentence presents.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Harmonic tremor, a steady seismic hum...' — is that a complete statement with its own subject and verb, or a naming phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The mark you picked demands independent clauses on both sides, but the right-hand side here is only a noun phrase naming the signal — so it fails that test. Re-check which mark may introduce a phrase after a complete clause.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud with a light pause at the mark — does the pause clarify or muddle the naming of the signal?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A small mark has small power. Ask whether this spot needs a formal introduction or just a breath.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The first part builds suspense — a decade of waiting — and then identifies the payoff. Can the lightest mark in English carry that introduction?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A comma here weakly splices the awaited thing onto 'waiting for' and blurs the boundary; the sentence needs a mark that formally introduces what follows a complete statement. Compare the versions with that in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say the sentence with no mark at all — where does your voice demand a boundary?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the grammar of the unpunctuated string: does every word find a role in the sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In 'the signal they had been waiting for harmonic tremor,' what job is 'harmonic tremor' doing — and does anything connect it to the rest?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With no punctuation, the naming phrase has no grammatical seat and simply collides with the clause; a mark must introduce it. Re-examine which version supplies that introduction.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What quality did the writer ask this verb to deliver — reread the goal in the question.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Grammatical isn't the bar here; the verb has to carry the stated feeling all by itself.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you heard only 'the column went ten kilometers up,' would you know whether that took minutes or days?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A neutral motion verb leaves the speed to the reader's imagination, so it can't stress how fast the climb was; the goal demands a verb whose very meaning is sudden force. Re-judge the verbs on that standard.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about the picture this verb paints — what pace do you see?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the verb's built-in speed against the speed the writer wants to stress.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Smoke drifts on a lazy wind. Is that the motion of a column that climbed ten kilometers within minutes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: That verb connotes slow, aimless movement and so works against the stated goal of emphasizing speed; the sentence needs a verb of sudden force. Re-compare the connotations.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking anything else, rank the four verbs from slowest-sounding to fastest-sounding.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Some verbs are technically accurate yet emotionally flat. Test whether this one adds any urgency.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A ladder extends; a table extends. Does that verb suggest the violence and speed the eruption scene calls for?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: That verb describes gradual lengthening without urgency, so it fails the goal of dramatizing speed; pick the verb whose connotation is fast and forceful. Rank them again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the original phrasing feel professional to you — walk me through its two key words.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Weigh each word's connotation separately: does the verb sound courteous or confrontational?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Refused' is how we describe someone digging in their heels. Does that shade match 'measured and professional,' or does it lean toward uncooperative?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The blunt verb gives the director a stubborn, standoffish edge that undercuts the intended professionalism; the goal needs language of polite, disciplined restraint. Re-weigh each phrase's tone.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the sentence should signal professionalism — and does your pick do that?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the phrase against the exact trait the writer wants to avoid, not just the trait they want.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Dodging' belongs to descriptions of politicians ducking scrutiny. Is that the portrait of a careful scientist?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: That phrasing explicitly casts the director as slippery — the very impression the writer wants to prevent; the sentence needs wording of principled restraint instead. Reassess the connotations.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How would a reader who knows nothing else about the director react to this phrasing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Extremes carry connotations too. Ask whether total silence reads as careful or as secretive.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A scientist who stays completely mute sounds like someone hiding something. Is silence the same as disciplined caution?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Absolute stonewalling suggests concealment rather than measured judgment, overshooting into evasiveness; look for wording that shows thoughtful restraint, not refusal. Compare again with the goal in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the proposed sentence again — what information does it actually contain?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A justification has to match the sentence's content, not just vote the right way. Compare reason to sentence, word by word.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the sentence about tripled output mention mounting hardware on a rim, or does it report a measurement over time?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The verdict may be right, but this reasoning misdescribes the sentence, which reports a striking measurement rather than any installation; a sound justification must name what the sentence really adds. Re-match reasons to content.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Scan the existing paragraph — can you point to a concrete incident already in it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before accepting a claim of repetition, hunt for the earlier twin it alleges.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The current sentences speak in general terms about magma and plumes. Where exactly is the earlier real-world instance this reasoning claims exists?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Nothing in the paragraph yet grounds the general claim in a particular event, so the charge of redundancy is false; concrete support is exactly what's missing. Re-evaluate what the addition contributes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if the proposed sentence ended before the words about lava?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Identify the sentence's center of gravity: which measurement is it really about?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The tripling of gas output is the star of the sentence — does mentioning lava's later arrival change the subject, or prove the warning came first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Lava appears only to time-stamp how early the chemical signal arrived; the sentence stays squarely on gas monitoring, so the off-focus objection fails. Reconsider what the sentence contributes to the paragraph's claim.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is this paragraph tracking, step by step, from slope to town?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Support has a job description: it must give evidence for the paragraph's claim. Test the hiking sentence against that job.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a colleague's weekend hobby tell readers anything about whether the alarm catches lahars?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The birdwatching detail offers no evidence about the alarm at all, so calling it support misreads it; it is a digression that breaks the paragraph's chain of events. Re-assess what the sentence does before keeping it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Trace the sequence: vibration, alarm, then sirens. Where does the hiking sentence fit in that chain?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A true bridge sentence touches what comes before it and what comes after. Check both of this sentence's edges.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does birdwatching pick up from the alarm, or hand off to the sirens? What does it share with either?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The sentence links to neither the alarm before it nor the sirens after it — it stalls the sequence rather than bridging it, so it cannot be defended as a transition. Reconsider which reading of the sentence is accurate.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Tell me why the sentence should go — does your stated reason match what the sentence actually is?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Right verdict, wrong warrant is still wrong. Test the claim that this material merely sits in the wrong place.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would moving the hiking detail elsewhere in the essay make it useful — or is placement not the real problem?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This reasoning treats the digression as good material misplaced, but no spot in the essay needs a colleague's hobby; the sentence fails on relevance, not position. Re-check which justification names that flaw.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Underline the scope words in the goal — how wide a survey does it ask for?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A justification can be factually true about the essay and still dodge the question. Compare scopes, not just facts.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The goal asks for a sweep across the observatory's whole kit; the essay lingers lovingly on one device. Do those scopes match?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: True statements about the essay's content cannot rescue a scope mismatch: an overview of the full array was requested, and a portrait of one device was delivered. Judge the verdicts by that comparison.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What exactly does the goal ask the essay to survey — devices in general, or the readings of one device?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A 'no' verdict still needs the right diagnosis. Ask which gap actually separates essay from goal.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Even if the essay catalogued every reading a tiltmeter makes, would it then survey the observatory's other devices?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The shortfall is breadth across different devices, not missing detail about this one; deeper treatment of a single meter would leave the mismatch untouched. Re-diagnose before settling on a reason.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide that depth could stand in for breadth here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Writers choose depth or breadth for good reasons — but the goal in the question already made the choice. Re-read it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If a reader wanted a map of the whole monitoring arsenal, would a beautiful portrait of one device satisfy them?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: However effective a single-device study may be, the stated goal explicitly demands an overview of the full array, and preference cannot rewrite the assignment. Match the verdict to the stated scope.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read only what comes after the period, as though it were its own sentence — does it finish a thought?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Every stand-alone sentence needs its own subject and main verb. Hunt for them in the second string of words.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A clause that opens with a relative pronoun exists to describe a noun. Which noun does this one need — and can it live apart from that noun?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A relative clause severed from its noun is a fragment no matter how long it runs; it must be attached to the word it modifies, not left after a full stop. Re-check how each version handles that attachment.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the mark you chose require of the words that follow it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Some punctuation upgrades are cosmetic. Ask whether this mark carries the same demand the period did.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the describing clause can't follow a period, can it follow a mark that also expects a complete clause after it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This mark and a period share the same rule — an independent clause on each side — so the fragment problem stays unsolved; the describing clause needs to be joined to its noun. Compare the versions on that requirement.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the second sentence would act as its verb if you had to point to one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An -ing word alone can't carry a sentence. Look for a subject plus a finite verb after the full stop.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Traveling hundreds of kilometers...' — who or what is doing that, and where is the completed verb that goes with it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swapping the pronoun for an -ing form leaves the same wound: no subject, no finite verb, so still a fragment; the description must hook onto the noun it describes. Re-test each version for a complete second clause or a proper attachment.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check each half around the comma: does each have its own subject and verb and finish a thought?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A comma is a pause, not a joiner. Recall what is allowed to sit between two complete statements.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'The alarm sounded' and 'the scientist reached the room' — both complete. Can a lone comma legally hold them together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Joining two independent clauses with only a comma is a splice; the seam needs an end mark, a semicolon, or a comma teamed with a coordinating conjunction. Re-inspect each version's seam.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What kind of word is 'therefore' — and what is it allowed to join?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Some connecting words are true conjunctions; others are adverbs in disguise. Sort this one before trusting it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try the seam test: with only a comma in front of 'therefore,' are the two complete clauses actually fastened together, or still spliced?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Therefore' is a conjunctive adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so a comma plus 'therefore' leaves the splice in place; it would need a semicolon before it. Re-run the seam test on the remaining versions.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence at speed — where did two separate statements collide?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Removing punctuation never joins clauses; it only hides the seam. Find the boundary between the two complete thoughts.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: '...sounded at 3 a.m. the duty scientist reached...' — what is missing at the spot where one sentence ends and the next begins?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With nothing at the boundary, the clauses fuse into a run-on; a legal connector or end mark is required at that seam. Re-evaluate which version installs one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Look at the two halves on either side of the boundary — can each stand alone?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Interrupting words set off by commas inside a clause don't change what the main seam between clauses requires.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'The gas plume kept thickening' is a complete statement even with 'however' tucked inside it. What does a lone comma between two complete statements create?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Both halves are independent clauses, so a bare comma splices them; the seam demands more than a comma alone provides. Re-test each version at the boundary.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship does 'because' assert between the fading tremor and the thickening plume?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check two things: the logic of the added word, and what the mark before it demands of the words after it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Did the tremor's fading cause the plume to thicken? And can that mark be followed by a clause that can't stand alone?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The added subordinator asserts a causal link the sentences don't support and leaves the mark followed by a dependent clause, which that mark forbids; both logic and structure fail. Reconsider the untouched relationship between the clauses.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say the sentence without any boundary — can you hear where one statement ends and the next begins?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Zero punctuation between clauses is only legal when one of them is dependent. Test both for independence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: '...had faded the gas plume...' — is 'faded' acting on the plume, or did two separate sentences just crash together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Removing the boundary fuses two independent clauses and even invites a misreading of 'faded' as acting on the plume; the seam must be marked. Re-examine which versions mark it legally.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who or what is doing the flying in this sentence — and where does that flyer appear?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An opening action phrase grabs the first noun after the comma as its actor. Identify that noun here.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can intense heat fly low over a lava lake? If not, what has the modifier accidentally latched onto?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The introductory phrase dangles: its real actor never appears in the subject slot, so the sentence claims the heat was flying; the doer must directly follow the comma. Look again for the version that puts the flyer there.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read your version literally, clause by clause — what is the phrase about flying attached to now?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Moving a modifier only helps if it lands beside the thing it describes. Check its new neighbor.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Set off by commas right after 'heat,' the flying phrase now describes the heat itself. Does that match reality?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Relocating the modifier next to the wrong noun turns a dangler into a misplaced modifier — the heat still seems to fly; the phrase must sit beside the machine that actually flew. Re-inspect which version does that.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the 'it was...' construction feel like it solved the problem?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the first noun-slot after the comma again in this version — what does the flying phrase attach to now?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'It' points to nothing that can fly, and the heat still claims the action. Has the modifier found its true actor anywhere nearby?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The cleft 'it was' construction shuffles emphasis without giving the opening phrase its real actor, so the modifier still dangles; the flyer itself must follow the comma. Re-check each version's first noun.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the second verb in this pair tell the reader that the first one didn't?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the deletion test on paired verbs: drop one and see if any meaning disappears.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If a team revised its estimate, hasn't it already, by definition, updated it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The two verbs are synonyms doing one job, and English never needs to pay twice for one meaning — a single exact verb carries it all. Apply the deletion test to every version.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking anything else, ask: can you revise something without going back to it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for warm-up phrases that restate what the main verb already implies.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Went back and' promises information — but doesn't the act of revising an earlier estimate already contain the going-back?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The lead-in phrase duplicates what the verb itself implies, adding words but no information; redundancy hides inside verbs as often as beside them. Re-test each version for stowaway repetition.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the words doing actual work in this version — which ones could vanish without loss?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Nouns like 'revisions' and 'changes' often smuggle in a verb's meaning twice. Convert them back to verbs and compare.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Made revisions and changes to their estimate' — how does that differ in meaning from simply revising it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This version stacks two redundant nouns on a weak verb, tripling the length while adding zero content; a single precise verb says it all. Re-run the deletion test on the set.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How many of these five words are carrying meaning the others don't already carry?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'In a ___ manner' is a classic scaffold. Ask what single part of speech does that scaffold's whole job.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Very' plus 'manner' plus 'in a' — what do they add beyond what the core adjective, turned into an adverb, would say alone?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The phrase is scaffolding around one idea that a lone adverb expresses completely; extra words with no extra meaning must go. Compare the versions by meaning per word.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: You trimmed some fat — is there any scaffold still standing in this version?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swapping one wordy frame for a slightly smaller one isn't the same as removing the frame. Look at the frame itself.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'In a ___ way' still wraps the idea in three spare words. What form of the word would need no wrapper at all?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The in-a-way frame survives, so this version is only half-trimmed; the same idea fits in a single adverb with nothing lost. Re-compare each version's word count against its meaning.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read this version slowly — do any of its words repeat each other's meaning?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test pairs inside the phrase: can a rate here be anything other than a speed?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Rate of speed' says the same thing twice, and the whole prepositional frame is doing an adverb's job. How much of this phrase is echo?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This version piles an internal redundancy onto a wordy frame, making it the least economical of the set; one adverb delivers the entire meaning. Re-rank the versions for economy.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the underlined phrase, what meaning would the sentence lose?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Interrupting phrases must earn their commas: emphasis, contrast, or new information. Audit this one's contribution.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is anything in the sentence actually surprising or disputed, so that a fact-insisting phrase earns its place?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The interrupter asserts factuality that no one questioned, contributing nothing but length; a phrase that changes nothing when dropped shouldn't stay. Rethink what this sentence truly needs between its subject and verb.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What's the difference in meaning between this phrase and the one it replaces?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Trading a phrase for its synonym only helps if the original's meaning was needed. First test whether it was.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the original insistence on fact added nothing, what does an identical insistence in different words add?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swapping filler for equivalent filler leaves the sentence exactly as padded as before; the real question is whether any interrupter is needed at all. Run the cover-up test again and re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read this version aloud — does the sentence gain force or lose it as the interrupter grows?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Longer isn't weightier. Measure this phrase's information against its word count.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'As it happens to be the case' spends six words — on what, exactly?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This version inflates the filler rather than questioning it, dragging the reader further from subject and verb for zero content; wordiness compounds the original problem. Reconsider whether the sentence needs the interrupter at all.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who — or what — is performing this verb? Picture the actor precisely.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Some verbs presume a casual human observer. Ask whether this sentence has one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a machine 'notice' something, the way you notice a new haircut? What kind of sensing does an instrument do?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Name the diction test: everyday noticing words fit people, not meters. Your option suits casual awareness, but the clause describes a device catching sub-threshold input — re-match the wording to that actor.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What scene does 'witness' conjure — who is present, and what are they doing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the verb's sensory channel. Which sense does it assume, and does the sentence support that?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Witnessing means seeing an event unfold. Can anyone see movements the sentence says are too faint even to feel?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Witness' presumes an observable event and an onlooker, yet these movements are imperceptible to people; the verb contradicts the sentence's own point. Re-test each verb against that fact.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about what 'uncover' usually describes — what kind of process ends in uncovering?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the verb's time frame to the sentence's: is this instant sensing or a long investigation?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Detectives uncover schemes after months of digging. Is that what a seismometer does with a passing tremor?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Uncover' implies deliberate investigation revealing something concealed, not an instrument's immediate registering of a signal; its connotation misfits the action. Re-compare the verbs' built-in stories.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the whole sentence in the voice of an official report — which words break that voice?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the diction to the document. Would this phrasing survive in an observatory's public statement?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Freaked out' belongs to hallway talk. Does the rest of the passage speak that way?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The slang clashes with the passage's formal, factual register, and it dramatizes emotion the report doesn't need; the sentence wants neutral wording centered on the action taken. Re-screen each version for tone.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made this version feel more formal than the original — test each word.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Softening slang isn't the same as replacing it. Check whether the idiom's casual core is still there.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would 'seriously rattled' appear in a scientific bulletin, or in a text to a friend?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The phrasing remains conversational — a gentler idiom is still an idiom — so the register mismatch stands; the passage needs plain, report-ready wording. Re-evaluate the versions against the passage's voice.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of this phrase is literal, and which part is a figure of speech?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Idioms carry baggage: informality plus implied drama. Weigh both against a factual account.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Was there an actual panic button — and does the passage report panic, or a prompt call to officials?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The idiom is both too casual for the register and adds panicked behavior the facts don't support; the wording should report the verifiable response in a neutral tone. Reconsider which version does only that.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through how the phrase right before the underlined verb usually behaves in a sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run an idiom check: some verbs and adjectives are locked to a specific preposition, and that preposition controls the form of the next verb.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try putting an ordinary noun after 'committed to' — if a noun fits there, what does that tell you about the kind of word 'to' is here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When 'to' works as a preposition, as it does after 'committed,' the verb after it must act like a noun and take its -ing form, so a bare infinitive breaks the pattern — look again for the form that fits.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the 'have + past participle' version feel right to you here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the time relationship: ask whether the sentence describes something finished in the past or an ongoing effort.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the students are still working at this skill, does a form meaning 'already completed' match the sentence's meaning — and is 'to' even acting as an infinitive marker after 'committed'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The perfect form claims the skill was finished before the commitment, which contradicts 'stay committed,' and 'to' after 'committed' is a preposition needing an -ing verb, so this version fails on both counts — reconsider your pick.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about why you swapped the preposition in that fixed expression.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do an idiom check: cover the sentence and ask which preposition standard English pairs with 'committed.'

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would you ever say someone is 'committed at' a goal in formal writing, or does that pairing sound off when you test it aloud?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Committed' takes 'to' in standard English, so the repair lies in the verb form after that preposition, not in the preposition itself — revisit the options with the original 'to' kept in place.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — then tell me which word in it the underlined pronoun points back to.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a number check: certain quantifier words at the front of a noun phrase force the whole phrase to count as singular.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'each on-call interpreter' talking about many people at once, or about every single interpreter one at a time?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Words like 'each' make an antecedent singular, so a plural pronoun clashes with it in formal writing — go back and find a singular pronoun suited to a person.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made you reach for the impersonal pronoun there?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a consistency check: a pronoun should stay in the same person and point of view as its antecedent.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The sentence names a specific role, 'each on-call interpreter' — does switching to a generic, impersonal form keep the reference tied to those people?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Shifting to the impersonal form breaks the link to 'each on-call interpreter,' which needs a third-person pronoun referring to a specific person — decide again with number and person both in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the underlined pronoun, what kind of noun would you expect it to stand in for?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the pronoun's kind, not just its number: English separates pronouns for people from pronouns for objects and organizations.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An interpreter is a person — does the pronoun you picked ever refer to a human being in formal prose?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: That pronoun is reserved for things, animals, and organizations, so it cannot stand in for a person like an interpreter — look for the singular pronoun that refers to people.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of the sentence forms a list, and where does each item in it start?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a parallelism check: read only the three list items back to back and listen for one that starts with a different verb form.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Analyzing the script..., ... rehearsals..., and building a signed translation' — what form do the first and last items share that the middle one currently lacks?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Items in a series must share one grammatical form; a finite present-tense verb cannot sit between two -ing phrases, so match the middle item to its neighbors and pick again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the to-form feel like the right fit for the middle item of the list?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare forms across the series: an item can be grammatical on its own and still be the wrong shape for its list.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the first item begins with 'analyzing' and the last with 'building,' does an item beginning with 'to' keep the pattern?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An infinitive breaks the -ing pattern set by 'analyzing' and 'building'; the series needs its middle item in that same -ing shape, so revisit the options with the pattern in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through what adding a subject pronoun does to the middle item of the series.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a structure check: decide whether each piece of the list is a phrase or a full clause, and whether they all match.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a complete clause with its own subject sit comfortably between two -ing phrases joined by 'and'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Dropping in a new subject turns one list item into a clause and splinters the series; keep every item a matching -ing phrase instead, then decide again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking the options, summarize each of the two sentences in a few words for me.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a direction check: decide whether the second sentence continues the first sentence's point or pushes against it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The first sentence praises the service; the second lists a drawback — is that a similarity the current transition can honestly signal?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A similarity word promises more of the same, but this passage pivots from strength to weakness, which calls for a contrast signal — reread and select the word that marks that turn.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship did you see between the drawback sentence and the sentence before it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the transition's promise: an example word commits the next sentence to illustrating the previous claim.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is slow conversation with an unfamiliar interpreter an example of fast, convenient calling — or a point pulling the other way?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The second sentence opposes the first rather than illustrating it, so an example transition mislabels the logic; find the word that signals opposition instead.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide that the second sentence follows as a result of the first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a cause check: a result word is only correct if the first sentence actually causes what the second describes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a fast, convenient connection cause interpreters to be unfamiliar with regional signs, or are these simply two opposing observations?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: No cause-and-effect link exists between the sentences — the writer is conceding a drawback after praise, so the passage needs a contrast word, not a result word; look again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your own words, what does the second sentence do to the claim made in the first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the direction of the logic: contrast words are earned only when the second sentence pushes against the first.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The first sentence says the films were made; the second says signs survive because of them — where is the opposition that a contrast phrase would announce?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The second sentence strengthens the first instead of opposing it, so a contrast phrase mislabels the connection; name the true relationship first, then pick the signal that matches it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What time relationship did you notice between the filming and the survival of those signs?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a timeline check: a while-that-was-happening phrase requires two actions unfolding during the same period.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Recording lecturers in the 1910s and signs surviving 'today' — do those two facts occupy the same window of time?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The sentences span a century rather than sharing one moment, so a simultaneity phrase distorts the logic; ask what the second sentence does to the first — confirm, oppose, or exemplify — and pick the signal for that job.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about why a concession word seemed to fit between these two sentences.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check what a concession sets up: it admits a weakness right before the writer pushes back with a rebuttal.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: After the underlined word, does the passage ever turn around and argue against the point it just admitted?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With no rebuttal following, a concession word leaves a promise unkept; the second sentence actually amplifies the first, so weigh which signal marks reinforcement.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the credentials angle feel like the right doorway into this paragraph?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a follow-through check: a good opener makes a promise that every later sentence helps keep.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the paragraph opened with coursework and mentorship, would the injury data and the twenty-minute rotation that follow feel like they belong?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Nothing after the blank mentions preparation or credentials — the sentences describe strain on the arms and how workers guard against it, so pick the opener that previews exactly that.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Take another look at the sentences after the blank — what single topic do they all share?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check scope: an opener about the language itself should lead into facts about the language, not about the people performing it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in the paragraph does regional variation ever come up again?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The paragraph never returns to differences among sign languages; it tracks fatigue, rotation schedules, and stretching, so the opener must frame the work's toll on the body — decide again with that in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through the connection you saw between earnings and the sentences that follow.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a topic-match check: underline the key noun in each later sentence and see whether your opener predicts those nouns.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Injury rates, paired shifts, stretching regimens — do any of those details develop a point about hourly pay?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compensation never resurfaces after the blank, so an opener about earnings promises a paragraph the writer didn't write; the details demand an opener about the job's physical cost.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up Sentence 5, what would a reader need to know before hearing that scoring takes months?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a dependency check: a sentence can't lead the paragraph if it leans on steps introduced later.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would 'scoring can take several months' make sense to someone who hasn't yet been told there's an exam, a film, or a rater?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Opening with the scoring delay puts the process's final stage before its first; the sentence must come after the step it depends on, so trace the sequence and place it accordingly.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where does the paragraph first mention anything that could be scored?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the chain of events: each sentence should only use ideas the previous sentences have already set up.

rows.subject: act-english
