rows.body_md: Right after the written test, do any films exist for raters to spend months on?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: At that point the performance exam hasn't happened, so a delay in scoring films would refer to nothing; slot the sentence after the stage that produces the scores it mentions.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if the paragraph jumped straight from filming to the months-long wait?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a missing-link check: ask whether every noun in the moved sentence has already been introduced.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sentence 5 hinges on 'scoring' — has the paragraph described anyone scoring the films before Sentence 4 does?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Between filming and the wait, the rating step still must be introduced; the delay only makes sense once raters have been mentioned, so position the sentence after that step.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What topic tag would you give Sentence 1, and what tag would you give Sentence 2?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a same-subject check: a paragraph break placed between two sentences on one subject splits a single idea in half.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sentence 2 is still describing what captions get wrong — has the passage moved to its second subject yet at that point?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Breaking there strands most of the captioning discussion in the second paragraph; the new paragraph should begin exactly where interpreters first appear, so scan for that turning point.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which sentence, in your reading, is the first one that stops talking about captions?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check each sentence's subject noun: the break belongs at the first sentence whose subject belongs to the new topic.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Emergency coverage scrolling too fast — is that a problem with captions, or a feature of the interpreter era?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sentence 3 still documents captioning's failures, so a break there splits the complaint from its evidence; find the first sentence where the stations' new solution enters.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide the complaints in Sentence 4 belong with what comes after rather than what comes before?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a glue check: ask which neighboring sentences Sentence 4 shares its subject with.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The mailroom complaints are about the caption delays — do they set up the new solution, or close out the old problem?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sentence 4 is the last word on the caption era, not the first word on the fix; the second paragraph should open with the stations' change, so locate where that change is introduced.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up 'a certified Deaf interpreter,' would the rest of the sentence still stand on its own?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a fence check: an interrupting phrase needs punctuation at both its entrance and its exit.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: You can see where the interrupter begins — where exactly does it end, and what marks that spot?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: One comma opens the appositive but nothing closes it before 'demonstrated'; nonessential interrupters take matching punctuation on both sides, so re-examine the options for a fully fenced version.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made you decide the renaming phrase needs no punctuation at all?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do an essential-or-extra check: delete the phrase and see whether the main statement survives untouched.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the sentence need 'a certified Deaf interpreter' to identify which leader is meant, or is it bonus information about a leader we already know?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Because the phrase merely adds detail, running it into the sentence unpunctuated misreads it as essential; extra information must be set off on both ends, so revise your pick.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through what job the semicolon is doing at the end of that phrase.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check what each mark is licensed to do: some punctuation joins full clauses, other punctuation fences interrupters.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'demonstrated how to voice a signed poem...' a complete sentence that could follow a semicolon on its own?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A semicolon must have an independent clause on each side, and the words after this one are just a predicate; the interrupter needs matching marks at both ends instead, so look again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read each half of the sentence aloud on its own — what do you notice about the two halves?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a clause count: identify whether the words on each side of the punctuation could stand alone as complete sentences.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Courtroom interpreters must render testimony exactly as it is spoken' and 'accuracy in this setting can decide the outcome' — what strength of punctuation do two such stand-alone statements require between them?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A comma by itself is too weak to join two independent clauses — that's the classic splice; pick the punctuation strong enough to hold a full clause on each side.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What role do you think the added interrupter word plays between those clauses?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the joiner's credentials: only a small set of coordinating conjunctions lets a comma connect two full clauses.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is that little adverb one of the FANBOYS conjunctions, or is it just a comment word dropped between two complete sentences?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Conjunctive adverbs set off by commas never repair a splice — both clauses remain unjoined; a mark built for clause boundaries has to carry the connection, so decide again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if there were nothing at all marking the spot where the first statement ends?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a boundary check: find the last word of the first complete thought and the first word of the second.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Reading 'spoken accuracy' straight through, can you tell where one claim stops and the next begins?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Removing the comma creates a fused sentence, an error even worse than a splice; two independent clauses still need a genuine boundary mark, so reconsider the options.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide where the announcement of the list ends and the list itself begins?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a signal check: when a complete statement promises items to come, a stronger mark than a comma flags the handoff.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With commas after 'essentials,' 'bottle,' and 'clothing,' can a reader tell which comma launches the list and which ones separate its items?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Using a comma both to introduce and to separate items blurs the list's starting line; the introduction after a complete clause deserves the mark designed for announcements, so revisit the choices.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the heavier mid-sentence mark feel right before the first item?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check each mark's contract: one joins two complete clauses, another introduces what a complete clause has promised.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'a water bottle, plain dark clothing, and a backup pair of glasses' a clause with its own subject and verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A semicolon requires full clauses on both sides, and a packing list can't satisfy that; the sentence needs the introducing mark instead, so trade it out.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about what 'such as' adds when the sentence already counts the items.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a flow check: some lead-in phrases run straight into their examples and reject any punctuation after them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the bag holds exactly three essentials, does 'such as' — which signals a partial sampling — fit the sentence's claim, and can a colon ever follow it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Such as' both contradicts the exact count and forbids a colon after it, since the phrase runs directly into its examples; drop the extra phrase and let the complete clause introduce the list properly.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the plainest verb of the group stand out to you?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a goal check: reread the stem's stated aim, then ask whether your verb carries that quality by itself.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you read 'her hands moved' with no other context, would you have any sense of how fast they were going?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A generic motion verb leaves the speed to the reader's imagination, and the writer's goal demands a verb that is fast all by itself — test each option against that bar.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which quality does 'worked' actually emphasize when you picture it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a connotation check: separate what a verb implies about effort from what it implies about pace.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Hands can work slowly and painstakingly — does that word ever guarantee quickness?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Effort and speed are different emphases, and the stem asks for speed; pick the verb whose core meaning is rapid motion.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before you settle, read the sentence aloud with your pick in place — what tempo does it suggest?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check register and pace together: some verbs are so stately that they slow a sentence down.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would you describe a sprinter as having 'proceeded' down the track during a record-setting race?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: That verb signals measured, formal movement — nearly the opposite of the writer's stated aim — so return to the options hunting for built-in quickness.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through what the original verb tells you about the pace at which the support grew.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the stem's own test: the goal names a manner — gradualness — so the verb must encode manner, not just existence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the current verb say anything about whether the support came all at once or bit by bit across those semesters?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb of mere existence can't dramatize a slow build; the phrase 'one persuaded administrator ... at a time' calls for a verb that means adding up piece by piece, so re-test the options.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What sense of timing does 'materialized' create when you picture it happening?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the verb's speed signature: some verbs quietly imply suddenness even when the sentence stretches across semesters.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When something materializes, does it build slowly before your eyes — or is it simply there where nothing was?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: That verb leans toward instant appearance, clashing with the three-semester, one-at-a-time detail; the goal needs a verb of steady piling up, so weigh the remaining options against that.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about the picture 'surfaced' paints — where was the support before, and what happens to it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a metaphor check: identify whether the verb describes growth in amount or a change in visibility.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If support 'surfaces,' it already existed and merely comes into view — is that the same as support being won little by little?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: That verb describes hidden support coming into view, not support growing in number; the sentence's tally of single conversions demands a verb of gradual buildup, so reconsider.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your own words, what does the proposed sentence actually show happening?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a reason check: for yes-or-no questions like this, the stated justification must match what the new sentence really does.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does moving a stool six times during class tell us anything about how schools hire or train their staff?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The justification about hiring and training describes content the sentence doesn't contain; an accepted reason must describe the sentence accurately, so re-evaluate what the anecdote contributes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Take another look at the proposed sentence and the chemistry-lab sentence — list what's different between them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a repetition test: two details only count as repetitive when the second adds no new information.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A stool moved six times in a middle school and an interpreter beside a fume hood — are those the same scene told twice?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The two moments differ in school, setting, and action, so the addition brings fresh support rather than an echo; judge it on whether it illustrates the paragraph's point.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who benefits from all that stool-moving in the proposed sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the focus: ask whose needs drive the action the sentence describes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the movement happens 'to stay inside the student's sight line,' has the spotlight really drifted away from the student?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The anecdote keeps the student's needs at the center — the movement serves the sight line — so the shifting-focus objection misreads it; reconsider what the sentence adds to the paragraph.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the directors detail feel like the sentence's main contribution?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run an accuracy check on the reason: a keep justification must describe information the sentence truly provides.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Reread Sentence 3 — does it ever tell us which directors these are, or when the first such production happened?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The sentence leaves the directors anonymous, so a justification about naming pioneers misdescribes it; ask instead what the patrons' reactions do for the paragraph's argument.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which sentences, exactly, discuss rehearsal schedules in this paragraph?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a flow check: an interruption charge sticks only if the sentences on either side continue one shared thread.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sentence 2 covers rehearsals and Sentence 4 covers stage placement — is Sentence 3 breaking a thread, or moving the paragraph from method to outcome?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Only one sentence concerns rehearsals, so there is no schedule discussion to interrupt; before deleting, weigh what the paragraph loses if no results are ever mentioned.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about why the patrons' reactions seemed beside the point to you.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the purpose of the staging itself: ask for whose benefit the whole technique exists.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If shadow staging exists so Deaf theatergoers can follow the action, are their reactions really unrelated to it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The patrons' experience is the technique's very purpose, so calling it unrelated inverts the paragraph's logic; reconsider whether the paragraph can spare its only sentence about results.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would a true overview of a certification process need to walk its reader through?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a coverage check: a goal question is settled by how much of the needed content appears, not by whether the topic gets a cameo.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Beyond the oath in the last line, where does the essay explain any exam, rating, or credential a candidate must earn?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A closing image is not an outline; since the essay never explains how certification works, it cannot serve as an overview, so revisit which reading matches the whole text.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where does the essay leave the writer at its final moment — what is happening in that scene?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a text check: a 'because' clause must square with what the passage literally says.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the writer raised a right hand to take the interpreter's oath, can it be true that the process was never finished?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The final sentence shows the writer sworn in, flatly contradicting the claim of an unfinished journey; a justification that contradicts the text is disqualified, so weigh the remaining readings.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: List the lessons the grandmother actually gives at that table — what are they?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the equivalence being claimed: family coaching and an official credentialing sequence are different things.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do fingerspelling drills and stories about a Deaf club map onto formal stages like exams and assessments?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Kitchen-table lessons are not official stages, so the claim that they cover the process overstates the text; the essay's heart lies elsewhere, and the accurate reading must say so.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read just the words before the period aloud — does that group feel finished?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a stand-alone test: any word group punctuated as a sentence must be able to survive by itself.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Because the stadium's video-board interpreter needed a clear line of sight to the podium' — what question does that leave hanging, and can a period legally follow it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A clause opened by a subordinator like 'because' is a fragment when cut loose; it must be attached to the main clause that completes it, so look for the version that joins them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the semicolon feel safer than the period here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the semicolon's requirement: it demands a complete clause on each of its two sides.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the 'Because...' clause on the left side of your mark able to stand as its own sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A semicolon has the same full-clause rule as a period, so it fails here for the identical reason; a dependent opener needs a smaller connector, so reconsider your options.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through what the added transition word fixes in the first word group.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a fragment check first, cosmetics second: no adverb can turn a dependent clause into a sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With 'Therefore' added after the period, has the 'Because...' group gained anything that lets it stand alone?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The transition only decorates the second sentence while the opening fragment remains stranded; repair the boundary itself by attaching the dependent clause to its main clause, then decide again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up everything before the comma, could the remaining words stand as a sentence — and what about the first half?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a splice test: count how many complete subject-verb clauses the single comma is being asked to hold together.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Demand ... has soared' and 'the national centers now schedule staff' — is a lone comma a strong enough joint for two full statements?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A bare comma between independent clauses is a splice; only a full stop, a semicolon, or a comma teamed with a coordinating conjunction can mark that seam — re-scan the options for a legal fix.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What role did you want 'consequently' to play between the two statements?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the word's category: transition adverbs comment on logic but lack the grammatical power to join clauses.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'consequently' on the FANBOYS list of coordinating conjunctions, or is it an adverb riding between two still-unjoined sentences?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A conjunctive adverb after a comma leaves the splice fully intact; the seam needs boundary punctuation, not a logical decoration, so return to the options with the FANBOYS test.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What happens at the spot where the first statement ends if all punctuation disappears?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a boundary audit: readers need some signal separating one complete thought from the next.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Reading 'soared over the past decade the national centers,' can you locate the border between the two claims without help?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Deleting the comma trades a splice for a fused sentence — an even weaker boundary; two independent clauses require a genuine stop or legal joiner between them, so pick again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which single word did you trust to connect these two complete statements?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a conjunction check: only a handful of short coordinating words can pair with a comma to join clauses.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Recite the FANBOYS list — does the time word after this comma appear anywhere on it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Then' is an adverb of time, not a conjunction, so comma-plus-'then' splices the clauses; the joint needs punctuation strong enough to stand between two sentences — look for it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What did the second comma around the time word seem to accomplish?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check whether extra pauses can substitute for structure: commas signal interruption, not clause boundaries.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With commas on both sides of the adverb, what mark is actually holding the two independent clauses together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Fencing the adverb changes nothing at the seam — the clauses are still joined by a lone comma; strengthen the boundary itself rather than decorating the adverb, then decide again.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before you settle, read the sentence straight through without any pause — where does the first thought end?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a two-sentence test: if each half could end with its own period, something must mark the meeting point.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: '...wrapped up the keynote at noon then she debriefed...' — what signals a reader that a brand-new clause has begun?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With no punctuation the clauses fuse into a run-on; an adverb like this one can open the second clause only after a genuine boundary mark, so revisit the options.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who, according to this sentence as written, is doing the signing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a modifier check: an opening -ing phrase silently attaches to the first noun after the comma.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a whole audience be 'signing at a furious pace' while also struggling to watch someone else do it?

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did the version starting with the possessive seem to fix the dangler?

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about what the sentence claims once the -ing phrase moves next to the crowd.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a logic check on the new attachment: placement decides who owns the action, so test the pairing it creates.

rows.subject: act-english

rows.body_md: What does the verb in the underlined portion mean all by itself?

rows.body_md: How does 'in turn' add to what the verb already tells the reader?

rows.body_md: Can you describe a scenario where people alternate but not in turn?

rows.body_md: Walk me through the difference between taking turns and alternating.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check for stacked synonyms: sometimes a version repeats an idea using two different expressions at once.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If taking turns and alternating are the same act, what does saying both accomplish?

rows.body_md: This version says the same thing twice in different clothes — the definition of redundancy; strip the duplicate and keep a single verb that covers it all.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What extra information does the longer verb phrase give the reader?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before you settle, tell me what 'the process of' contributes to the sentence's meaning.

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How do the two qualifiers in that version differ from each other in meaning?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a doubling check: when two expressions qualify the same verb, ask whether each earns its place.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'In most cases' and the adverb beside it — do they hedge the claim in two different ways, or the same way twice?

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the rule-of-thumb phrasing add beyond its length?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check for inflated idioms: a familiar saying can occupy five words while carrying one word's meaning.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you compressed 'as a general rule of thumb' into one word, would the sentence lose anything?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The idiom is a five-word costume for a one-word idea, and crisp prose refuses that trade; find the version that hedges the claim without the padding.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your own words, what does 'for all intents and purposes' actually mean?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does that stock phrase say the pairing happens in most instances, or does it say something more like 'effectively so'?

rows.body_md: The phrase is both filler and a meaning shift — it signals 'in effect,' not 'usually'; the sentence needs its frequency hedge kept intact and lean, so reconsider.

rows.body_md: Why did the size-change verb feel equal to the job here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When an hour of debate becomes a useful two-minute summary, is the point merely that it's smaller — or that its essentials survived the squeeze?

rows.body_md: A pure shrinking verb drops the idea that the content was preserved, which is the sentence's whole point; pick the verb that carries both compression and preservation.

rows.body_md: What image does 'deflated' put in your mind when applied to the debate?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check emotional shading: some verbs carry a negative or mocking tone that the context may not want.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the sentence intend to belittle the debate, or simply to report it being distilled for latecomers?

rows.body_md: That verb imports a dismissive, air-out-of-a-balloon tone the neutral context never asks for; the sentence needs a neutral verb of skilled compression, so re-examine the choices.

rows.body_md: Where do you usually see 'abbreviated' used — what kinds of things get abbreviated?

rows.body_md: Run an object-fit check: some verbs pair naturally only with certain nouns, like words, titles, or schedules.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can you abbreviate an hour of debate into a summary, or do you abbreviate a word or a meeting itself?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The verb suits shortening a form or duration, not distilling arguments into a signed digest; precision means matching the verb to its true object, so weigh the alternatives once more.

rows.body_md: Where else have you heard the underlined phrase — in what setting?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does an image borrowed from tag-team wrestling match a sentence about professional colleagues at a panel?

rows.body_md: Would a clear writer describe a colleague resting her hands with a phrase like 'commenced the performance of her duties'?

rows.body_md: Walk me through how you tested the verb in the original sentence.

rows.body_md: This is a verb-form question — say the verb's three principal parts to yourself before trusting your ear.

rows.body_md: Say more about why you changed more than one thing in the span.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The sentence describes what happens to every donation as a routine — does a past-tense verb fit that routine, and does a plural pronoun fit the subject *Every one*?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This version keeps the plural pronoun and adds a tense shift; the antecedent is singular and the routine is present-time, so both parts of this version fail — re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide on the time frame for this clause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Once the pronoun's number is fixed, do a tense sweep: every verb should match the sentence's habitual present.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The sentence says each item *is tested* as an ongoing practice — should the second clause suddenly describe the past?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The singular pronoun here is right, but the past-tense verb clashes with the sentence's present-time routine — keep the number, fix the time frame, and re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking the options, how would you describe the pattern this list sets up?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a parallelism check: name the form of the first two list items, then test the third against it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The first two habits each start with an -ing verb — does a *to*-form item match that pattern?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Every item in a series must share the form the list establishes, and this version's infinitive breaks the -ing pattern set by the first two items — re-test each option against that pattern.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job is the underlined portion doing inside the list after the colon?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Compare shapes: list items should be phrases of matching form, not a mix of phrases and clauses.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could you drop a whole subject-plus-verb statement into a list whose other items are verb phrases without a subject?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A full clause with its own subject cannot sit beside two subjectless -ing phrases in the same series; this version breaks the match, so re-examine which options preserve it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — where does the rhythm of the list stumble?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for nominalizations: turning an action into a 'the ___ of' noun phrase often disguises a parallelism break.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The other habits are expressed as direct -ing actions — does wrapping the last one in 'the ... of' keep that same shape?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Recasting the final item as a bulky noun phrase abandons the series' established -ing form and adds words without adding meaning — re-choose with the pattern in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your own words, how does the second sentence relate to the first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the connector's job: a contrast word promises the second sentence will push against the first.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does an overflowing back room push against the idea of a donation surge, or follow from it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A contrast transition requires opposition between the two sentences, and here the second sentence is a consequence of the first, not a reversal — match the connector to that relationship and re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What relationship were you expecting the connector to announce?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An example transition should introduce a specific instance of the previous claim — check whether that's what follows.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the overflowing back room one instance of households cleaning closets, or something the surge causes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'For example' promises an illustration of the prior statement, but the second sentence reports a result instead, so this connector mislabels the logic — re-choose with cause and effect in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the transition, what link would you naturally supply between the two sentences?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Time connectors only mark simultaneity — make sure the sentences aren't tied by something stronger.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Are these two disconnected events that merely share a month, or does the first one make the second happen?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Meanwhile' treats the sentences as parallel events with no logical tie, yet the overflow happens because of the surge — pick the connector that names that causal link.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide what the word 'Therefore' is claiming here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Cause-effect connectors make a promise: the second sentence must be produced by the first. Verify that promise.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does denim selling quickly cause board games to sit unsold, or are these simply two opposite outcomes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Therefore' asserts that the first sentence logically produces the second, but nothing about fast denim sales makes games linger — the sentences pull in opposite directions, so choose the connector built for that.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about what the two sentences have in common.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A similarity connector needs both sentences moving the same direction — check each sentence's direction before trusting it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: One item flies off the rack while the other gathers dust — is that a matching pair of outcomes?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Likewise' promises the second sentence mirrors the first, yet these outcomes are opposites; a connector signaling difference, not sameness, is required — re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try restating the first sentence — does the second sentence say the same thing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Restatement connectors mean 'same idea, new wording.' Test whether any new information appears.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The second sentence brings up a different product with the opposite sales pattern — can that count as rephrasing the first?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'In other words' fits only when the second sentence repeats the first idea in fresh wording, but here it introduces an opposing fact about different merchandise — pick the connector that marks that opposition.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is the paragraph mainly tracking from its first sentence to its last?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A closing line should stay with the paragraph's subject — check which noun this option actually follows.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: After the opening sentence, does the paragraph ever return to the mill's equipment, or does it stay with the shop and its neighbors?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A conclusion must land on the paragraph's central subject, and this option wanders off to machinery the paragraph never revisits — re-read the final sentences and choose the option that stays with them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking the options, how wide is this paragraph's lens — one community or the whole country?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch scope: a conclusion that suddenly widens to a national trend often abandons the paragraph's actual claim.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do the details about the repair café and lingering neighbors support a statement about nationwide habits?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This option zooms out to a countrywide trend the paragraph never discusses; a conclusion must match the paragraph's local, specific scope — re-choose with that scope in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which parts of the paragraph would you expect a final sentence to echo?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Distinguish 'on the same subject' from 'making the same point' — a conclusion needs the second.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The paragraph dwells on repair lessons and neighbors lingering — does a note about furniture prices capture why those moments matter?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This option adds a stray sales fact instead of drawing together the paragraph's images of people connecting at the shop — pick the option that pulls those threads into one closing idea.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up Sentence 3, what setup would a reader need before meeting the word 'Disagreements'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a first-mention check: a paragraph's opening line can't lean on people or conflicts that haven't been introduced.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the paragraph began with disputes being settled, would a reader know who is disagreeing or about what?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An opening sentence must stand on its own, and this placement makes the paragraph start with a conflict whose participants haven't appeared yet — trace where the disagreements first make sense and re-place the sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What earlier information does Sentence 3 quietly depend on?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the reference chain: each sentence should follow the sentence that makes it intelligible.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Disagreements between whom? If the sentence lands before the members and their categories are described, is that question answered?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This placement puts the dispute-settling before the paragraph explains the specialists whose opinions clash, breaking the logical chain — position the sentence after its cause is established.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Take another look at Sentence 4 — what job does it do for the paragraph?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for wrap-up sentences: details appended after a paragraph's summary tend to dangle.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sentence 4 passes judgment on 'the system' as a whole — should a new working detail of that system arrive after the verdict?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Placing the sentence after the paragraph's summarizing final thought leaves a stray detail hanging past the conclusion — the detail belongs inside the description the summary evaluates, so re-place it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through the label you'd give each sentence — past or present.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A paragraph break should fall where the topic flips, not just after the first sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sentences 2 and 3 still describe lantern light and a long-ago fire — do those belong in a paragraph about the current layout?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Breaking after the opening line dumps decades of history into the layout paragraph; the split must fall where the past ends and the present begins, so re-scan for that seam.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the fire feel like the right dividing line?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Dramatic events can still be history — sort sentences by era, not by excitement.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the 1994 fire part of the shop's past, or part of what shoppers see on the floor today?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The fire and rebuilding are still chapters of the shop's history, so beginning the second paragraph there leaves historical material stranded in the layout paragraph — find the sentence where the present actually starts.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which sentences work together to describe what shoppers see on the floor?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check what the candidate opening sentence refers back to — a new paragraph shouldn't split a description from its partner.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The signs in Sentence 5 point toward the wings introduced just before — can those two sentences live in different paragraphs?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Starting the new paragraph at the final sentence severs the signs from the wings they describe and leaves the layout paragraph one sentence long — back up to where the present-day description begins.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the sentence aloud — where does the opening description hand off to the main statement?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This is an introductory-phrase check: find where the modifier ends and the subject begins.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Without any punctuation, can a reader tell whether 'groups' or 'the shop' is what the sentence is about?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A modifier that opens a sentence must be closed off with a comma before the subject arrives; leaving the seam unmarked lets the phrase crash into the subject — re-choose with that boundary marked.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job is each comma doing in the version you picked?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count your commas and name each one's purpose — an unneeded pair can carve out words the sentence can't spare.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The second comma fences 'the shop' off as an aside — if you lift out that aside, what is left to do the funding?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Commas in pairs mark removable material, but removing what this pair encloses leaves the sentence without its subject — keep the comma that closes the opening phrase and drop the one that isn't doing a job.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking the options, where would you naturally pause when reading this sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two comma rules collide here — one about openers, one about subjects and verbs. Test the option against both.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does this version mark the end of the opening phrase, and does it keep the path from subject to verb clear of stray commas?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This version pauses in exactly the wrong spot: it leaves the introductory phrase unclosed and then splits the subject from its verb with a lone comma — apply both rules and re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Say more about what sits on each side of that comma.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the stand-alone test on both halves before deciding how heavy the punctuation should be.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If both halves could each end with a period, is a bare comma strong enough to hold them together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences — that's a splice — so this version needs either a stronger mark or a joining word; re-test the options against that rule.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would change if you read only the words after the punctuation mark?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A semicolon has a strict contract: check what qualifies to sit on each side of it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'most arriving before the store unlocks' contain a finished verb that could carry its own sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A semicolon must have a complete clause on both sides, and the -ing phrase after the mark in this version can't stand alone — verify each side's independence before re-choosing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide what kind of word 'however' is?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Some connecting words are full conjunctions and some are adverbs in disguise — the punctuation they need differs.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can 'however' plus a mere comma legally weld two complete sentences, the way 'but' can?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'However' is a conjunctive adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so a comma before it still leaves a splice — and the word signals a turn the logic doesn't take; re-choose with both tests in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up everything after the punctuation mark, what would be left standing?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Colons have an entry requirement — test what comes before the mark, not what comes after.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'The shop's most contested treasures are' a sentence that could take a period on its own?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A colon may only follow a clause that is already complete, and here it cuts in directly after the verb, mid-thought — apply the cover-up test to each option and re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made a semicolon feel right at this spot?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Recall the semicolon's contract and check whether both sides of this one honor it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a list of cameras, paperbacks, and quilts amount to the complete clause a semicolon demands on its right side?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A semicolon joins two stand-alone clauses, but here it splits a verb from the items it introduces, leaving a fragment — reconsider whether any mark belongs at this seam.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What job is that comma doing between the verb and what follows?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for punctuation splitting a clause's core parts — verb and complement travel together.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would you write 'the treasures are, cameras' in any sentence — what does that pause interrupt?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: No comma may separate a verb from the words that complete it; the pause in this version breaks the clause's spine — re-read the seam and choose accordingly.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is the stated goal asking this verb phrase to accomplish?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match wording to purpose: the goal names two qualities the phrase must convey — check for both.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'are stored' let a reader picture overflowing color, or just inventory sitting in a warehouse?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The goal calls for wording that dramatizes plenty and cheer, and this flat storage verb conveys neither — re-test each option against the goal's two qualities.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking the options, what picture should the winning phrase paint?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Beware neutral verbs: stating that something is visible is not the same as showing abundance.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If a reader is told the sweaters 'can be seen,' what do they learn about how many there are or how they look?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This phrasing only confirms the sweaters are visible, adding no image of quantity or color, so it fails the writer's stated aim — pick the wording that shows rather than reports.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your own words, what does the sweater display need to feel like to the reader?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test each verb for what it adds: some verbs only tell us an object continues to exist.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'remain' suggest joyful excess, or just that nothing has moved?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A verb that merely says the sweaters stay in position gives the reader no sense of cheerful overflow, so it cannot accomplish the goal — re-choose with the goal's imagery in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What clues in the sentence tell you who is speaking and in what setting?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do a register check: hold the underlined words up against the formality of 'written appraisal.'

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would an auction house's official document describe an instrument as 'super cool'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The wording must match the document's professional register, and this casual slang breaks it — re-read each option in the voice of a formal report and re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How would you describe the level of formality this sentence sets up?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Energy and appropriateness are different tests — screen each option for slang before judging its enthusiasm.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'insanely great score' sound like language from an official appraisal or from a text to a friend?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This phrasing is even more conversational than the original, piling an informal intensifier onto slang, so it deepens the register clash — choose the wording a professional document would use.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Try restating the sentence in the voice of the person who wrote the appraisal.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check each noun and modifier for words you'd hear in casual speech but not in professional writing.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would the word 'pickup' for a valuable violin appear in a formal valuation?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Seriously awesome pickup' belongs to casual conversation, not a professional document, so it fails the tone the sentence establishes — re-choose with register in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is this paragraph mainly built to explain?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the addition against the paragraph's job, not against whether it's pleasant to know.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would knowing about the manager's weekend hikes help a reader understand how the shop sets its prices?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A sentence earns its spot only by advancing the paragraph's main idea, and humanizing the manager does nothing for an explanation of how prices are calculated — re-weigh the verdict and its reason.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Take another look at the proposed sentence — what does it actually claim?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A justification must match the sentence's real content; check whether the reason invents information.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where in a sentence about hiking is there anything about weekend closing hours?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This reason attributes an explanation the proposed sentence never gives — hobbies don't account for store hours — so even the approval it supports is built on nothing; re-examine what the sentence truly adds.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide the sentence clashes with the paragraph?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Separate two different flaws: conflicting with earlier statements versus simply wandering off the topic.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does anything about a hiking hobby actually deny or reverse what the paragraph says about the manager?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The verdict here may feel right, but the stated reason fails — no earlier statement is disputed by the new sentence; the real problem is drift from the paragraph's subject, so choose the reason that names it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the final sentence actually tell us about Dara?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match the reason to the sentence's content — a keep vote needs an accurate account of what the sentence contributes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the sentence describe how volunteers are found, or what one volunteer went on to do?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This reason misdescribes the sentence, which traces one volunteer's outcome rather than any recruiting process — a justification must fit the evidence, so re-match verdicts to reasons.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which earlier sentence, if any, already covers what the final one says?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run a redundancy check: repetition means the same information, not the same topic.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do the earlier sentences mention Dara, the bank, or any specific person's outcome?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Nothing earlier states this information — the final sentence adds a new, specific case rather than repeating one — so a deletion built on redundancy fails; reconsider what the sentence contributes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through how the final sentence relates to the paragraph's opening claim.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Distinguish a topic shift from a topic payoff — specifics often look like departures because they zoom in.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the paragraph claims volunteering builds job skills, what does a volunteer landing a bookkeeping job do for that claim?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Far from wandering, the sentence delivers the proof the paragraph's claim needs; deleting it would leave the generalization unsupported — re-evaluate which verdict-and-reason pair reflects that.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What question is this paragraph trying to answer for the reader?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Relevance means feeding the paragraph's specific claim, not just mentioning the same shop.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the year the shop opened explain anything about why its prices can undercut chains?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The founding date is background that does no work in a cost explanation; the winning fact must help account for deep markdowns — re-test each option against that job.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking the options, restate the claim the underlined portion must support.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for decorative details: colorful facts can be true and still do nothing for the argument.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How would a repainted sign lower what customers pay at the register?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: An artist's sign says nothing about costs or prices, so it cannot support the paragraph's explanation — choose the fact that plugs into the cost logic.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made this option feel connected to the paragraph?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Same topic isn't same point — check whether the fact explains the claim or merely mentions a related subject.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the timing of donation waves explain why the shop can charge less, or just describe supply rhythms?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This fact shares the subject of donations but explains schedule, not cost, so it leaves the paragraph's price claim unsupported — pick the option that accounts for cheapness itself.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the first part aloud, up to the period — does it feel finished?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check for a subordinating opener: certain first words promise a second half is coming.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: After 'Because the loading dock floods every spring,' what has the reader been promised that never arrives before the period?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A clause that begins with 'Because' is dependent and cannot end at a period by itself; the original leaves that promise unfulfilled — re-join the halves and re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What test do you run before allowing a semicolon?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Semicolons are for two stand-alone statements — audit each side of this one.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can 'Because the loading dock floods every spring' stand as its own complete sentence to the left of a semicolon?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A semicolon requires independence on both sides, and the 'Because' clause fails that test, so this version misuses the mark — a lighter connection is required; re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How many joining words does this version use to connect the two ideas?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Count the conjunctions: one connection needs exactly one connector.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If 'Because' already links the flooding to the staff's response, what work is left for 'so' to do?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Pairing 'Because' with 'so' puts two conjunctions on a single joint, which English doesn't allow — keep one causal signal only, then re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which words on each side of the comma could serve as a subject and main verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do the two-period test: try replacing the comma with a period and see if both halves survive.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If both halves pass the period test, what does that tell you about a lone comma's strength here?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Two complete clauses cannot be held together by a comma alone; the original commits that splice — apply the legal joining patterns and re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What changed, grammatically, when the comma disappeared?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Removing punctuation is also a punctuation decision — test what now sits between the clauses.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With no mark at all, where does the first statement end and the second begin for a reader?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Deleting the comma swaps a splice for a fused sentence, leaving the clauses with no boundary whatsoever — the joint needs to get stronger, not vanish; re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What kind of word is 'however,' and what punctuation does it demand?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sort connectors into true conjunctions versus adverbs before trusting a comma.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Even if 'however' were punctuated correctly, does the second clause actually reverse the first, or explain it?

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: That stronger mark and a coordinating conjunction are alternative connectors, not partners; stacking both over-joins the clauses — pick the version that uses exactly one legal connector.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Could 'A smart taper includes' stand alone as a finished thought?

rows.body_md: Say more about what job that mark usually does in a sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Recall the mark's legal uses — joining full clauses, or separating supersized list items — and test whether either applies here.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'fewer miles, extra sleep, and familiar meals' a second complete clause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, or commas already inside list items; neither condition holds, so it illegally severs the verb from its list — reconsider how the verb should meet its objects.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What exactly is this comma separating?

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: No mark belongs between a verb and the list it governs; the comma interrupts that direct link for no grammatical reason — re-choose with the verb-object connection in mind.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What picture does the verb in this version put in your head?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Hold the sentence against the writer's stated aim and ask how much force the verb carries.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'went' show strain and speed, or just movement in a direction?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A colorless verb of motion records the trip without conveying effort; the stated goal demands a verb with power behind it — re-read the options for the one whose energy matches the pumping arms.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you weigh the goal in the question against this verb?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the verb for energy: does it suggest pushing harder, or merely keeping on?

rows.body_md: Would a reader feel the hill in the word 'continued'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Continued' emphasizes persistence, not intensity; it tells us the interval went on but not that Jonah attacked it — re-choose the verb that dramatizes the effort.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up the rest of the sentence, what tone would this verb set?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Match register and force: the surrounding details are vivid, so check whether the verb keeps up with them.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does 'traveled' sound like an all-out effort or like an itinerary?

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How would you describe the sentence's overall register?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the option inside the full sentence and listen for a register clash.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do 'kept tabs' and 'pretty much' match phrases like 'hesitant jog' and 'preparation'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Casual idioms drop the sentence into conversational register while everything around it stays measured and reflective; consistency requires matching the passage's level — reconsider which phrasing blends in.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made this metaphor feel at home in the sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check both slang and hedges: little words like 'basically' carry a register of their own.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does calling a training log 'a receipt' fit the sentence's earnest, reflective mood?

rows.subject: act-english

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which words in this version stand out from the rest of the sentence?

rows.body_md: Compare formality piece by piece: the verb and the noun each pull the sentence somewhere new.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'the whole saga' the way the rest of this sentence talks about her preparation?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Jotted down' sounds offhand and 'whole saga' exaggerates playfully, both breaking the sentence's steady, earnest register — re-choose the option whose tone stays level.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Walk me through how tax paperwork connects to a Saturday long run.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test the sentence against the paragraph's stated job, not against whether the fact is true or flattering.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Even if the fact makes the club look organized, does it develop the morning-run scene?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A true and even admirable fact still fails if it belongs to a different topic; the paragraph is about the runs, and finances sit outside that frame — reconsider whether adding it serves the stated goal.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where does the paragraph talk about leadership or trust?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A justification must match something actually on the page; scan the paragraph for the idea this reason claims to support.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the paragraph ever raise the question of trusting the club's officers?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: This reason invents a purpose the paragraph never pursues; the passage is a portrait of the weekly run, so a sentence about spring paperwork serves no goal stated or implied — re-judge the addition against what the paragraph actually does.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which earlier sentence did you think already covered this information?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: For a repetition claim, point to the first occurrence — can you actually find one?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is tax paperwork mentioned anywhere else in the paragraph?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The right verdict can rest on the wrong reason: nothing here repeats, because the paperwork detail never appears elsewhere; the real problem is relevance, not redundancy — re-check the reason attached to each verdict.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made the Keiko sentence feel like a bridge?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A transition claim means the sentence sets up what follows; test whether the closing warning depends on it.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Would the coaches' caution still follow smoothly from the first sentence alone?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: The closing caution connects directly to the opening practice, so this sentence is not needed as a bridge; it is doing a different job for the opening claim — re-examine what it actually contributes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Where exactly do the Keiko sentence and the coaches' warning clash?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Contradiction requires incompatible claims; line the two statements up side by side.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a runner both wear a long-sleeve shirt at midday and keep her sessions short with careful rehydration?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A case of a practice does not contradict advice about doing that practice safely; the two statements coexist, so this deletion rests on a false conflict — reconsider both the verdict and its reason.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Tell me what new information, if any, the second sentence adds.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Repetition means the same content appears twice; compare the general claim with the Keiko details point by point.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does the opening sentence already mention August, midday miles, or the long-sleeve shirt?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Moving from a general claim to one runner's particulars adds support rather than repeating; cutting it would leave the opening assertion bare, defeating the writer's stated goal — re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is the paragraph's subject, in one phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Sort the choices by topic before judging them; equipment and nutrition are different threads.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Do carbon-plated shoes deliver any carbohydrate?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Shoe technology, however helpful late in a race, belongs to a gear discussion; the paragraph develops in-race nutrition, so this sentence changes the subject — re-check which detail feeds the actual topic.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: When does the action in this sentence happen relative to the race?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check the time window the paragraph cares about: before, during, or after the event.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a celebration meal the night after the finish affect fueling during the miles themselves?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Post-race dining falls outside the paragraph's window, which concerns intake while the race is under way; a detail after the finish line cannot develop that point — reconsider the timing of each choice.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you weigh this choice's timing against the paragraph's focus?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the paragraph's first sentence again and mark its key phrase about when fueling matters.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is loading up on carbohydrates in the days beforehand the same practice as taking in fuel once the race has begun?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Eating extra in the days before is preparation, not mid-race intake; the paragraph explicitly concerns fueling after the start, so this near-miss detail addresses the wrong phase — re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Read the first 'sentence' aloud on its own — does it finish a thought?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Any statement starting with 'Because' owes the reader a payoff clause; check whether the period cuts that payoff off.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If someone said 'Because the course climbs steeply at mile sixteen' and then stopped, what would you ask them?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A subordinate 'Because' clause cannot stand alone; the period turns it into a fragment and orphans the very clause that completes it — re-join the two parts with the mark that attaches an opener to its main clause.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does each side of that stronger mark need in order to qualify for it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the stand-alone test on the left side of the mark before anything else.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is 'Because the course climbs steeply at mile sixteen' a complete sentence by itself?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A semicolon demands independence on both sides, and the 'Because' clause fails that test; the opener needs to lean on the main clause, not be walled off from it — reconsider the lighter connection.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What two things is 'and' trying to link in this version?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Coordinating words join equals; check whether both pieces carry equal rank.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is the 'Because' clause an equal partner to the main clause, or a dependent setup for it?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'And' coordinates two like units, but a subordinate clause already hangs on the main clause by itself; adding a coordinator garbles the hierarchy — re-choose the simple attachment an introductory clause takes.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Which part of this sentence did you treat as the main clause?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Split the sentence at the comma and test each half for independence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can a comma alone carry two complete statements?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Both halves are full clauses, so a bare comma splices them; the join needs a real connector or a stronger mark, and the two ideas also pull in opposite directions — re-check the connectors on offer.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What kind of word is 'consequently,' and what punctuation does it demand?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Adverbs that connect ideas are not conjunctions; check what must accompany them between two clauses.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Even with 'consequently' added, what is still the only thing holding the two clauses together?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A conjunctive adverb after a comma leaves the splice intact — that word needs a semicolon before it — and it also claims a cause-effect link the sentence never makes; re-examine both the grammar and the logic.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If you covered up everything after the name, what would remain of the sentence?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Find the boundary between the two complete thoughts and ask how it is marked in this version.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With no punctuation or joining word at all, how does a reader know where the first clause ends?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Deleting the comma creates a fused sentence, a step worse than a splice; two independent clauses require a genuine connector, ideally one signaling the sentence's turn from dread to reassurance — re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Before checking anything else, count the complete clauses in this sentence.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Find where 'Rain began just after the halfway mark' ends, and test what separates it from what follows.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: With nothing between 'mark' and 'the crowds,' how would a reader know a new statement has begun?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Running two independent clauses together with no mark fuses them; each complete statement needs a real boundary, especially with a third clause already chained on by 'but' — re-check the separators.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What would this comma be responsible for joining?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Test both sides of the comma for independence, then recall what a lone comma may legally join.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Since 'but' already links the last two clauses, can a bare comma also carry the first join?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A comma alone between independent clauses is a splice, and stacking it before the existing ', but' chain makes the boundaries even murkier; the first clause needs clause-strength separation — reconsider.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does 'because' claim about the rain and the crowds?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Check two things at once: the mark's requirements and the logic the joining word asserts.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Does a semicolon still work when the clause after it has been demoted by a subordinating word?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but 'because' makes that clause dependent — and the sentence never argues that causal point; both the grammar and the logic misfire, so re-choose.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Who, in this sentence, skipped the long runs?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Find the opening phrase's implied actor, then check the first noun after the comma.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Did the marathon's final miles skip anything?

rows.body_md: An opening participial phrase attaches to the nearest following subject, and here that subject is the miles, not the runner; the sentence must be rebuilt so the skipper sits where the modifier can reach him — re-inspect each version's first noun after the comma.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In this version, what noun follows the comma?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Run the attachment test on the revision too: modifier, comma, then who?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can 'the punishment' be the one who skipped training runs?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Swapping in a new abstract noun does not fix the dangle — a punishment cannot have skipped workouts any more than the miles could; test each version by asking whether its post-comma noun is the true doer.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the interrupting phrase sit next to in this version?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Modifiers describe what they touch; identify the noun this one now hugs.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Placed between the miles and the verb, whose action does the skipping become?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Relocating the phrase mid-sentence parks it beside the miles again, so the wrong noun still owns the skipped runs; the modifier must neighbor the person it describes — re-evaluate where each version puts him.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What does the verb in this span mean all by itself?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Circle each word after the verb and ask what new information it adds.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Can two courses merge apart, or merge into more than one route?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: How did you decide which extra words to cut and which to keep?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Is it possible to merge in any way other than 'together'?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: 'Together' is baked into the meaning of the verb, so keeping it preserves a redundancy even after the larger cut; re-test each remaining word against the verb's built-in meaning.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What is the difference between the two verbs this version uses?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Watch for synonym stacking: paired verbs often duplicate rather than add.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: If the courses combine, what does the second verb contribute that is new?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Joining two synonymous verbs and re-adding the one-route idea triples the same point; revision should remove repetition, not multiply it — reconsider which version says it once.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: In your own words, what does 'the fact that' add to this sentence?

rows.body_md: Try compressing the underlined phrase and re-reading: is any meaning lost?

rows.body_md: What is the logical job of this whole five-word phrase?

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: Constructions built on 'the fact that' are filler around a simple causal link; the same logic survives with the padding gone, so the original fails the concision test — re-weigh each option for wasted words.

rows.subject: act-english
rows.body_md: What made this version feel more formal or precise?

rows.body_md: Swapping one padded phrase for another is worth checking: count what each word contributes.

rows.body_md: Does this phrasing differ in meaning from the original wording at all?
